items.title: [Bug]: chatgpt/ device-code auth is synchronous and blocks the proxy event loop for up to 900s, killing the worker
items.body:
- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. Searched `is:issue "device code"` — 9 results, none reports this. #27175, #24562 and #17065 are different faults. ### What happened? A single request for a `chatgpt/*` model froze both of our proxy replicas for ~6.5 minutes each, until Kubernetes killed them. The proxy stopped answering every request, including `/health/liveliness`, and emitted no log output at all for the duration. The cause is that ChatGPT's device-code login is synchronous, and it is reached from an `async def` request handler: ``` async def async_response_api_handler() llms/custom_httpx/llm_http_handler.py:2730 → provider_config.validate_environment() llm_http_handler.py:2764 ← plain def, runs inline on the loop → ChatGPTResponsesConfig.validate_environment() llms/chatgpt/responses/transformation.py:41 → Authenticator.get_access_token() llms/chatgpt/authenticator.py:43 → _login_device_code() authenticator.py:143 → print(device code to stdout) authenticator.py:152 → _poll_for_authorization_code() authenticator.py:199 _get_httpx_client() :200 ← sync client while time.time() - start < DEVICE_CODE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS: :203 time.sleep(...) :224, :230, :241 ``` The budget is set by the constants at `authenticator.py:25-28`: | Constant | Value | | --- | --- | | `DEVICE_CODE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `15 * 60` — 900 s | | `DEVICE_CODE_POLL_SLEEP_SECONDS` | `5` | | `DEVICE_CODE_COOLDOWN_SECONDS` | `5 * 60` | So one request can hold the event loop for up to 900 seconds. `_wait_for_access_token()` (`:362`, `while` at `:364`, `time.sleep` at `:373`) does the same for a second request arriving inside the cooldown. ```mermaid flowchart TD R["POST /v1/responses, model chatgpt/*"] --> H["async def async_response_api_handler()"] H --> V["validate_environment() — sync, no await point"] V --> P["device-code poll loop
time.sleep, up to 900 s"] P -.->|"event loop never yields"| S["starved on the same thread"] S --> S1["/health/liveliness and /health/readiness
never dispatched → orchestrator kills the worker"] S2["every other in-flight request"] --- S S3["uvicorn's own access log → total silence"] --- S ``` Three things turn this from slow into fatal on a proxy: 1. `validate_environment` is part of the sync provider-config interface. Every other provider returns headers in microseconds; this one waits on a human. Network I/O with sleeps does not belong behind a synchronous interface method. 2. It blocks during header construction, *before* any call to the model — so the model name after the prefix is irrelevant, and every `chatgpt/*` model is affected. 3. With `NUM_WORKERS=1` there is no sibling worker to answer the health probe, so the container fails its liveness check and is killed. Our probe error was `Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers` — the TCP connection was accepted, but no HTTP response ever came. This is not a one-time setup problem. The token file lives at `~/.config/litellm/chatgpt/auth.json` inside the container, so it is lost on every restart, and `_is_token_expired` re-arms the flow whenever the token expires. `llms/github_copilot/authenticator.py` has the same shape — sync `_get_httpx_client()`, `time.sleep(5)` at `:325`, `print(` at `:349` — so a fix should probably cover both. **What I expected instead:** a request that cannot authenticate returns an error promptly. A server should never print an interactive prompt to stdout, and should never block its event loop waiting for one to be answered. Either refuse the device flow when no TTY/interactive session exists and return a clear "ChatGPT auth not configured, run the login flow first" error, or run it in a thread with a short timeout so the loop keeps serving. ### User Flow **Before a (hypothetical) fix** — one user's request takes the proxy offline for everyone until the container is restarted. 1. User A sends `POST https:///v1/responses` with `{"model": "chatgpt/gpt-5.6-terra", "input": "hi"}` and a valid virtual key. 2. The request never returns. User A's client hangs with no status code and no error. 3. User B sends `POST https:///v1/messages` with a Claude model that has always worked. It returns `503 Service Unavailable` from the load balancer in front of the proxy. 4. User B sends `GET https:///health/liveliness`. The connection is accepted but no response headers ever arrive; the client times out. 5. This continues for ~6.5 minutes across ~300 requests from other users, all `503`. 6. The container is killed and restarted. Requests then succeed again, and User A's original request is gone with no response. 7. Any user holding a valid key can repeat step 1 at will and take the proxy down for every other user. **After a (hypothetical) fix** — the same request fails on its own and nobody else notices. 1. User A sends `POST https:///v1/responses` with `{"model": "chatgpt/gpt-5.6-terra", "input": "hi"}` and a valid virtual key. 2. The request returns promptly with an error explaining that ChatGPT authentication has not been completed for this deployment. 3. User B sends `POST https:///v1/messages` with the same Claude model. It returns `200 OK`. 4. User B sends `GET https:///health/liveliness`. It returns `200 OK`. 5. No other request is affected, and nothing is logged as an outage. 6. The container is not restarted. 7. A user holding a valid key can no longer affect any other user's requests. ### Proof the bug occurs **Setup.** Proxy on Kubernetes, one replica set of 2 pods, `NUM_WORKERS=1`, `litellm-gateway:v1.99.0`. Relevant config (models unrelated to the trigger removed, credentials redacted): ```yaml general_settings: store_model_in_db: true master_key: litellm_settings: callbacks: [...] model_list: - model_name: gpt-5.6-terra litellm_params: model: bedrock/openai.gpt-5.6-terra aws_region_name: us-east-1 model_info: mode: responses use_openai_responses_path: true ``` Liveness probe: `/health/liveliness`, `periodSeconds: 15`, `timeoutSeconds: 10`, `failureThreshold: 6`. Readiness probe: `/health/readiness`, `periodSeconds: 10`, `timeoutSeconds: 10`, `failureThreshold: 3`. No `chatgpt/*` model was in `model_list`. This was not a synthetic test — it is a production incident, and I have not re-run it deliberately because doing so takes the gateway offline. **Step 1-2 — the request that hangs.** A developer ran `codex --model chatgpt/gpt-5.6-terra` against the proxy. Both pods printed this to stdout within 533 ms of each other, with a different code each, and then went completely silent. Note there is no access-log line for the triggering request, because uvicorn logs only on completion: ``` 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z Sign in with ChatGPT using device code: 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z 1) Visit https://auth.openai.com/codex/device 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z 2) Enter code: XXXX-XXXXX 2026-09-02T15:23:37.192Z Device codes are a common phishing target. Never share this code. ``` Log output per pod, showing the gap — normal traffic right up to the prompt, then nothing until the replacement process boots: ``` pod A: 513 events 15:20:03 → 15:32:58, largest gap 403.8 s (15:23:37 → 15:30:20) pod B: 378 events 15:20:00 → 15:32:59, largest gap 410.9 s (15:23:37 → 15:30:28) ``` **Step 3 — other users get 503.** Load-balancer metrics per minute. `ELB_5XX` is generated by the load balancer itself; `Target_5XX` is what the proxy returned: ``` minute ELB_5XX ELB_503 Target_5XX TargetConnectionError 15:24 30 30 - - 15:25 22 22 - - 15:26 63 63 - - 15:27 45 45 - - 15:28 41 40 - - 15:29 65 65 - - 15:30 36 36 - - ``` `Target_5XX` and `TargetConnectionError` are empty for the whole window: the proxy returned nothing, so all ~301 errors were synthesised by the load balancer once both targets had dropped out of rotation. **Step 4 — health endpoints stop answering.** From the orchestrator, for both pods: ``` Liveness probe failed: Get "http://:4000/health/liveliness": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers) Readiness probe failed: Get "http://:4000/health/readiness": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers) ``` The connection was accepted and no headers came, i.e. the process was alive with a stalled loop. For contrast, a pod that was genuinely shutting down later reported `connect: connection refused`. **Step 6 — the container is killed.** Container state after the event, both pods: ``` reason=Error exit=137 (SIGKILL from the failed liveness probe, not OOMKilled) pod A: died 15:30:08, restarted 15:30:08, back up 15:30:20 pod B: died 15:30:15, restarted 15:30:15, back up 15:30:28 ``` The kill arrived at ~400 s, i.e. it interrupted the 900 s poll budget less than half way through. **Line references** were verified against the `litellm==1.99.0` wheel from PyPI, not the `main` branch. ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? Proxy ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.99.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details No response

gold.rationale: A synchronous, blocking device-code auth flow (with time.sleep loops up to 900s) is reachable from an async request handler with no await point. This blocks the entire event loop, starving health checks and all other in-flight requests on the same worker, leading to orchestrator-triggered container kills. This is a severe availability bug affecting all users of the proxy (not just chatgpt/* requests), with no workaround for a single-worker deployment, and it is triggerable by any valid key holder — effectively a DoS vector against the shared proxy. It behaves entirely differently from expected behavior (a request that cannot authenticate should fail fast), so this is a bug, not a feature or docs issue. Same defect pattern exists in github_copilot's authenticator, meaning multiple providers are affected via the shared request-handling path. Given it can take down the whole proxy for all users with no workaround, and is trivially repeatable by any user, this meets the bar for P0 (broken for most users on affected paths, no workaround, easily triggered denial of service). This requires maintainer judgement to decide the right architectural fix (thread offloading vs. refusing device flow when non-interactive) and to assess blast radius across two providers, so needs_human is true.

items.title: [Bug]: 41 of 85 openrouter/* entries disagree with openrouter.ai's own API on price (20 of them cite the page that contradicts them)
items.body:
### What happened?

41 of the 85 comparable `openrouter/*` entries in `model_prices_and_context_window.json` disagree with OpenRouter's own published price on at least one cost field — in both directions, from -89% to +3025%. **20 of the 41 carry a `source` field pointing at the exact OpenRouter model page that contradicts them.**

Anything that computes spend from `openrouter/*` entries — `completion_cost()`, the proxy's cost tracking, budgets and alerts — is off by these factors.

Verified 2026-09-03 against `GET https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models`, which is the same source `.github/scripts/auto_update_price_and_context_window_file.py` names, and spot-corroborated against the public model pages:

| model | registry | openrouter.ai API | public page |
|---|---|---|---|
| `openrouter/qwen/qwen3.5-plus-02-15` | $0.40 / $2.40 | $0.26 / $1.56 | "$0.26 / $1.56 per 1M" |
| `openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-120b` | $0.18 / $0.80 | $0.037 / $0.17 | "$0.03 / $0.17 per 1M" |

That OpenRouter's listed price is the intended value is confirmed by your own curated entries: `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5` has `source: https://openrouter.ai/anthropic/claude-opus-5` and matches that page exactly on all four cost fields.

### The drift is concentrated, not uniform

Correct today: **anthropic 11/11, google 6/6, openai 18/21**. Wrong today: **qwen 1/12, deepseek 1/9, z-ai 0/5, xiaomi 0/2, mistralai 4/9**. The frontier-lab families get audited; the open-weight long tail does not.

And these are not 41 independent typos. Several are one upstream repricing each — entries whose input *and* output are wrong by the identical factor:

- **×1.5385 (+53.8%) on both fields, n=4:** `qwen/qwen3-coder-plus`, `qwen/qwen3.5-27b`, `qwen/qwen3.5-flash-02-23`, `qwen/qwen3.5-plus-02-15` — consistent with a single ~35% Qwen price cut upstream that was never picked up.

### Why CI does not catch this

`.github/workflows/test-model-map.yml` runs exactly two things: `jq empty` (is it JSON) and `ci_cd/generate_model_prices_schema.py --check` (is the schema in sync).

The second one **generates the schema from the data file it is validating** — `build_schema(prices)` takes `all_keys` from the union of keys present, and takes the `mode` enum from `{entry["mode"] for entry in entries.values()}`. A schema derived from the data cannot reject that data's content. It can only reject a key name `classify()` can't place — and `classify()` sends anything containing `"cost"` to a non-negative number and anything starting with `"supports_"` to a boolean, so most novel names land softly too.

That is a useful thing to have (it keeps types and docs honest) but it is not a check on whether a number is *true*, and nothing else in CI is either. A cost value only has to be a non-negative float.

### Please don't fix this by switching on the existing auto-updater

`.github/workflows/auto_update_price_and_context_window.yml` is scheduled weekly, but no PR with its hard-coded title (`Update model_prices_and_context_window.json file`) has ever been opened, and the file's history is entirely hand-written commits — so it appears dormant. Three things in it would need fixing first; I'm flagging them as latent, not as live damage:

1. **`"max_tokens": row["context_length"]` writes the wrong field.** Your schema documents `max_tokens` as *"max output tokens if the provider specifies it, else max input tokens"*, and the curated entries use it that way — `openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-5` has `max_tokens: 128000` against a 1,000,000 context. Because `sync_local_data_with_remote()` does `local_data[key].update(remote_data[key])`, a run would overwrite the curated max-output value with the context window on every entry that has both.
2. **The `supports_vision` test is dead.** It fires on `architecture.modality == 'multimodal'`, and **0 of the 424** models in today's API use that value — the field is now `text+image->text` and 14 other compound forms. 256 live models accept image input. In the registry this shows up as 7 entries that are vision-capable upstream with no `supports_vision` (`openrouter/openai/gpt-5`, `-mini`, `-nano`, `openrouter/openai/gpt-5.2-codex`, `openrouter/mistralai/mistral-small-3.1-24b-instruct`, `-3.2-`, `openrouter/bytedance/ui-tars-1.5-7b`) and 3 that still carry `supports_vision: true` although upstream is now `text->text` (`openrouter/minimax/minimax-m2.1`, `openrouter/z-ai/glm-4.7`, `openrouter/z-ai/glm-4.7-flash`). None of the 7 are rescued by `fallback_generalizations` — all 7 rules are Claude/Bedrock-specific. `.update()` merges, so it can add or overwrite a field but never remove one; a flag that goes stale stays.
3. **It would fail your own schema check.** `openrouter/auto` and `openrouter/bodybuilder` return `"prompt": "-1"` as a sentinel; the importer does `float(...)` on it, and the generated schema gives every `*cost*` field `minimum: 0`.

### What I did not check

- Only the `openrouter/*` namespace. I did not look at any other provider.
- OpenRouter prices change whenever they like; this is a 2026-09-03 snapshot, and small deltas (the four entries under 10%) may just be recent moves rather than neglect.
- I excluded `openrouter/auto` and `openrouter/bodybuilder` from the 85 — the registry's `0` is arguably more sensible than the API's `-1`, and I'm not calling those defects.
- 60 live models now carry `pricing.overrides` (time-of-day and day-of-week rates) which this registry has no field for. I compared only the headline rate and am **not** counting those as errors — noting it only because it means a straight import wouldn't be complete either.
- I have not traced runtime resolution end to end, so what I am reporting is that the file disagrees with the source it names, not a measured billing delta in a running proxy.

Related but distinct: #33068 (openrouter Claude entries *missing*; still missing as of today — `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-5`, `claude-opus-4.8` and `claude-fable-5` are live upstream and absent here). This issue is about entries that exist and are wrong.

### Reproduce

```bash
curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models -o or.json
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
reg={k:v for k,v in json.load(open('model_prices_and_context_window.json')).items()
     if isinstance(v,dict) and v.get('litellm_provider')=='openrouter'}
live={f"openrouter/{r['id']}": r for r in json.load(open('or.json'))['data']}
for k in sorted(set(reg)&set(live)):
    e,pr=reg[k],live[k]['pricing']
    for rf,lf in [('input_cost_per_token','prompt'),('output_cost_per_token','completion'),
                  ('cache_read_input_token_cost','input_cache_read')]:
        if rf in e and lf in pr and abs(e[rf]-float(pr[lf])) > 1e-9*max(e[rf],float(pr[lf])):
            print(f"{k:55s} {rf:30s} registry={e[rf]:<12g} live={float(pr[lf])}")
PY
```

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented, evidenced bug report: pricing data in model_prices_and_context_window.json for many openrouter/* entries disagrees with OpenRouter's own published API/page prices, causing incorrect cost accounting for completion_cost(), proxy spend tracking, and budgets/alerts. This is "incorrect cost accounting" which per the rules is explicitly a bug category ("Provider X returns the wrong price" is a bug). It affects a widely-used shared path (cost calculation) across many providers/models (41 of 85 entries, spanning multiple provider families), which triggers the "many providers or shared core path affected → raise one level" modifier. Impact is broad (any spend tracking relying on openrouter pricing) though a workaround (manually overriding prices) exists, which would normally lower urgency by one level, but the widespread nature affecting core cost path pushes it to at least P1. Given the scale (41 entries wrong, affecting real billing/budget decisions) and no automated test catching this, it warrants prompt attention — P1. This requires a maintainer to verify the extensive claims and decide on a scoped fix/update process, so needs_human is true (per rules, "claims needing reproduction to confirm" and it's P1).

items.title: mid-stream fallback asymmetry: chat completions may lose partial usage, Responses API preserves it
items.body:
A third finding from the 30-project conformance check, following #39057 (cache-hit accounting) and #39455 (retry log inflation).

**The observation**

The router handles mid-stream failures differently depending on the API surface (`litellm/router.py`):

- **Chat completions**: if a stream has already produced content and then receives `MidStreamFallbackError` (~L2471-2477), the original exception is re-raised — no fallback. Whether the partial stream's usage was already logged depends on whether the failure logging path carries the accumulated usage (static analysis suggests it may not).

- **Responses API**: only pre-first-chunk failures trigger fallback (~L2479-2485, L2521). When fallback does occur, `stream_chunk_builder` extracts partial usage from the failed stream and merges it into the fallback stream (`_combine_fallback_usage` ~L2382-2404).

- **`FallbackStreamWrapper`** (~L2443-2450) reuses the original `model_response.logging_obj`, so the final success logging carries combined usage in one record.

**The question**

For the chat-completions "content already produced, no fallback" path: is the partial stream's usage (tokens consumed by the provider before the mid-stream error) captured in the failure log? If not, the cost of that partial generation exists on the provider bill but is invisible in spend_logs — a measurement blind spot for mid-stream failures.

The asymmetry itself is worth documenting: the Responses API path explicitly preserves partial costs via `_combine_fallback_usage`, while the chat-completions path may not.

Context: AgentMeasure conformance check; LiteLLM has been the most responsive project in the campaign (independent enforcement case + published fixture + maintainer engagement). This is the last high-priority finding from our audit.

gold.rationale: This is a well-researched conformance finding pointing to a real code-level asymmetry: chat completions may fail to capture partial usage on mid-stream errors, while the Responses API path explicitly merges partial usage via _combine_fallback_usage. This is incorrect/missing cost accounting behavior against the expected contract that provider usage should be logged — this is a bug (wrong/incomplete cost accounting), not just a docs issue, since the code's behavior (potentially dropping usage data) diverges from what spend_logs should reflect. It's narrower in scope (only affects mid-stream failures with partial content before fallback fails), and a workaround isn't stated but this is a narrow edge case with static-analysis-level uncertainty ("static analysis suggests it may not", "is the partial stream's usage... captured... If not"). This needs confirmation/reproduction by a maintainer since the report itself is hedged with uncertainty ("depends on whether... research suggests"), and it's part of a series of related findings needing judgement on how to handle. Given the narrow blast radius (mid-stream failures specifically) and lack of confirmed impact, P2 is appropriate rather than P1. Needs human because it requires confirmation of behavior via investigation/reproduction, and is a nuanced accounting/logging correctness issue requiring maintainer judgement.

items.title: router retries: how should consumers derive logical operations from inflated log counts?
items.body:
A follow-up measurement question from the 30-project conformance check, building on the cache-hit discussion in #39057.

**The observation**

The router's retry loop (`litellm/router.py`, ~L7152, `async_function_with_retries`) calls `self.make_call(original_function, ...)` for each attempt (~L7210, L7254). Each attempt is a complete `litellm.acompletion` invocation with its own Logging object, triggering success/failure callbacks independently.

Dollar spend is handled correctly: failed attempts without usage produce failure logs without spend, so the dollar total is not double-counted. But request/log counts inflate: a logical operation that succeeded on retry 3 produces 3 log entries (2 failure + 1 success), and any analytics counting "requests" or "calls" from the logs table counts 3 where the user intended 1.

The `attempted_retries` / `max_retries` metadata written into each request (~L7180, with the comment "used for spend logs retry tracking") suggests the authors are aware of the multi-entry shape.

**The question**

Is there guidance for consumers on how to derive "logical operations" from the logs table? E.g., group by a request correlation ID and count groups rather than rows? Or would an `operation_id` or `retry_group_id` field be considered useful on spend_logs entries?

Context: AgentMeasure conformance check; the attempt/operation boundary is our core invariant. LiteLLM has been one of the most responsive projects to this campaign — the cache-hit discussion in #39057 produced an independent enforcement case and a published fixture.

gold.rationale: The issue asks whether there is existing guidance for consumers to derive logical operations from inflated log counts, and whether a new field (operation_id/retry_group_id) would be useful. This is primarily a question about existing behavior/guidance, but also floats a feature idea (new field on spend_logs). Since no concrete demand beyond this single reporter, and the core ask is "is there guidance" / "would this be useful" - it's framed as a question first, with a feature suggestion embedded. Per the category rules, question takes precedence if the author is asking how to do something without claiming misbehavior - here the observation is about a known/documented multi-entry shape (not a bug, since dollar spend is correctly handled and the retry metadata suggests intentional design), and the actual ask is "is there guidance" - a question. The feature request (operation_id field) is speculative, single-requester, no evidenced demand, so it would be P3 if categorized as feature. Since the primary framing is a question seeking clarification/guidance, category=question. This requires judgement/product-direction call about whether to add new fields, and is part of a broader conformance campaign referencing related issues, so a maintainer should look at it rather than being routed as a simple duplicate or typo.

items.title: [Bug]: /v1/messages streaming delays message_start until the model's thinking pass finishes, even with no fallbacks configured
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

Streaming `/v1/messages` requests to an adaptive-thinking Bedrock model (e.g., Claude Sonnet 5 with `thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}`) deliver `message_start` and `content_block_start` only after the model's entire thinking pass finishes, instead of immediately when Bedrock actually sends them. The identical request sent directly to Bedrock, bypassing the proxy entirely, delivers `message_start` within about two seconds every time, regardless of how long the model then thinks before producing visible content.

Depending on `output_config.effort` and `max_tokens`, a model's thinking pass can take anywhere from a few seconds to several minutes. For that entire window, a client of the proxy sees nothing but periodic SSE keepalive pings, with no way to tell a genuinely slow request apart from a hung one, even though the underlying provider already answered with its lifecycle frames in about two seconds.

This reproduces with zero fallback deployments configured for the model, so there is no fallback attempt this behavior could be protecting.

Expected: `message_start` and `content_block_start` reach the client as soon as the provider sends them, independent of how long the model then takes to produce its first real content.

## Suggested fix

`Router._aanthropic_messages_streaming_iterator` wraps every streaming `/v1/messages` response so a mid-stream provider error can retry against a fallback deployment before any lifecycle frame commits the client to the current attempt. To make that safe, it buffers `message_start`, `content_block_start`, and any `ping` behind buffered frames, only releasing them once the first `content_block_delta` arrives, since forwarding `message_start` and then falling back would produce two overlapping message lifecycles on one SSE stream

That buffering is applied unconditionally, with no check for whether the router has any fallback deployment configured to retry against in the first place. For an adaptive-thinking model, Bedrock's first `content_block_delta` does not arrive until the entire thinking pass finishes, so the buffering ends up holding `message_start`, an event that carries no content and is not itself part of what a fallback would need to redo, hostage for the full length of that pass, even when there is nothing to fall back to

The fix: gate the buffering behind whether any fallback (general, context-window, content-policy, or a catch-all default) could actually resolve for the requested model group. With no fallback destination configured, forward the source stream live, exactly as it streams without this wrapper, since there is nothing left to protect. When a fallback is configured, keep the existing buffer-until-content behavior unchanged

This router-level fix needs to land together with the existing httpx `chunk_size=1024` fix on the Bedrock invoke reader (already present at the commit this proof was captured against). Tested in isolation, the router fix alone gets `message_start` out in about two seconds, but `content_block_start` still doesn't arrive until the thinking pass finishes: httpx's byte-chunker slices the raw stream into fixed 1024-byte pieces regardless of where an event-stream frame boundary falls, so `content_block_start`'s frame can get split across that boundary and its remainder sits buffered inside httpx until more bytes happen to arrive. Both fixes together are needed for every lifecycle frame to forward live, not just the first one


### User Flow

Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer streaming a request through the proxy's `/v1/messages` endpoint sees no bytes at all for as long as the model spends thinking, even though the exact same request straight to Bedrock starts streaming in about two seconds

1. They send `POST https://<proxy-domain>/v1/messages` with `model` set to a Bedrock adaptive-thinking model (e.g. `us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5`), `"thinking": {"type": "adaptive"}`, `"output_config": {"effort": "max"}`, and `"stream": true`
2. Their client's own timing log shows no data for many seconds, with only an `event: ping` frame arriving roughly every 15 seconds
3. The first real event, `event: message_start`, does not appear until the model finishes its entire thinking pass, which for a large `max_tokens` ceiling can be a minute or more later
4. Sending the identical request body directly to Bedrock, bypassing the proxy, returns `event: message_start` within about two seconds every time, so the developer has no way to tell in advance whether their next call through the proxy will start in two seconds or two minutes

After a (hypothetical) fix: the same developer sees `event: message_start` arrive within about two seconds, matching a direct call to Bedrock, and only the model's own thinking time (not the proxy) accounts for any further wait before visible content

1. They send the same `POST https://<proxy-domain>/v1/messages` with the same body
2. `event: message_start` and `event: content_block_start` arrive within about two seconds
3. `event: ping` keepalives may still appear while the model keeps thinking, but only after the real lifecycle events already reached the client
4. The remaining wait for `event: content_block_delta` matches the model's own thinking time exactly, the same as calling Bedrock directly


### Proof the bug occurs


Config the proxy ran with (no fallbacks configured anywhere in the file):

```yaml
model_list:
- litellm_params:
    model: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
    aws_region_name: us-west-2
  model_info:
    litellm_provider: bedrock
    input_cost_per_token: 2.2e-06
    output_cost_per_token: 1.1e-05
    id: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
  model_name: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
```

Ran with `AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` set (a short-term Bedrock API key), which rules out AWS credential resolution as a factor

Version / commit: `x-litellm-version: 1.101.0`, commit `2ffe6a1dc846d5168b375110b5ab3ffb36439a93`

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

gold.rationale: This is a clear behavioral bug: streaming /v1/messages through the router unconditionally buffers lifecycle SSE frames (message_start, content_block_start, ping) even when no fallback deployments are configured, causing significant client-perceived latency that diverges from documented/expected streaming behavior and from calling the provider directly. The reporter provides a detailed reproduction, root cause analysis (buffering logic in Router._aanthropic_messages_streaming_iterator plus httpx chunk_size splitting frames), and a concrete suggested fix. This affects the shared router streaming path used by all providers/models going through /v1/messages with streaming enabled, not just Bedrock adaptive-thinking models specifically, since the buffering logic itself is unconditional in the shared core path. This qualifies as "many providers or shared core path affected," pushing urgency up. It's not a security issue, not a docs issue, and not a question—it's a functional defect with real-world impact (client can't distinguish slow model from hung proxy, no workaround for streaming latency other than disabling thinking mode). Given the shared-core-path impact and lack of workaround (short of not using streaming or not using adaptive thinking), this is P1: affects a widely-used path (any model that thinks long before first delta, streamed through this proxy) and there's no clean workaround. It requires maintainer judgement because the fix involves two coordinated changes (router-level buffering gate, plus httpx chunk_size fix) and confirming the claimed behavior/for correctness before implementing, so needs_human=true.

items.title: [Bug]: least-busy starves deployments — response-cache hits drift the counter negative, ties always pick the first, and the counter isn't shared across workers
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

This is a root-cause follow-up to #25323, which is open since 2026-04-08 and was nearly auto-closed as stale. That report says traffic "gradually drops to zero" for some deployments but does not identify what makes the counter drift in the first place. This issue names a **deterministic, non-race trigger** (a response-cache hit), plus a second, independent bias that survives any clamp, and a third reason the counter is not actually shared across workers. All three are reproduced below on **1.99.0** (current PyPI) and verified present in `main`.

### What happened?

With `routing_strategy: least-busy` and three healthy deployments in one model group, traffic pins itself to a single deployment for long stretches, then jumps to a different one. Over 24h on our proxy: 689 / 785 / 82 requests across three equal-purpose upstreams, with individual hours as lopsided as 195 / 0 / 5. No cooldowns, no failures, `litellm_deployment_state` clean throughout — the upstreams were all healthy the whole time.

There are three separate defects behind this. The first is the trigger, the second makes the "obvious" fix insufficient, and the third explains why a shared Redis cache does not help.

---

#### 1. A response-cache hit decrements the counter without a matching increment

`LeastBusyLoggingHandler` increments in `log_pre_api_call` and decrements in the success/failure callbacks. A cache hit never calls the LLM, so `log_pre_api_call` never runs — but `caching_handler.py` still dispatches the success callbacks with `cache_hit=True`:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/litellm/caching/caching_handler.py#L691-L706

So the decrement fires alone. This is **not** a race: it is one guaranteed `-1` per cache hit. Anyone running `cache: true` together with `least-busy` drifts negative at a rate proportional to their cache hit rate.

Then, in `_get_available_deployments`, unused deployments are seeded to `0`, so a negative count always wins the `min()` and never recovers — every later request goes to the same deployment, whose counter only sinks further on the next cache hit:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/litellm/router_strategy/least_busy.py#L155-L185

#### 2. Even at zero drift, ties always resolve to the first deployment

`if v < min_traffic` is a strict comparison over `dict` iteration order, so when all counts are equal — which is the normal state under light traffic, and the state you land in *if* the counter is clamped at 0 — the first-listed deployment wins every time. #38746 measured 30/30 requests landing on one deployment with two identical upstreams.

This matters for the fix: **clamping alone converts "always the drifted deployment" into "always the first deployment."** Both are total starvation. #25325 and #34444 clamp only; #25393 and #38746 also address the tie-break. The clamp and the tie-break have to land together.

#### 3. The counter is not shared across workers, despite a Redis cache

`Router` builds its cache without an in-memory TTL:

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/litellm/router.py#L776-L778

`DualCache.async_get_cache` returns the in-memory tier first and only falls through to Redis when it misses, and `InMemoryCache.default_ttl` is 600s. `InMemoryCache.set_cache` calls `allow_ttl_override`, which refuses to change a live key's expiry, so repeated increments never shorten it. With `--num_workers 2` each worker therefore routes off its own private counter for up to 10 minutes while overwriting the other's value in Redis. Observed live, same key, seconds apart:

```
{"30950da0(A)": -9, "0fdc2169(B)": 0, "f499c2e9(C)": 0}
{"0fdc2169(B)": -8, "30950da0(A)": 0, "f499c2e9(C)": 0}   <- the other gunicorn worker
```

Docs present `least-busy` + `redis_host` as the way to coordinate in-flight counts across workers, so this is a silent gap between documented and actual behavior.

### Steps to Reproduce

No network access needed — the upstreams are `mock_response`.

```python
import asyncio
import litellm
from litellm import Router


async def main() -> None:
    litellm.cache = litellm.Cache(type="local")

    router = Router(
        model_list=[
            {"model_name": "grp",
             "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/fake-a", "api_key": "x", "mock_response": "ok"},
             "model_info": {"id": "A"}},
            {"model_name": "grp",
             "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/fake-b", "api_key": "x", "mock_response": "ok"},
             "model_info": {"id": "B"}},
        ],
        routing_strategy="least-busy",
        cache_responses=True,
    )

    key = "grp_request_count"
    msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "same prompt every time"}]

    for i in range(6):  # 1 miss + 5 hits
        await router.acompletion(model="grp", messages=msgs, max_tokens=4, temperature=0)
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)  # let the async logging worker drain
        print(f"after call {i + 1}: {await router.cache.async_get_cache(key=key)}")

    picked: dict[str, int] = {}
    for _ in range(20):
        d = await router.async_get_available_deployment(
            model="grp", request_kwargs={}, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "new"}]
        )
        picked[d["model_info"]["id"]] = picked.get(d["model_info"]["id"], 0) + 1
    print("20 selections:", picked)


asyncio.run(main())
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
$ pip install litellm==1.99.0 && python repro.py
after call 1: {'A': 0}
after call 2: {'A': -1, 'B': 0}
after call 3: {'A': -2, 'B': 0}
after call 4: {'A': -3, 'B': 0}
after call 5: {'A': -4, 'B': 0}
after call 6: {'A': -5, 'B': 0}

counter: {'A': -5, 'B': 0}
20 selections: {'A': 20}          # expected ~10/10
```

Defect 3, same version:

```shell
litellm.default_in_memory_ttl  : None
DualCache.default_in_memory_ttl: None
InMemoryCache.default_ttl      : 600 seconds
ttl unchanged by later writes  : True
```

### Expected behaviour

1. A cache hit should not decrement a counter that was never incremented — the counter should track in-flight upstream calls only.
2. With all counts equal, selection should spread across the tied deployments rather than always returning the first.
3. With `redis_host` configured, the in-flight counter should be shared across workers rather than served from a 600s-stale per-process copy.

### Suggested fix

The three defects need three changes, and 1+2 must ship together or starvation simply moves:

1. Skip the decrement when the callback is a cache hit (`kwargs.get("cache_hit") is True`), or gate the whole handler on it. Clamping with `max(v - 1, 0)` is a useful backstop for genuine races but treats the symptom here.
2. Collect all ids tied at the minimum and `random.choice` among them — the approach in #25393 / #38746.
3. Have `Router` pass an explicit short `default_in_memory_ttl` (or read the counter with `local_only=False`) so the shared tier is authoritative when Redis is configured.

There are currently **five open PRs against this one function** — #25325, #25393, #34444, #38746, #38910 — the oldest open since April. None is merged, and none covers all three defects. I'm happy to open a PR combining 1+2 (+3 separately, since it touches `Router`) if a maintainer indicates which of the existing PRs to build on rather than adding a sixth. Please say which and I'll rebase onto it.

### Are you a ML Ops Team?

No

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.99.0 (also reproduced on 1.98.0; `least_busy.py`, `dual_cache.py` and `in_memory_cache.py` are byte-identical to `main` at time of filing)

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-researched bug report identifying three concrete, reproducible defects in the least-busy routing strategy: (1) cache hits decrement the busy counter without a matching increment, causing negative drift and starvation; (2) tie-breaking always picks the first deployment due to strict comparison, meaning even a clamp fix is insufficient; (3) the in-memory TTL default prevents proper cross-worker sharing via Redis, defeating documented multi-worker coordination. Code behaves contrary to reasonable/documented expectations (least-busy should distribute load evenly), so this is a bug, not a feature or docs issue. It affects a widely-used routing strategy (least-busy) combined with caching and multi-worker deployments — a common proxy configuration — causing near-total starvation of deployments in production with no failures/cooldowns to explain it and no workaround mentioned (other than not using cache+least-busy together, which is not a real workaround for a documented supported combination). This is a significant correctness issue on the core routing path affecting many users running multi-worker or cached setups, warranting P1. It doesn't rise to P0 since it doesn't cause data loss and isn't a security issue, and it's not literally "broken for most users on current release" — only those combining least-busy with caching or multi-worker Redis setups, but that's a widely-documented supported combination. Given three distinct root causes bundled together, and the need for a maintainer to decide how to sequence/land the clamp + tie-break + TTL fixes together (explicitly called out as needing to land together), this requires human judgement to confirm and coordinate the fix strategy.

items.title: [Feature]: Route by requested `service_tier` capability within a model group
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature

When multiple deployments share the same `model_name`, LiteLLM should be able to use the request's OpenAI-compatible `service_tier` value as a **deployment eligibility constraint** before applying the normal routing strategy.

This matters when only some providers/deployments for a logical model support a requested tier such as `flex` or `priority`.

For example:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: zai-org/GLM-5.3
    litellm_params:
      model: hosted_vllm/zai-org/GLM-5.3
      order: 1
    model_info:
      # does not support flex

  - model_name: zai-org/GLM-5.3
    litellm_params:
      model: some_provider/zai-org/GLM-5.3
      order: 2
    model_info:
      # supports flex
```

A standard OpenAI-style request:

```json
{
  "model": "zai-org/GLM-5.3",
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "..."}],
  "service_tier": "flex"
}
```

should cause the router to exclude deployments that cannot satisfy `flex`, then run the configured routing/load-balancing strategy across the remaining eligible deployments.

#### Current behavior in LiteLLM 1.99.0

`service_tier` is treated as an inference/provider parameter, not as a router constraint. A deployment may advertise/support the `service_tier` **parameter name** without supporting the requested **value**, and deployments that do not support `flex` remain candidates in the same model group.

`enable_pre_call_checks` does not currently make `service_tier` a deployment-selection discriminator. The practical workarounds are either:

1. expose a separate public model slug such as `model-flex`, or
2. use tag-based routing and require the client to send an additional LiteLLM-specific constraint such as:

```json
{
  "service_tier": "flex",
  "metadata": {
    "tags": ["tier:flex"]
  }
}
```

That leaks gateway deployment topology/policy into clients even though `service_tier` already expresses the client's intent in the OpenAI wire format.

### User Flow

Desired behavior:

1. The administrator configures multiple providers under one public `model_name`.
2. Each deployment either explicitly declares its supported service tiers, or LiteLLM obtains that information from provider/model metadata when authoritative metadata exists.
3. A client sends only the normal request parameter:

```json
{"model": "zai-org/GLM-5.3", "service_tier": "flex", ...}
```

4. LiteLLM filters the candidate deployments to those supporting `flex`.
5. The normal `order`, routing strategy, cooldown, rate-limit, etc. logic chooses among those remaining deployments.
6. `service_tier: "flex"` is still forwarded to the chosen provider as it is today.
7. If no deployment can satisfy the explicitly requested tier, LiteLLM should fail clearly rather than silently select a deployment that cannot honor the requested service class. If fallback-to-default semantics are desired, that should be an explicit policy rather than an accidental consequence of routing.

When `service_tier` is absent (or otherwise means "no explicit tier requirement"), existing routing behavior should remain unchanged.

### Possible implementation shape

A generic per-deployment capability would make this straightforward, for example:

```yaml
model_info:
  supported_service_tiers:
    - default
    - flex
```

The exact configuration/API shape is not important; the important distinction is between:

- `supported_openai_params` / `allowed_openai_params`: whether the deployment accepts the **parameter**, and
- a service-tier capability: which **values** the deployment can actually satisfy.

Provider adapters that already know their valid service-tier values could populate this capability automatically where reliable. Explicit deployment metadata would cover custom/OpenAI-compatible endpoints.

I would not infer capability solely from fields such as `input_cost_per_token_flex`: pricing metadata and serving capability are related but not equivalent.

This should ideally apply consistently to Chat Completions and Responses routing.

### Motivation, pitch

The proxy should preserve the abstraction provided by the OpenAI-compatible API. A client requesting `service_tier="flex"` has already stated its routing requirement; it should not also need to know which LiteLLM deployment tags represent flex-capable infrastructure.

This becomes particularly useful for heterogeneous model groups where the same logical model is available through several providers but only one or a subset offers flex/priority processing. It also generalizes beyond `flex` to future service-tier values without requiring a proliferation of public model aliases.

This is distinct from existing issues around forwarding/mapping `service_tier` or calculating tier-specific costs (for example #10307, #13810, #17808, #17828, #34914, #37326, and #37647). Related #38061 discusses attaching settings such as `service_tier` to Auto Router tiers, but does not address using a client's `service_tier` value to filter eligible deployments within a normal model group.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy / Router

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

1.99.0

### LiteLLM is hiring a founding backend engineer, are you interested in joining us and shipping to all our users?

No

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified feature request for new router capability (filtering deployments by service_tier support within a model group) that does not currently exist. It's a single requester with a detailed write-up but no evidence of corroborating demand from multiple users or maintainer signal — per rules, a detailed write-up alone does not count as demand, so it defaults to P3. It's not a bug since current behavior (treating service_tier as a pass-through param) is not violating any documented contract; it's proposing new routing logic. This is a product-direction decision about whether/how to build a new routing discriminator, so it needs maintainer judgement before being routed/queued.

items.title: [Bug]: ValkeySemanticCache crashes at import with redis-py >= 5 — stale camelCase import of redis.commands.search.indexDefinition
items.body:
**Title:** `ValkeySemanticCache` crashes at import with redis-py >= 5 — stale camelCase import of `redis.commands.search.indexDefinition`

**Affected versions:** 1.94.0 through 1.99.0 (latest at time of writing)
**Affected code:** `litellm/caching/valkey_semantic_cache.py`

## Summary

`ValkeySemanticCache` imports the Redis search module by its **pre-5.0 camelCase name**, which no longer exists in any modern redis-py. The import happens unconditionally at module level, so any deployment that enables `litellm_settings.cache_params.type: "valkey-semantic"` fails at startup with `ModuleNotFoundError` — regardless of LiteLLM version or redis-py version installed.

## The bug

`litellm/caching/valkey_semantic_cache.py` (verified in the 1.94.0 sdist from PyPI, line 27, and in the 1.99.0 sdist, line 26 — the import is unchanged between both):

```python
from redis.commands.search.indexDefinition import IndexDefinition, IndexType
```

redis-py renamed this module to **snake_case** (`index_definition`) in **redis-py 5.0** (released 2023). The camelCase path has been removed from redis-py 5.x, 6.x, 7.x and 8.x — the versions installed by every official LiteLLM image.

## Reproduction

1. Official image `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:1.94.0` (or any version up to 1.99.0) — ships redis-py 8.x.
2. Configure a semantic cache:

   ```yaml
   litellm_settings:
     cache: true
     cache_params:
       type: "valkey-semantic"
       redis_url: "os.environ/REDIS_URL"
       valkey_semantic_cache_embedding_model: "openai/text-embedding-3-small"
       valkey_semantic_cache_index_name: "litellm_semantic_cache_prd"
       similarity_threshold: 0.85
       ttl: 172800
   ```

3. Start the proxy. Startup crashes:

   ```
   ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'redis.commands.search.indexDefinition'
     File "/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/litellm/caching/valkey_semantic_cache.py", line 27, in <module>
       from redis.commands.search.indexDefinition import IndexDefinition, IndexType
   ```

Verified independently:

- redis-py **4.6.0** (last version with the camelCase module) — the import resolves.
- redis-py **8.0.1** and 7.4.0 — the module is `redis/commands/search/index_definition.py` (snake_case); the camelCase import fails.

## Fix

One line — import the snake_case name (with a fallback for old redis-py, if backwards compatibility with redis-py 4.x is desired):

```python
try:  # redis-py >= 5 (module renamed to snake_case)
    from redis.commands.search.index_definition import IndexDefinition, IndexType
except ModuleNotFoundError:  # redis-py 4.x (last version with camelCase name)
    from redis.commands.search.indexDefinition import IndexDefinition, IndexType
```

## Context

- This makes the `valkey-semantic` cache backend unusable on any current install — not just with the official images, but with **any** environment running redis-py >= 5, which is every redis-py released in the last two years.
- The incompatibility is silent in the docs: `docs/my-website/docs/proxy/caching.md` still documents `type: "valkey-semantic"` as a supported backend without mentioning the redis-py version requirement.

Happy to open a PR with the one-line fix if that speeds things up — just say the word.

gold.rationale: A stale import name (`indexDefinition` instead of `index_definition`) causes an unconditional ModuleNotFoundError at import time for any redis-py >= 5, which is essentially every currently installed version, including the official LiteLLM docker images. This makes the entire valkey-semantic cache backend completely unusable — a clear code defect vs. documented/expected behavior (bug, not docs, since the code itself is broken). There is a clear, well-understood one-line fix and reproduction steps provided, so a maintainer doesn't need to investigate further to understand the issue, though it should be verified before merging. Given it breaks a documented feature for all users on current releases with no workaround (other than pinning to redis-py 4.x, which is not a real workaround for most), this is high impact — P1. It's not P0 since it's a single narrower feature entirely broken, not core broken for most users, but it's also close to "widely-used provider" wide-impact since it affects every current redis-py install. Given the affected component (valkey-semantic cache) is not the shared core cache path (default caching type is different), P1 for a fully broken widely-affected feature is appropriate. No security concern applies. needs_human is set true because P1 severity triggers escalation policy, even though the fix is well-specified, to allow verification/PR review.

items.title: [Bug]: OpenRouter wildcard routing causes duplicated irrelevant warnings about unknown costs
items.body:
The dashboard UI offers to create a single "model" which covers all models exposed by openrouter. 
This "model" slug is checked and does not match anything in  the costs database.
So, at startup, the application server emits two warning (one for the model by name, one by id, for some reason) complaining of unknown cost.  But, since #13653 and #32255, pricing for OpenRouter relies on usage data it reports back in response metadata, so the cost database isn't needed or used.

So there are several bugs here:
1. wildcard models shouldn't be matched as if they represent a specific model for cost purposes, at the site that generates this warning.
2. the check should not report the same issue with the same model seperately, once via model name and once via model id.
3. for providers that provide costs through responses, which litellm knows how to ingest, this warning should not evoked. Certainly, not for openrouter since the PRs above were merged .

gold.rationale:
This is a bug report describing incorrect/misleading warning logs at startup: (1) wildcard OpenRouter models are matched against a cost database as if they were specific models, (2) the same warning is emitted twice (once by name, once by id), and (3) the warning is spurious for providers like OpenRouter that report costs via response metadata, which litellm already ingests per prior PRs (#13653, #32255). The code's behavior (warning generation) diverges from the actual/intended cost-accounting logic already implemented elsewhere, so this fits "bug" rather than "docs" or "feature". It's not a security issue, and the author is reporting broken/misleading behavior rather than asking how to do something. Impact: affects any OpenRouter users using the wildcard-model dashboard feature — it's a warning/logging issue, not breaking core functionality, and there's no data loss or blocking crash. A workaround exists (ignore the warning), so it's a narrower, cosmetic-ish issue rather than P1. This affects an OpenRouter integration but only produces noisy logs, not broken behavior, so P2 seems too high; it's mostly cosmetic/log noise. Given it's confined to warning messages and doesn't break functionality, P3 is appropriate, but since it does touch shared cost-computation logic and affects clarity for many OpenRouter+wildcard users, P2 fits better upon reflection due to multiple related bugs bundled and core cost-check path affected. I'll go with P2.
Needs_human: true because this bundles three distinct sub-issues requiring judgement on how to fix (matching logic, dedup, provider-specific suppression), which is more than a trivial routing decision.

items.title: Translate CC Session id header to OpenRouter's session_id for sticky routing and tracing
items.body:
Related to #39145 

In the absence of a `session_id` key in the top-level request, OpenRouter resorts to using the `prompt_cache_key` field as a session identifier ([OR Docs[(https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching#using-session_id-for-sticky-sessions)):
```markdown
# Using session_id for sticky sessions

For more explicit control over sticky routing, you can pass a session_id in
your request. When a session_id is present, OpenRouter uses it directly as the
sticky routing key instead of deriving one from message hashing. 

This is especially useful for multi-turn agentic workflows where the 
opening messages may change between requests but you still want 
to route to the same provider.

***You can provide session_id in two ways**: 
- Request body: Include session_id as a top-level field in your request body. If both are provided, the body value takes precedence. 
- Header: Set the x-session-id HTTP header. The session_id must be at most 256 characters. 

If neither is set, OpenRouter **falls back** to the OpenAI-style `prompt_cache_key` request field as the sticky routing key.
Clients that already send prompt_cache_key get session-pinned routing without
any changes.
```

 with the bug described in #39145, that means each and every generation end up in the same session titled: "\"device_id\":\"xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx".

Claude Code sends:
- `X-Claude-Code-Session-Id: <SESSION_GUID>` as a header.
- and also places `SESSION_GUID` under `metadata.user_id.session_id`.

So if #39145 is fixed to use the session_id as `prompt_cache_key`, the behavior should  be ok. But if openrouter is treated as a top-tier (7B$ *cough*) provider/router, a `session_id` key is the [documented](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/best-practices/prompt-caching#using-session_id-for-sticky-sessions) [way](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/broadcast#optional-trace-data) to support tracing.

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified feature request: translate Claude Code's X-Claude-Code-Session-Id header (or metadata.user_id.session_id) into OpenRouter's documented top-level session_id field for sticky routing/tracing. It's related to another issue (#39145) about a similar mapping bug, showing some corroborating context/demand around OpenRouter session handling, but this specific request is a new capability (mapping a header to a new field), not existing broken behavior. No explicit multiple-user demand beyond the linked issue's author. Default feature requests to P3; the related issue provides some evidence of impact but not strong corroborated demand, and OpenRouter is a widely used provider so it could be borderline P2. Given it's a clear, well-specified feature request that can be queued without deep judgement, needs_human is false.

items.title: Discussion: trust-card verification for MCP servers used through LiteLLM
items.body:
## Context

LiteLLM is increasingly used as a unified gateway, including for MCP server routing. For deployments that proxy untrusted MCP servers, there's no canonical way to verify the *issuer* of a server's credential before routing.

## What we built

**Universal Trust Adapter (UTA)** — https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter

- 8 credential formats: ATC v3, JWT, W3C VC, A2A, EAT-AI, ZTA, MCP Cards, X.509
- 12-stage pipeline
- 6,744 verifications/sec
- Live API: https://www.marketnow.site/api/trust

## Proposal

Add an optional `trust_verifier` config to LiteLLM's MCP routing layer. When set, the verifier is called before the request is routed. Failed verification returns a structured error.

## Non-goals

- Not asking LiteLLM to bundle UTA.
- Not asking for changes to the core proxy.

## Ask

1. Is this in scope?
2. Where should the hook live — in the MCP router, or as a global middleware?

## References

- Repo: https://github.com/alicelabs-llc/universal-trust-adapter
- API: https://www.marketnow.site/api/trust

gold.rationale: This is a proposal/discussion for a new optional feature (trust verification hook for MCP routing) that does not currently exist in LiteLLM. The author explicitly asks whether it's in scope and where a hook should live — a product-direction question requiring maintainer judgement. There's no evidence of broken behavior, and this is a single requester (self-promoting their own project) with no corroborated demand from other users, so it defaults to P3. Since it requires a maintainer decision on scope/architecture, needs_human should be true.

items.title: Design intent: on cache hits, spend is zeroed but token columns replay the original usage — which basis should token reports aggregate?
items.body:
Opening question about a semantics boundary we hit while auditing agent-telemetry accounting.

**Observed shape (proxy + response cache enabled)**

When the same prompt hits the response cache a second time, a new `spend_logs` row is added with `spend = 0` — expected, per `litellm/proxy/hooks/proxy_track_cost_callback.py` (~L275: `if kwargs.get("cache_hit", False) is True: response_cost = 0.0`). But the `prompt_tokens` / `completion_tokens` / `total_tokens` columns replay the original response's full usage, because a cache hit flows through the complete success-logging path with `cache_hit=True` (`litellm/caching/caching_handler.py`, `_async_log_cache_hit_on_callbacks` calls `async_success_handler(result=cached_result, ...)`), and `StandardLoggingPayload` reads token columns from that usage (`litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py`, ~L6103).

**The question**

What is the intended contract for the token columns on a cache-hit row?

- If they mean "real provider token consumption", then token-based rollups (token reports, token-denominated budgets) double-count every cache hit, while dollar rollups correctly show zero.
- If they mean "tokens attributable to this request for user-facing accounting", that's a legitimate choice — but then the two columns in the same row follow different accounting conventions (dollars = provider cost, tokens = served volume), which is worth stating in the docs explicitly so consumers know which basis to aggregate on.

If useful, I can send a minimal repro script (two identical calls with cache on) showing the two rows, or a small doc PR clarifying the convention. Context: I maintain AgentMeasure, a measurement-conformance project; we treat "a cache hit is not a new provider measurement" as a core invariant and are mapping how major frameworks handle it. Not claiming a bug — asking where the intended boundary is.

gold.rationale: The author explicitly frames this as a design/semantics question ("Not claiming a bug — asking where the intended boundary is"), asking which accounting basis (tokens vs spend) is the intended contract for cache-hit rows. This is not a claim that the software misbehaves relative to documented behavior, nor a simple how-to question with an existing-behavior answer — it's a request for clarification on intended design and potentially documentation of that convention. It fits the docs category best if code is working as intended and the ask is to clarify/document the convention, but the underlying question is really "what should the contract be," which is a product-direction judgement call that a maintainer needs to make (docs would follow from that decision). Given the explicit "not a bug" framing and request for clarification/doc, docs is the best fit, but the ambiguity about which basis is correct requires maintainer judgement before any doc change lands. Urgency is low — no evidenced widespread demand, no broken system, workaround (aggregate by known convention) implicitly exists. This is a single-reporter thoughtful design query, defaulting to P3. Needs_human=true because this requires a product-direction decision on the accounting contract before it can be routed as a simple docs fix.

items.title: [Bug]: Sentinel test connection bypasses Sentinel and redis-py 8.x compatibility is not enforced
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues and did not find this Sentinel test/dependency compatibility bug reported.

### What happened?

LiteLLM v1.97.0 runtime Redis operations can use Sentinel, but `RedisCache.test_connection()` constructs a plain `redis.asyncio.Redis` client with Sentinel-only kwargs. The administrative test returns a constructor failure even when real Sentinel coordination works.

Separately, LiteLLM filters Sentinel connection kwargs through runtime inspection of redis-py constructor signatures. With redis-py 8.x, decorator signatures can yield an empty allowlist and drop the master password/transport options. The exact LiteLLM v1.97.0 image includes redis-py 5.3.1 and works, but compatibility is not enforced for a rebuild or dependency update.

Evidence:

- [`test_connection()` bypasses Sentinel](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.97.0/litellm/caching/redis_cache.py#L1362-L1397).
- [Runtime Sentinel clients use `Sentinel.master_for()`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.97.0/litellm/_redis.py#L509-L566).
- [Connection kwargs are derived from constructor introspection](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.97.0/litellm/_redis.py#L39-L62).
- [v1.97.0 records redis-py 5.3.1](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.97.0/uv.lock#L7936-L7939).

Expected: the administrative test uses the same Sentinel path as runtime; supported redis-py versions are constrained/tested, and unsupported majors fail clearly.

Actual: the test yields `unexpected keyword argument 'sentinel_nodes'` while runtime ping/GET/SET succeeds on 5.3.1; redis-py 8.x can silently omit password/options during argument filtering and fail authentication.

### What this blocks

- Using `RedisCache.test_connection()` as Sentinel readiness evidence.
- Unreviewed LiteLLM image rebuilds or redis-py major-version upgrades.
- Claiming Sentinel authentication/options are stable across redis-py versions without a compatibility matrix.

This does **not** block the exact pinned LiteLLM v1.97.0 image with redis-py 5.3.1 after real Sentinel operations pass; it blocks using the broken administrative test and changing that dependency set without proof.

### User Flow

Before a hypothetical fix: a proxy administrator tests a healthy Sentinel configuration and receives a false failure, while a dependency rebuild can silently break runtime auth.

1. The administrator configures Sentinel nodes, `mymaster`, and a Redis password.
2. The v1.97.0 runtime successfully performs coordination operations on redis-py 5.3.1.
3. The administrator invokes the Redis connection test and sees a `sentinel_nodes` constructor error.
4. A later image rebuild resolves redis-py 8.x.
5. Sentinel master authentication then fails because required kwargs were filtered out.

After a hypothetical fix: test and runtime use the same path and unsupported dependencies are rejected.

1. The administrator configures the same Sentinel target.
2. Runtime coordination succeeds.
3. The administrative test succeeds through Sentinel.
4. Dependency CI exercises supported redis-py versions.
5. An unsupported major cannot be installed or start silently.

### Proof the bug occurs

With v1.97.0 and redis-py 5.3.1:

```text
runtime ping/GET/SET through Sentinel: success
RedisCache.test_connection(): failed — Redis.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'sentinel_nodes'
```

With redis-py 8.1.0 in an isolated reproduction, constructor introspection produces an incomplete/empty allowlist and Sentinel master authentication fails. The official pinned v1.97.0 image remains on 5.3.1; this report asks that compatibility be explicit and tested.

### Proposed fix

- Route `test_connection()` through the runtime Sentinel-aware helper.
- Add sync/async Sentinel integration tests with auth, failover, GET/SET, increment, and Lua.
- Enforce a tested redis-py version range.
- Replace fragile signature introspection where possible.
- Add dependency-update CI for Sentinel.

### Acceptance criteria

- `test_connection()` succeeds whenever runtime Sentinel ping succeeds.
- Discovery and master-auth failures are reported distinctly.
- redis-py 5.3.1 passes the full matrix.
- redis-py 8.x either passes or is rejected clearly by dependency constraints.
- Credentials never appear in logs/errors/artifacts.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.97.0

### Cross-check roster

The investigation and issue framing were cross-checked using GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude Opus 5, Grok 4.6, and GLM-5.3. Not every model independently executed every reproduction.

gold.rationale: The issue reports that RedisCache.test_connection() constructs a plain Redis client instead of using the Sentinel-aware runtime path, causing the admin test to fail even though real Sentinel operations succeed. This is a clear behavioral bug: documented/expected behavior is that the test should validate the actual connection path, but code takes a different path and produces false failures. There's also a secondary concern about redis-py 8.x compatibility via fragile constructor introspection, which is a real but more speculative/forward-looking risk (not yet manifesting in the pinned version). The core bug (test_connection bypassing Sentinel) is reproducible and specific with code references and evidence of failure, so it is a bug rather than a feature or question. It affects Sentinel users specifically (a subset of Redis users), and a workaround exists (rely on runtime behavior instead of the test, or pin redis-py 5.3.1), so urgency stays at P2 rather than higher. It doesn't affect most users (only Sentinel-configured deployments), and the redis-py 8.x issue is speculative/not yet triggered in the shipped version. Given the specificity of the code pointers and clear reproduction evidence, a maintainer could route this to the caching/redis module without much ambiguity, but the issue also bundles multiple asks (fix test_connection, add version constraints, CI tests, replace introspection) which suggests judgement is needed to decide scope of the fix — warranting human review.

items.title: [Bug]: cached AsyncHTTPHandler finalizer closes the pooled httpx client under in-flight SSE streams (hourly batched stream deaths)
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

On a production proxy serving streaming traffic, active SSE streams die in same-second batches once per hour per proxy process, phase locked to process start and drifting a few minutes per day. The stream ends with a clean EOF and no terminal event; clients (for example Claude Code) show a retry banner and re-run the turn. We expected in-flight streams to be unaffected by anything periodic inside the proxy.

Root cause (verified in source and in production): the proxy caches its provider httpx clients with a 1 hour TTL. When the cache evicts a handler, the handler object is finalized immediately, and the finalizer's sole-referrer refcount guard cannot see requests in flight, because a live request references the pooled connection rather than the client object. The finalizer then closes the client, tearing the pool down under every live stream on it. The EvictedClientCloser introduced by #35492 fixed the cache's eviction-time close but the finalizer path still closes directly.

Server-side fingerprints while it happens: Cloud Run logs "Truncated response body" warnings in hourly clusters, the proxy records httpx.ReadError raised from `response.aiter_bytes()`, and downstream captures show unrelated clients' streams dying at the same second.

Fix is up as #38242 (finalizer defers busy clients to the EvictedClientCloser; idle clients still close immediately).

### User Flow

Before a (hypothetical) fix: a developer running long streaming turns through the proxy loses whichever turns are in flight at one fixed minute each hour

1. They send POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages with "stream": true (their coding agent points at the proxy)
2. Tokens stream normally, then mid-response the SSE simply ends: no message_stop, clean close, always at the same minute past the hour
3. Their client shows "Waiting for API response" and retries the whole turn, losing the partial generation
4. Every other user with a stream open at that minute sees the same thing at the same second

After a (hypothetical) fix: the same turns stream to completion across that minute

1. They send the same POST https://litellm-domain/v1/messages with "stream": true
2. The stream runs through the hourly boundary and ends with message_stop
3. No retry banner, no lost turns for any user

### Proof the bug occurs

Config / setup the proxy ran with: stock image, `--config config.yaml --num_workers 1`, `DISABLE_AIOHTTP_TRANSPORT=True`, Anthropic models via `model_list` entries with per-model api_key, `litellm_settings.request_timeout: 2400`

Version or commit: v1.97.0

The kill fires at the client-cache TTL, so it cannot be triggered by a single curl on demand; it can be reproduced on schedule:

1. Start the proxy and note the boot time; the first Anthropic request after boot creates the cached client and starts the 1 hour clock
2. At ~58 minutes after that first request, start a long streaming request, e.g. `curl -N https://localhost:4000/v1/messages -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" -d '{"model":"claude-opus-5","max_tokens":4000,"stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"write a very long story"}]}'`
3. At the TTL minute the stream ends without message_stop; the proxy logs `httpx.ReadError` from `response.aiter_bytes()` and (on Cloud Run) a "Truncated response body" warning

Production observations at v1.97.0, before patching: hourly truncation clusters at :38 to :46 past each hour for 17+ hours (matching instance start times 19:38/19:44/19:52), stream deaths in same-second multi-tenant batches (2 at 12:42:13, 3 at 12:46:45 on 2026-08-25), and a steady 50 to 100 ReadErrors per 30 minutes. After deploying exactly the #38242 change as a runtime patch: zero truncation clusters, zero ReadErrors, for 5+ days and counting. The deterministic regression test in #38242 (`test_collected_handler_never_kills_a_stream_in_flight`) fails on the unpatched merge base and passes with the fix.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.97.0

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented, reproducible bug in the core proxy client-caching/connection-pool lifecycle affecting all streaming providers (not just Anthropic) — the finalizer closes the shared httpx client out from under in-flight streams, killing all concurrent SSE streams hourly. This is the shared core path (client cache TTL/finalizer) so it affects many users broadly, not a narrow edge case. There's a clear root cause, reproduction steps, evidence from production (log clusters, error counts), a regression test, and a fix already up as a PR (#38242). Because the shared core connection-handling path is affected across all providers, and it causes silent data/turn loss for every concurrent user at the TTL boundary with no workaround (developers can't disable the TTL or avoid the eviction), this qualifies as very high impact — broken for most users with active streams on a current release, no workaround. That maps to P0, and since a fix is already proposed, this could arguably be routed without much debate, but given it's P0/P1-severity and touches core behavior, per rules P0/P1 issues need human judgement to confirm and merge. Category is bug: this is a violation of expected behavior (streams should not die due to internal cache housekeeping), not a feature request or docs issue.

Despite following up multiple times on your Discord server and via email, i still haven't received any response from your security team, and my report has still not been triaged after **more than 30 days**.

My report was submitted privately via Github Security Advisories, and it also included the mandatory PoC video showing the full attack chain, that you guys request as a mandatory step in your security policy. Thanks for your attention,
Best of regards.

This is a security report escalation - the underlying issue is a vulnerability report that has not been reviewed. Per rules, security takes precedence over everything else. Since this involves an unaddressed, potentially high-impact vulnerability with an exploit path already demonstrated (PoC video), and no maintainer response, this requires immediate human/maintainer judgement to assess severity and respond. This is not something that can be auto-routed - it needs a security team's direct attention.

There is no description of an actual problem, error, question, or feature request.
