items.title: Title: Bounding spend on destinations with no provider account
items.body:
The budget system here is thorough — reservation before the call, fail-closed enforcement, per-key and per-session caps. I've been building the same primitives and yours cover more ground than mine.

One case I can't see how to express: spend against a destination we have no account with. Every budget scope resolves to a provider relationship — our OpenAI key, our Bedrock contract. But agents increasingly hit endpoints where there's no account and no invoice: pay-per-call APIs, another team's agent, an MCP server that charges at the door.

Is that in scope for the gateway, out of scope by design, or has nobody asked? Any of those three answers is useful to me.

Asking because I've built the settlement side of exactly this and I'd rather understand where the boundary is than assume it's a gap.

gold.rationale: The author is asking a clarifying question about scope/design intent ("Is that in scope for the gateway, out of scope by design, or has nobody asked?") rather than reporting broken behavior or requesting a specific feature. They explicitly frame it as wanting to understand a boundary, not claiming the software misbehaves. This fits the question category test: the answer is a clarification of existing design, not necessarily a code change (though it could lead to one). However, since this touches on a product-direction question about whether a new budget/settlement capability should be built, it requires maintainer judgement to answer definitively - a single requester describing a novel use case without corroborated demand. It's not a bug, not docs, and while it gestures at a feature, the ask itself is explicitly a scoping question, so 'question' fits best per the category ordering rules. Urgency is low - no broken system, no urgent demand signal, single requester - so P3. But since this asks about product direction/scope, a maintainer needs to weigh in to give an authoritative answer, so needs_human should be true.

items.title: Allow disabling background health-check history persistence
items.body:
## The Feature

Allow proxy admins to disable persistence of background health-check history while keeping background checks, shared health state, metrics, and routing updates enabled

Large deployments can accumulate health-history rows quickly. Each background persistence cycle currently reads the existing history before deciding which model results to write, so operators who do not use historical health data need a supported way to avoid that database work

## User Flow

Before this feature: an admin cannot run background health checks without also persisting their history

1. They set `background_health_checks: true` under `general_settings` and start the proxy
2. They observe healthy and unhealthy deployment counts through `GET https://litellm-domain/health`
3. PostgreSQL continues receiving health-history reads and writes on every persistence cycle

After this feature: the same admin keeps live health checks but opts out of historical persistence

1. They also set `persist_background_health_check_results: false` and restart the proxy
2. They observe the same healthy and unhealthy deployment counts through `GET https://litellm-domain/health`
3. PostgreSQL receives no background health-history reads or writes

## How far you got

Current `litellm_internal_staging` has no supported configuration field for this behavior. Disabling background checks also disables the live health information needed for routing and operations

## Component

Proxy

## Duplicate check

I searched existing issues and did not find this configuration option

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified request for a new configuration option (persist_background_health_check_results) that does not currently exist. It's a feature request rather than a bug, since the current behavior is as designed but lacks flexibility. There's no evidence of multiple users requesting this (single reporter), so it defaults to P3 per the rubric despite being a detailed write-up. It's well-specified enough to be queued without maintainer discussion on scope - the feature and its behavior are clearly defined, so needs_human is false.

items.title: [Bug]: vertex_ai rerank drops document text from response even when return_documents is true
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When calling `litellm.rerank()` with a Vertex AI semantic-ranker model and `return_documents=True` (the default), none of the results carry a `document` field. The results only contain `index` and `relevance_score`.

What makes this different from a simple omission: the request side already does the right thing. `transform_rerank_request` sets `ignoreRecordDetailsInResponse = not return_documents` (`litellm/llms/vertex_ai/rerank/transformation.py:146`), so Vertex returns `content` and `title` on every record when `return_documents=True`. The response transformer then reads only `id` and `score` from each record and silently discards `content`. Vertex is paying to return the text and LiteLLM throws it away.

The result is that `results[i].document.text` is always absent regardless of what the caller passes for `return_documents`, making the parameter a no-op on the response side.

### User Flow

Before a fix: a RAG pipeline using Vertex rerank to retrieve ranked source passages gets no document text back

1. They call `litellm.rerank(model="vertex_ai/semantic-ranker-default@latest", query="...", documents=["doc 0", "doc 1", ...], return_documents=True)`
2. The response comes back with `results: [{"index": 1, "relevance_score": 0.95}]`, no `document` field, despite Vertex having returned the record content
3. They access `results[0]["document"]["text"]` and get `KeyError: 'document'`
4. Setting `return_documents=False` produces identical output, so the parameter is a no-op

After a fix: the same call returns document text in each result

1. Same call with `return_documents=True`
2. The response comes back with `results: [{"index": 1, "relevance_score": 0.95, "document": {"text": "doc 1"}}]`
3. `results[0]["document"]["text"]` returns the ranked source passage
4. Setting `return_documents=False` omits the `document` field as expected

### Proof the bug occurs

Verified on commit 8fb4545dd0 (litellm v1.97.0).

The bug is in the response transformer and reproduces without a live Vertex call. Running the regression test before the fix:

```
FAILED test_vertex_rerank_return_documents_true_populates_document_text
  AssertionError: return_documents=True must populate document
  got {'index': 1, 'relevance_score': 0.95}  -- no document field

FAILED test_vertex_rerank_return_documents_true_async  
  KeyError: 'document'
```

Root cause in `transform_rerank_response` (`transformation.py:182-186`):

```python
results.append(
    {
        "index": int(record["id"]),
        "relevance_score": record.get("score", 0.0),
        # record["content"] is present when ignoreRecordDetailsInResponse=false
        # but is never read here
    }
)
```

The fix is to read `record.get("content")` and populate `document.text` when `return_documents` is truthy, which is simpler than the Bedrock equivalent because Vertex returns the text directly in the response rather than requiring back-fill from the original request.

This is the same class of bug as #38006 (Bedrock rerank), which was fixed in #38007.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK (litellm Python package)

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.97.0

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

https://www.linkedin.com/in/abhay-tiwari-/

gold.rationale: This is a clear bug: documented/expected behavior (return_documents=True should populate document text) is violated by the response transformer, which discards the content field even though the request already requests it. The issue includes precise root cause, code location, and regression tests demonstrating the failure, similar to a previously fixed Bedrock bug (#38006/#38007). This affects a subset of users (Vertex AI rerank users using return_documents=True), and a workaround may exist by manually mapping index back to original documents client-side, though that's not stated by the reporter. Given clear reproduction and well-scoped fix, it doesn't require maintainer judgement to route to the Vertex AI rerank module owner - it's straightforward to fix by reading record.get("content"). Urgency is P2 since it's a narrower path (single provider, single parameter) rather than a core/widely used path, with no explicit regression or workaround mentioned but scope is limited.

items.title: [Bug]: Router silently load-balances a raw model string across unrelated model_name groups when it collides on litellm_params.model
items.body:
[Bug]: Router silently load-balances a raw model string across unrelated model_name groups when it collides on litellm_params.model

### What happened

`Router._get_deployment_by_litellm_model` is used as a fallback when a client sends a `model`
string that doesn't match any configured `model_name`:

```python
def _get_deployment_by_litellm_model(self, model: str) -> List:
    """
    Get the deployment by litellm model.
    """
    return [m for m in self.model_list if m["litellm_params"]["model"] == model]
```

This matches purely on the literal `litellm_params.model` string across **every** deployment in
`self.model_list`, with no awareness of which `model_name` group each deployment belongs to.
`Router._common_checks_available_deployment` takes whatever this returns straight into the
normal load-balancer.

If the same literal `litellm_params.model` string happens to be used by deployments across
multiple unrelated `model_name` groups — for example, several independent model groups all using
a generic `openai/<model>` passthrough to route to different actual backends — then a client
that sends that raw string directly in `model` gets load-balanced across *all* of those
unrelated groups, silently borrowing capacity from model groups it was never configured to call.

We hit this in production: ~20 unrelated model groups in our proxy config all used the literal
string `openai/gpt-oss-120b` as their `litellm_params.model` (each pointing at a different real
backend via the generic `openai/` passthrough). A misconfigured client sent `model:
"openai/gpt-oss-120b"` directly (instead of one of our named model groups) and was silently
load-balanced across all ~20 of them, including model groups it had no business calling.

### Expected behavior

At minimum, this fallback path should not silently span multiple unrelated `model_name` groups.
Some options:
- Raise a clear error when the literal-string match spans more than one distinct `model_name`
  group, rather than load-balancing across all of them.
- Or: scope the fallback lookup to require an exact, unambiguous match (e.g. restrict to groups
  where every deployment shares the same `model_name`), falling through to the existing
  "no healthy deployments" error otherwise.

Whichever approach is taken, it'd be good to have it behind a flag so existing users who
(knowingly or not) rely on the current behavior aren't broken by a version bump — something like:

```python
router = litellm.Router(
    model_list=[...],
    enable_cross_model_group_collision_check=True,  # opt in - default (unset) preserves current behavior
)
```

with an env var equivalent (e.g. `LITELLM_ENABLE_CROSS_MODEL_GROUP_COLLISION_CHECK`) for
rollout/rollback without a code/config change, and a
`router_settings.enable_cross_model_group_collision_check` proxy-config equivalent for anyone
running the proxy rather than the SDK directly. Naming it `enable_*` (defaulting to off) rather
than `disable_*` avoids upgraders being silently opted into new behavior, and avoids the
double-negative confusion of `disable_x: false` meaning "on".

### Reproduction

```python
import litellm

router = litellm.Router(
    model_list=[
        {"model_name": "chain-a", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/some-shared-string"}},
        {"model_name": "chain-b", "litellm_params": {"model": "openai/some-shared-string"}},
    ]
)

# Neither "chain-a" nor "chain-b" was requested - the raw litellm_params.model string was.
# This resolves successfully today, load-balanced across BOTH unrelated groups.
router.get_available_deployment(model="openai/some-shared-string")
```

### Relevant code

`litellm/router.py`, `Router._get_deployment_by_litellm_model` and its call site in
`Router._common_checks_available_deployment` (the `if len(healthy_deployments) == 0:` /
"check if the user sent in a deployment name instead" branch).

### Version

v1.93.0 (confirmed present; have not checked whether later versions changed this)

gold.rationale: The router's fallback lookup by litellm_params.model matches across unrelated model_name groups, causing requests to be silently load-balanced across model groups the client never configured to call. This is a genuine behavioral defect (violates expected isolation between model groups) rather than a missing feature, though the reporter also proposes a flag-based fix. It's a real bug with a clear reproduction and production impact (capacity leaking across groups, potential security/isolation concern in multi-tenant proxy setups). It's not framed as an exploit against auth/credentials, so security category doesn't strictly apply, though there is a governance/isolation angle. Given the production impact but narrow trigger condition (requires literal string collisions across model groups, which is a specific misconfiguration/coincidence), this affects a subset of users - impacts the shared router core code path though, which affects many users if they hit this collision pattern. Since it can silently borrow capacity from unrelated groups without any config granting that, and is confirmed in production, this needs prompt attention. There's no user-side workaround other than avoiding collisions. Given decision requires judgement on whether to add a flag (product-direction call) and it's a subtle correctness/isolation bug, needs_human should be true.

items.title: MiniMax‑M2.7: message.content empty, usage all zero while reasoning_content has valid output, finish_reason=stop
items.body:
### Title: MiniMax‑M2.7: message.content empty, usage all zero while reasoning_content has valid output, finish_reason=stop

**Environment**

- LiteLLM version: xxx
- Model: MiniMax‑M2.7

**Bug description**
When calling MiniMax‑M2.7, upstream returns `finish_reason: stop` with valid text inside `reasoning_content / thinking_blocks`, but `message.content` is empty string. All usage token fields are zero. LiteLLM returns 200 OK to downstream client. Downstream application receives empty content and triggers massive client‑side retries.

Root cause:

1. Minimax adapter does not map `reasoning_content` to top‑level `message.content` for M2.7 new response schema.
2. Token usage parsing path outdated for M2.7 nested provider‑specific token payload, resulting all tokens=0.
3. `finish_reason=stop` makes LiteLLM treat it as successful completion, no retry triggered.

**Expected behavior**

1. If `reasoning_content` exists and `content` empty, fill `content` with reasoning content (configurable toggle).
2. Correctly parse token usage from M2.7 provider‑specific response fields.
3. Provide validation hook to detect this malformed response and raise error instead passing bad payload downstream.

gold.rationale: This is a clear bug report affecting a specific provider (MiniMax M2.7): the adapter fails to map reasoning_content to message.content, token usage is parsed incorrectly (all zeros), and finish_reason=stop causes LiteLLM to treat malformed responses as successful, leading to silent failures downstream. This is incorrect behavior relative to expected output/usage accounting, matching the 'bug' category (wrong output, incorrect token accounting). It's not security, not purely docs, and not a question - the reporter describes concrete malfunction with reproduction context (empty content, zero usage, stop reason) tied to a specific provider/model. Since it affects only MiniMax M2.7 (a single, narrower provider) rather than the shared core path or multiple providers, and it's unclear if a workaround exists, but the impact is a subset of users (specific model) rather than most users - this points to P2. However, the fact that malformed responses are silently passed through as 200 OK with zero usage is a data-integrity/reliability concern that could cause significant downstream issues (retries storms) for users of that model - but limited to one provider/model, so no multi-provider or core-path escalation applies. This warrants human review because it requires reproduction confirmation and judgment on whether to add a generic validation hook (product-direction feature ask bundled with the bug), and it bundles three distinct asks (content mapping, usage parsing, validation hook) which is a multi-issue bundle needing maintainer triage.

items.title: [Bug]: Initial Prisma connection failure ignores allow_requests_on_db_unavailable, returns 401, and never recovers
items.body:
## Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that this issue is not a duplicate. Issues #27704 and #34934 and PR #35837 cover adjacent startup, readiness, and post-connect recovery behavior, but not the initial-connect nil-client authentication path reported here.

## What happened?

When LiteLLM starts with a configured PostgreSQL database and the initial Prisma connection fails, `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true` intentionally permits startup to continue. In this path, the global Prisma client is set to `None`.

Passing readiness in this fail-open mode is not inherently incorrect: the purpose of `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable` is to let requests proceed during a database connectivity failure. The defect is that the initial-connect-failure path does not actually honor that contract:

1. `/health/readiness` returns HTTP 200, consistently with the requested fail-open policy, so Kubernetes routes requests to the replica.
2. Virtual-key authentication raises `NoDatabaseConnectionError` before consulting the cache.
3. That exception is not recognized as the database-connectivity failure that caused it, so LiteLLM skips its intended restricted fail-open identity and returns a generic HTTP 401. If the request cannot be served under the fail-open policy, the correct result is a retryable 503—not a credential-invalid 401.
4. The failed initial connection does not get the reconnect watchdog used by an already-connected Prisma client, so restoring database availability does not repair the replica; it remains in this state until it is restarted.

In a multi-replica deployment, this produces intermittent 401 responses for valid credentials depending on which replica receives the request. A client may incorrectly conclude that its credentials are invalid and rotate or discard them.

The observed query-engine startup failure occurs inside the Prisma runtime that LiteLLM initializes and distributes in its official container image. It is therefore a LiteLLM integration and reliability failure even if the eventual low-level fix belongs in the bundled Prisma dependency. We have not yet isolated why the subprocess failed to listen on its local port. The mismatch between the advertised fail-open state and the authentication path, the incorrect 401, and the lack of recovery are separately deterministic LiteLLM application behaviors. The HTTP 200 readiness result is a relevant symptom of that mismatch, not a standalone defect when fail-open is enabled.

## User Flow

Before a hypothetical fix: an operator whose application uses a valid LiteLLM virtual key is told that the credential is invalid after a startup database outage, and the proxy does not recover when the database returns.

1. They start LiteLLM at `http://127.0.0.1:4000` with `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true`, an existing database-backed virtual key, and the configured PostgreSQL endpoint temporarily unavailable.
2. They send `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/models` with `Authorization: Bearer ${VIRTUAL_KEY}`.
3. They receive HTTP 401 with `Authentication Error, No DB Connected`, even though the virtual key is valid and the configured policy allows requests during a database outage.
4. They restore the configured PostgreSQL endpoint without restarting LiteLLM.
5. They repeat `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/models` with the same `Authorization` header.
6. They continue to receive the same HTTP 401 indefinitely.
7. They restart LiteLLM while PostgreSQL is reachable.
8. They repeat the same `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/models` request.
9. They receive HTTP 200, confirming that the credential was valid and the prior 401 described a dependency failure as an authentication failure.

After a hypothetical fix: the same operator can use the configured restricted fail-open behavior during the outage, and the proxy automatically resumes database-backed authentication when PostgreSQL returns.

1. They start LiteLLM at `http://127.0.0.1:4000` with `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true`, an existing database-backed virtual key, and the configured PostgreSQL endpoint temporarily unavailable.
2. They send `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/models` with `Authorization: Bearer ${VIRTUAL_KEY}`.
3. They receive the response permitted by LiteLLM's restricted database-unavailable identity rather than HTTP 401. If that route cannot safely use fail-open behavior, they receive a retryable HTTP 503 instead.
4. They restore the configured PostgreSQL endpoint without restarting LiteLLM.
5. They repeat `GET http://127.0.0.1:4000/v1/models` with the same `Authorization` header.
6. They receive HTTP 200 under the restored database-backed identity.
7. They do not restart LiteLLM.
8. They continue making the same request.
9. Requests continue to succeed after automatic recovery.

## Proof the bug occurs

This report is based on a live production LiteLLM proxy, not a mocked test. The sanitized configuration, exact image digest and runtime versions, observed HTTP status and response bodies, and same-pod timing evidence are included below. The deployment-level reproduction section gives the complete `curl` flow against `http://127.0.0.1:4000`; no provider call or paid API is required because the failure occurs while authenticating `GET /v1/models`.

The exact original customer request was not retained as a matching APM span, so that limitation is stated rather than presenting reconstructed telemetry as a trace-level E2E transcript. The repeatedly observed sequence on affected live replicas was: Prisma query-engine `/status` connection failure, HTTP 200 readiness with `db: "Not connected"`, valid virtual-key requests returning the shown HTTP 401 body, no recovery after the database was available, and successful authentication only after restart.

## Environment

- LiteLLM image: `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.95.0`
- Image digest: `sha256:af806882b7a6ced41658db5b6a7e98ed7b9b51d03b935e0417bf1c8552d688af`
- Source commit for tag `v1.95.0`: `72a4a55f43ea7266de589f005d0d33624fe5d555`
- Latest release checked for persistence: `v1.98.0` (source inspection; the original production incident was on `v1.95.0`)
- Python: 3.13.14
- `prisma` Python package: 0.11.0
- Base image: Wolfi (`VERSION_ID=20230201`)
- OpenSSL: 3.6.3
- glibc: 2.43
- Prisma query engine:
  - Path: `/opt/prisma/binaries/node_modules/prisma/query-engine-debian-openssl-3.0.x`
  - Engine commit: `ac9d7041ed77bcc8a8dbd2ab6616b39013829574`
- Deployment: large multi-replica Kubernetes deployment on EKS
- Pod resources: 4 CPU and 16 GiB memory requests/limits; Guaranteed QoS
- Database: external PostgreSQL-compatible Amazon Aurora cluster
- Documented database connection limit: 5,000

The issue was observed on more than one pod and ReplicaSet.

## Relevant LiteLLM configuration

The following is the relevant, sanitized portion of our configuration:

```yaml
general_settings:
  use_redis_transaction_buffer: true
  allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true
  database_connection_pool_limit: 10
  user_api_key_cache_ttl: 600
  enable_jwt_auth: true
  store_model_in_db: false

litellm_settings:
  # Other deployment-specific callback and routing settings omitted.

environment:
  DATABASE_URL: >-
    postgresql://$(DATABASE_USERNAME):$(DATABASE_PASSWORD)@$(DATABASE_HOST)/$(DATABASE_NAME)
  LITELLM_MASTER_KEY: <from Kubernetes Secret>

database:
  deployStandalone: false
  useExisting: true
  endpoint: <Aurora/PostgreSQL global endpoint>
  database: litellm
  secretName: <Kubernetes Secret>

redis:
  # An external Redis deployment is used.
  enabled: false
```

`DATABASE_URL_READ_REPLICA` and `DIRECT_URL` are not set. The database schema is managed separately from the LiteLLM application deployment.

The application and health probes use port 4000:

```yaml
startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/readiness
    port: 4000
  initialDelaySeconds: 120
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 30

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/liveliness
    port: 4000
  periodSeconds: 30
  timeoutSeconds: 5

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /health/readiness
    port: 4000
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 5
  failureThreshold: 3
  successThreshold: 1

separateHealthApp: false
```

## Actual behavior

After a Prisma connection failure during startup, the affected replica continues serving and reports Ready. A request authenticated with a valid virtual key receives:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
content-type: application/json
```

```json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "Authentication Error, No DB Connected. See - https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/virtual_keys",
    "type": "auth_error",
    "param": "None",
    "code": "401"
  }
}
```

At the same time, readiness reports HTTP 200 and indicates only in the response body that the database is disconnected:

```json
{
  "status": "healthy",
  "db": "Not connected"
}
```

Restoring database availability does not repair a client that failed its initial connection. The replica continues returning the same authentication response until it is restarted.

## Expected behavior

For a deployment that is configured to use the database for virtual-key authentication:

1. With `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true`, a genuine database-connectivity failure should use LiteLLM's documented restricted fail-open identity. Readiness may remain HTTP 200 if the configured request path can actually operate under that policy.
2. If a route or deployment policy cannot safely use fail-open behavior, the dependency failure should produce a retryable 503 and the replica should not report Ready for that mode. It should never become a 401 indicating invalid credentials, because the credential was not evaluated.
3. With `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: false`, initial database connection failure should fail startup or result in 503 readiness and request responses.
4. LiteLLM should retry and recover when the database becomes reachable after an initial connection failure, or it should fail startup so the process can be restarted by its supervisor.
5. A deployment that intentionally has no database configured should remain distinguishable from a database-configured deployment whose client failed.

## Production evidence

All times below are UTC on 2026-08-19.

On one affected pod, APM recorded three failed Prisma query-engine status probes during startup:

| Time | Request | Error |
|---|---|---|
| 18:36:44.249 | `GET http://localhost:60987/status` | `httpx.ConnectError: All connection attempts failed` |
| 18:36:46.933 | `GET http://localhost:60987/status` | `httpx.ConnectError: All connection attempts failed` |
| 18:36:49.412 | `GET http://localhost:60987/status` | `httpx.ConnectError: All connection attempts failed` |

The first sampled `NoDatabaseConnectionError` responses from that pod appeared at 18:38:21. More than 100 such errors were sampled. Kubernetes health probes began timing out at 18:45:43 and later received connection-refused errors, after which the pod was removed.

The same ordering was seen on pods from multiple ReplicaSets: local Prisma `/status` connection failures were followed by persistent `No DB Connected` authentication failures. In another instance, `/status` failed between 19:21:09 and 19:21:13, and the resulting `No DB Connected` failures began at 19:22:46 and continued until 21:27.

The exact original customer request was not retained as a matching APM span, so we cannot claim trace-level identity between that request and the sampled errors. The repeated same-pod sequence nevertheless identifies the server-side path responsible for the observed response.

### Resource checks

The evidence does not indicate gross pod or database resource saturation during the initial failure window:

- Affected pod maximum memory: approximately 4.07 GB out of 16 GiB.
- Affected pod maximum CPU: approximately 0.91 cores out of 4.
- No OOM-kill metric was present and the pod restart count remained zero during the relevant window.
- Aurora connections remained below 30% of the documented maximum.
- Aurora CPU remained low and free memory remained ample throughout the window.

These checks make broad capacity exhaustion unlikely, but they do not rule out a short-lived network, TLS, authentication, query-engine process, or binary-compatibility failure.

### Internal observability evidence

Private Datadog deep links and internal pod identifiers are intentionally omitted from this public report. The underlying same-pod traces supporting the timing above can be shared privately with maintainers if needed.

## Code path and suspected defects

The line references below refer to the `v1.95.0` tag unless stated otherwise.

### 1. Initial Prisma connection failure is converted into a `None` client

File: [`litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py`, `ProxyStartupEvent._setup_prisma_client`, lines 8456–8507](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py#L8456-L8507)

`_setup_prisma_client()` constructs a `PrismaClient` and awaits `prisma_client.connect()` at lines 8474–8481. If that connection fails, the catch block at lines 8505–8507 calls `PrismaDBExceptionHandler.handle_db_exception(e)` and returns `None` when `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable` permits startup to continue.

As a result, the process loses the distinction between:

- no database was configured, and
- a database was configured, but its required client failed to initialize.

The reconnect monitor belongs to a successfully initialized client. Returning `None` after an initial failure therefore also leaves no object to monitor and reconnect.

`PrismaClient.connect()` itself uses a retry envelope of three tries and ten seconds in [`litellm/proxy/utils.py`, lines 4217–4247](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/utils.py#L4217-L4247).

### 2. Readiness advertises fail-open availability, but the initial nil-client authentication path cannot fail open

File: [`litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, detailed readiness, lines 1450–1479](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py#L1450-L1479)

When `prisma_client` exists but is unhealthy, the detailed readiness path returns 503. When the client is `None`, it instead returns HTTP 200 with `{"status":"healthy","db":"Not connected"}`.

File: [`litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, public readiness resolution, lines 1534–1571](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py#L1534-L1571)

`_resolve_public_readiness_db()` immediately returns `"Not connected"` for a `None` client without changing the response status to 503. Kubernetes uses only the HTTP status, so the pod remains Ready.

That result can be correct when `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true`: a deliberately degraded but usable proxy may remain Ready. The problem in this initial-failure state is that the authentication path described below does not provide the fail-open behavior that readiness advertises. Kubernetes therefore continues sending traffic to a pod that rejects valid virtual keys with 401.

This behavior remains present in the latest release, v1.98.0, in the [detailed readiness path](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.98.0/litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py#L1518-L1549) and [public readiness path](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.98.0/litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py#L1604-L1618).

### 3. A missing Prisma client is raised before the authentication cache is checked

File: [`litellm/proxy/auth/resolvers/store.py`, `IdentityStore._resolve_key`, lines 101–107](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/auth/resolvers/store.py#L101-L107)

`IdentityStore._resolve_key()` checks whether `_prisma is None` before it consults the cache. It raises `NoDatabaseConnectionError("No DB Connected")`, so `user_api_key_cache_ttl: 600` cannot make this state fail open even for a key that was previously cached in the process.

This prevents cached authentication from supporting the advertised fail-open state. It also means the initial-connect-failure path depends on the exception handler's restricted fallback, but the exception is not classified in a way that reaches that fallback.

### 4. `NoDatabaseConnectionError` falls through to generic HTTP 401 handling

File: [`litellm/proxy/auth/resolvers/exceptions.py`, lines 8–14](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/auth/resolvers/exceptions.py#L8-L14)

`NoDatabaseConnectionError` inherits from the plain `IdentityResolutionError`. It does not carry a `ProxyException` error code or HTTP status.

File: [`litellm/proxy/auth/auth_exception_handler.py`, lines 66–90](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/auth/auth_exception_handler.py#L66-L90) and [`litellm/proxy/auth/auth_exception_handler.py`, lines 147–177](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.95.0/litellm/proxy/auth/auth_exception_handler.py#L147-L177)

When `allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true`, lines 66–90 are designed to return a restricted `INTERNAL_USER` fallback identity for exceptions recognized by `is_database_connection_error()`. When fail-open is disabled, recognized database-service-unavailable errors are mapped to 503 at lines 163–172.

`NoDatabaseConnectionError` is not recognized by either database-error classifier. It therefore skips both the intended fail-open identity and the 503 dependency-error mapping, reaches the generic authentication branch, and becomes a 401.

This remains unchanged in v1.98.0: [`exceptions.py`, lines 8–14](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.98.0/litellm/proxy/auth/resolvers/exceptions.py#L8-L14), [`auth_exception_handler.py`, lines 66–90](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.98.0/litellm/proxy/auth/auth_exception_handler.py#L66-L90), and [`auth_exception_handler.py`, lines 146–176](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.98.0/litellm/proxy/auth/auth_exception_handler.py#L146-L176).

### 5. The local `/status` failures originate in the Prisma Python runtime

Runtime file in the image: `/app/.venv/lib/python3.13/site-packages/prisma/engine/query.py`, approximately lines 144–232.

LiteLLM constructs the Prisma client and calls `connect()` during `ProxyStartupEvent._setup_prisma_client()`. The Prisma runtime packaged in the LiteLLM image then selects an available local port, starts the query-engine subprocess, and polls `GET /status` every 100 ms for up to the default ten-second connection timeout. The observed `httpx.ConnectError` means no service accepted the local connection during those probes. Normal Prisma queries use `POST /`, so these requests are the engine startup/health path rather than application traffic.

This startup chain is invoked and distributed by LiteLLM, making it appropriate to report the failure against LiteLLM. The runtime starts the subprocess with stdout and stderr inherited by the LiteLLM process. We were unable to find the corresponding query-engine stderr in our indexed container logs, so the exact failure mode within the LiteLLM-distributed stack remains unknown. The process may have:

- exited immediately,
- taken longer than ten seconds to listen,
- failed a database/TLS/authentication initialization step, or
- encountered a Wolfi/engine binary compatibility issue.

## Steps to reproduce

### Deployment-level reproduction

This reproduction requires a LiteLLM database whose schema has already been migrated and a valid virtual key created before the test.

1. Start PostgreSQL and LiteLLM v1.95.0 with the sanitized settings above.
2. Generate a virtual key while the database is healthy and save it as `VIRTUAL_KEY`.
3. Stop LiteLLM.
4. Make the database endpoint temporarily unreachable from the LiteLLM process. For a local test this can be done by stopping PostgreSQL after its data volume and schema have been preser

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented bug affecting the core proxy auth/db-availability path. The documented contract of allow_requests_on_db_unavailable is violated: readiness reports 200 (fail-open) but auth still hard-fails with 401 instead of using the fail-open identity or a 503, and the failed initial connection never gets the reconnect watchdog, so it never recovers without a restart. This affects the shared authentication/core path used by all proxy deployments with a Postgres backend, and in multi-replica deployments causes intermittent false 401s for valid credentials with no recovery except restart (no real workaround other than restarting pods). This is a core reliability/auth defect, not a docs or feature issue. Given it affects the shared core auth path across many users/replicas and has no real workaround (restart is not a fix, it recurs), and combines multiple related issues, this needs maintainer judgement to reproduce/confirm and decide the right fix (503 vs fail-open identity, watchdog reuse). Impact: affects widely-used core auth path for DB-backed deployments, workaround (restart) is painful and doesn't prevent recurrence — raising to P1. Given the complexity and multiple facets (auth bypass logic, readiness inconsistency, reconnect watchdog gap) this needs human triage.

items.title: [Performance] Guidance for scaling LiteLLM Proxy to 500M TPM with input-heavy traffic
items.body:
## Summary

We are running LiteLLM Proxy in a single-layer production topology and would like guidance on whether our deployment can scale from the current ~100M TPM to 500M TPM.

We are looking for recommended LiteLLM configuration values and capacity-planning advice, especially for PostgreSQL connections, Redis pools, worker count, billing/wallet hot paths, and background jobs.

## Current topology

```
Users
  -> Nginx load balancer
  -> 4 LiteLLM Proxy VMs
  -> shared Redis + PostgreSQL
  -> upstream model APIs
```

- 4 LiteLLM VMs
- 32 vCPU / 64 GiB RAM per VM
- 24 LiteLLM workers per VM (96 workers total)
- One separate node currently hosts Nginx, Redis, and PostgreSQL
- This is a single LiteLLM layer; the upstream is not another LiteLLM Proxy
- We use the Proxy for authentication, budgets, spend tracking, wallet admission, routing, and Prometheus metrics

## Current measured traffic

The attached Grafana panel covers the last 15 minutes:

- System TPM mean: approximately 99.6M
- System TPM peak: approximately 117M
- Input TPM mean: approximately 98.9M
- Output TPM mean: approximately 684K
- At one sample: 110M input TPM and 743K output TPM

The traffic is therefore heavily input-dominant (roughly 99% input tokens). We want to reach 500M TPM without changing the request distribution substantially.

## Relevant configuration

```yaml
litellm_settings:
  request_timeout: 600
  set_verbose: false
  json_logs: true
  callbacks:
    - prometheus
  turn_off_message_logging: true
  redact_user_api_key_info: true
  cache: true
  cache_params:
    type: redis
    ttl: 600
    max_connections: 100
    mode: default_off

billing:
  enabled: true
  enforce_wallet_admission: true
  wallet_redis_hot_path_enabled: true
  reservation_ttl_seconds: 7200
  pro_wallet_max_in_flight_team: 60
  pro_wallet_max_in_flight_key: 30

general_settings:
  database_connection_pool_limit: 10
  database_connection_pool_timeout: 20
  database_connection_timeout: 20
  allow_requests_on_db_unavailable: true
  proxy_batch_write_at: 120
  use_redis_transaction_buffer: true
  disable_error_logs: false
  disable_spend_logs: false
  disable_spend_updates: false
  store_prompts_in_spend_logs: false
  background_health_checks: true
  use_shared_health_check: true
  health_check_interval: 1800
  health_check_concurrency: 10
  store_model_in_db: true

router_settings:
  routing_strategy: simple-shuffle
  cache_params:
    type: redis
    max_connections: 500
  timeout: 120
  stream_timeout: 300
  enable_pre_call_checks: true
  optional_pre_call_checks:
    - encrypted_content_affinity
  cooldown_time: 120
  retry_policy:
    AuthenticationErrorRetries: 0
    TimeoutErrorRetries: 0
    RateLimitErrorRetries: 3
    ContentPolicyViolationErrorRetries: 1
    InternalServerErrorRetries: 2
```

## Observed cross-model contention

The current deployment also shows cross-model resource contention and queue buildup. In practice, the system can only monitor and sustain roughly 150M TPM reliably before backlog becomes visible. A representative pattern is:

- Qwen3.7 reaches approximately 100M TPM.
- DeepSeek was previously serving approximately 100M TPM.
- After Qwen3.7 reaches that level, DeepSeek throughput is squeezed down to approximately 50M TPM.
- The reduction appears correlated with shared worker, Redis, PostgreSQL, or other proxy-side resources rather than an upstream quota change.

This suggests that model traffic is not sufficiently isolated: one high-volume model can consume shared worker capacity, connection pools, queue slots, Redis operations, or billing/spend-processing capacity and create backlog for other models. We would like to know whether LiteLLM has recommended per-model or per-deployment concurrency limits, queue isolation, weighted routing, separate Router instances, or dedicated worker pools for this situation.

## Questions

1. With 4 VMs (24 workers each), is 500M TPM a realistic target for this input-heavy workload, assuming the upstream providers can supply the required quota?
2. Is `database_connection_pool_limit: 10` unsafe with 96 workers (theoretical maximum of about 960 PostgreSQL connections)? What pool size would you recommend?
3. What Redis `max_connections` values would you recommend for the response cache and Router cache per worker at this scale?
4. Should background health checks and scheduled jobs run only on a dedicated control instance rather than on all serving workers?
5. Is `use_redis_transaction_buffer: true` appropriate for this workload, and what Redis/PostgreSQL metrics should we monitor?
6. Would you recommend changing retry counts, `proxy_batch_write_at`, request/stream timeouts, or worker recycling settings?
7. Are there known limitations or production issues with this topology or with Redis Cluster/Sentinel that we should account for?

items.title: [Feature]: [Feature] Support httpx2 / plans to drop httpx<1.0 pin in Python SDK
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature

```markdown
## Summary

The `httpx` package is no longer actively maintained and has been succeeded by `httpx2` (a separate package starting at v2.0.0 on PyPI). We'd like to understand LiteLLM's plans regarding the httpx dependency in the Python SDK.

## Current State

LiteLLM v1.97.0 pins:
- `httpx>=0.28.0,<1.0`
- `openai>=2.20.0,<3.0.0`

The `openai` SDK already supports httpx2 as an optional extra (`pip install 'openai[httpx2]'`) and plans full httpx2 migration in v3.0.0.

However, LiteLLM's `openai<3.0.0` pin blocks downstream users from adopting openai v3.0.0, and the `httpx<1.0` pin blocks direct httpx2 adoption.

## Context

We use LiteLLM as a dependency in an enterprise AI platform. Our security tooling flags `httpx` as an unmaintained package (inactive community risk). We cannot migrate to httpx2 because LiteLLM (and its transitive dependencies) hard-pin `httpx<1.0`.

## Questions

1. With the Rust migration underway for the gateway, will the **Python SDK** (`pip install litellm`) eventually drop or replace the `httpx` dependency?
2. Are there plans to support `openai>=3.0.0` (which will use httpx2 natively)?


### User Flow

```markdown
## Before this feature (today)

Today, a platform team building an AI service on top of litellm cannot remove the unmaintained `httpx` package from their dependency tree, because litellm v1.97.0 hard-pins `httpx>=0.28.0,<1.0` and `openai>=2.20.0,<3.0.0`.

1. Developer adds `litellm==1.97.0` to `pyproject.toml` and runs `pip install -e .`
2. Pip resolves `httpx==0.28.1` into the environment (required by litellm)
3. Developer's enterprise security scanner runs nightly and flags `httpx` as **ESW4 — inactive community / unmaintained package**
4. Developer attempts workaround: replaces `httpx` with `httpx2==2.12.0` in the lockfile
5. `pip install` fails — litellm's metadata demands `httpx>=0.28.0,<1.0`, and httpx2 is a different package name
6. Developer attempts second workaround: upgrades to `openai==3.0.0` (which uses httpx2 natively) hoping litellm will pick it up
7. `pip install` fails — litellm pins `openai>=2.20.0,<3.0.0`, rejecting v3.0.0
8. Developer is stuck: the security finding stays open, no code change can resolve it

**Current workaround:** Accept the security finding as a known risk, document it as "waiting for upstream," and carry the exception through every release audit.

## After this feature (ideal user flow)

With httpx2 support in litellm, the same developer can eliminate the unmaintained httpx package entirely.

1. Developer adds `litellm==<new-version>` to `pyproject.toml` and runs `pip install -e .`
2. Pip resolves `httpx2>=2.7.0` into the environment (litellm now accepts httpx2 as transport)
3. Developer's enterprise security scanner runs nightly — **no findings** for httpx (it is no longer installed)
4. Application starts: `POST http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions` with a JSON body containing `model` and `messages`
5. LiteLLM proxy forwards the request to the configured provider and returns `200 OK` with the completion response — same as before, no behavior change
6. Developer ships the release without a dependency-exception ticket

### How far you got

Dead-end: litellm can't even start without httpx.
  
  $ pip install litellm==1.97.0 httpx2==2.12.0
  $ pip uninstall httpx -y
  $ python3 -c "import litellm"
  
  ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'httpx'
  
  httpx2 is installed but litellm doesn't know it exists — different package name, no fallback, no config option. The proxy never starts, so there's nothing further to test.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK (litellm Python package)

### LiteLLM is hiring a founding backend engineer, are you interested in joining us and shipping to all our users?

No

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a request for the library to support a new dependency version (httpx2) / relax pins on httpx and openai to enable future compatibility. No existing behavior is broken — litellm works fine with current pins. This is a forward-looking feature/roadmap question about dependency management, not a bug or a "how do I use X" question. It requires a maintainer/product decision about dependency strategy (whether to support httpx2, whether to relax openai pin), which is a product-direction call. It's a single requester (enterprise security tooling concern) with no evidence of broader community demand, so default to P3 per feature request rules. Since it requires a product-direction judgement call about dependency strategy, needs_human should be true.
