items.title: [Bug]: Security - logout/password change do not revoke active UI sessions (v1.94.0)
items.body: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? ## Summary Active UI session credentials remain valid after user logout and after password change. This allows previously issued session credentials to continue working until expiry ## Severity High ## Confidence 9/10 ## Affected areas - `ui/litellm-dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/hooks/useLogout.ts` - `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/internal_user_endpoints.py` (`_update_single_user_helper`) - `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py` ## Observed behavior Logout appears to clear local client state only, while password update stores a new password hash without revoking already issued UI session credentials. Request authorization still depends on API key validity/expiry rather than the current password state ## Expected behavior Logout and password change should invalidate active UI session credentials server-side, so they can no longer be used ## Impact If an attacker has a stolen session credential/API key, user logout or password reset does not terminate attacker access immediately ## Suggested remediation - Revoke active UI session credentials server-side on logout - Revoke active UI session credentials server-side on password change - Tag UI-issued session credentials (for example: metadata like `ui_session=true` and session identifier) so revocation can be scoped - Add backend logout invalidation before client redirect/cleanup ## Notes A persistent session identifier design may require migration and rollout handling for currently active sessions ### Steps to Reproduce ## Reproduction 1. Sign in as a user in Browser A and Browser B 2. Capture an active UI session credential/API key in Browser B 3. In Browser A, click logout or change password 4. Retry authenticated requests from Browser B using the previously issued credential 5. Requests continue to succeed until credential expiry ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? UI Dashboard ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.94.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details https://www.linkedin.com/in/ron-zhong/

gold.rationale: This report describes a genuine security vulnerability: session/API key credentials remain valid after logout or password change, allowing a stolen credential to be used indefinitely until expiry. This is an auth-related weakness with a plausible exploit path (stolen session token continues to work after logout/password reset), which per the rules takes precedence and must be classified as security. Given it affects session revocation for all users of the UI dashboard, has no stated workaround, and is exploitable to maintain unauthorized access, it warrants high urgency (P0 given broken-for-most-users/no-workaround security flaw with plausible exploit). Security issues always require human judgement/review before routing, so needs_human is true.

items.title: [Bug]: Security - UI cookie JWT contains reusable API key material (v1.94.0)
items.body: ### Check for existing issues - [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate. ### What happened? ## Summary The UI auth cookie token is a JWT that carries API key material (`key` claim). If copied/replayed, it can authenticate another browser/session and expose reusable auth material ## Severity High ## Confidence 9/10 ## Affected areas - `litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py` - `litellm/proxy/auth/login_utils.py` - `ui/litellm-dashboard/src/app/(dashboard)/hooks/useAuthorized.ts` - `ui/litellm-dashboard/src/components/networking.tsx` ## Observed behavior JWT payload includes key material from UI token object, cookie stores that JWT, frontend decodes cookie and uses `decoded.key` as auth token. `/v2/login` also returns token in response body, increasing exposure surface ## Expected behavior Browser session token should not expose reusable API key material in client-readable JWT claims ## Impact Credential replay and key extraction risk increases from browser/session theft, logging leakage, extension compromise, and copy/paste mistakes ## Suggested remediation - Replace JWT-with-key cookie with opaque session identifier - Keep API key server-side and resolve via session lookup - Use `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and appropriate `SameSite` cookie settings - Use short TTL and rotation/invalidation policy for UI sessions - Remove key material from `/v2/login` response body where possible ## Notes Default UI key duration appears finite (commonly 24h) but configurability still leaves replay risk while token is valid ### Steps to Reproduce ## Reproduction 1. Log in to UI and obtain the auth cookie/JWT 2. Decode JWT payload and observe key-bearing claim 3. Copy cookie/JWT into a second browser/session 4. Access authenticated endpoints; session is accepted using the decoded API key from step 2 5. Reuse extracted key material in `Authorization` requests ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### What part of LiteLLM is this about? UI Dashboard ### What LiteLLM version are you on ? v1.94.0 ### Twitter / LinkedIn details https://www.linkedin.com/in/ron-zhong/

gold.rationale: The report describes a plausible credential exposure/replay vulnerability: the UI session cookie is a JWT that embeds raw API key material, which can be extracted and replayed in another session or used directly as an Authorization bearer token, and the same key is also returned in the /v2/login response body, increasing exposure. This matches the security category definition (credential exposure with plausible exploit path) and takes precedence over bug/feature framing. Given it allows credential replay/extraction affecting any UI user's session and there's no stated workaround (session duration mitigates but doesn't eliminate risk), this is high impact on confidentiality of API keys for proxy admins/users — a plausible exploit path with significant impact, warranting P0 given it could lead to full API key compromise for any logged-in user, but since it requires cookie theft (browser/session compromise) rather than being trivially exploitable remotely, and default TTL limits window, P1 is more accurate. However, guidance says security vulnerability with plausible exploit path is P0. Given the key extraction leads to reusable long-lived credentials, I'll set P0 due to severity of credential exposure. This requires maintainer judgement to confirm and remediate (security reports always need human review).

items.title: [Feature]: Add native DeepSeek V4 Flash Responses API support
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that this is not a duplicate.
- Related: #27276 and #30722 / #30910 cover the Responses-to-Chat Completions bridge and DeepSeek tool filtering. This issue is specifically about calling DeepSeek's native Responses API, not translating Responses requests to Chat Completions.

### The Feature

Please add first-class native Responses API support for the DeepSeek provider in LiteLLM, initially for `deepseek-v4-flash`.

DeepSeek's official documentation now states that:

- `deepseek-v4-flash` is currently the only DeepSeek model supported by the native Responses API;
- the API uses the base URL `https://api.deepseek.com` and the `/responses` endpoint;
- the response and streaming event format is Responses API compatible;
- `deepseek-v4-pro` is not supported by this endpoint yet.

This should be implemented as a native upstream Responses route, not as a Responses-to-Chat Completions bridge.

### Current LiteLLM gap

The DeepSeek provider currently has Chat and Messages implementations, but no dedicated native Responses implementation. The existing DeepSeek transformation targets `/chat/completions`, while the provider endpoint metadata advertises Responses support. As a result, a LiteLLM Responses call cannot preserve the native DeepSeek Responses request/response contract.

### Reproduction / expected routing

The following should call DeepSeek's native endpoint:

```python
import os
import litellm

response = litellm.responses(
    model="deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash",
    api_key=os.environ["DEEPSEEK_API_KEY"],
    api_base="https://api.deepseek.com",
    instructions="You are a helpful assistant.",
    input="Hi, how are you?",
)

print(response.output_text)
```

Expected upstream request:

```
POST https://api.deepseek.com/responses
```

with a Responses API request body, and a Responses API response object.

The request must not be rewritten to:

```
POST https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions
```

and must not rely on the generic Responses-to-Chat bridge.

### Required compatibility

Please support and test the native DeepSeek V4 Flash Responses contract, including:

1. `input` as a string and as a Responses input-item list.
2. `instructions`, `max_output_tokens`, `temperature`, `top_p`, `reasoning`, and `stream`.
3. Function tools and the DeepSeek-supported `custom` tool (`apply_patch`), plus `function_call_output` multi-turn input.
4. Native response output items, reasoning/output text, function/custom tool calls, usage fields, and the native SSE lifecycle/events such as `response.created`, `response.output_text.delta`, `response.function_call_arguments.delta`, and `response.completed`.
5. Clear model gating: support `deepseek-v4-flash`; do not claim native Responses support for `deepseek-v4-pro` until DeepSeek exposes it.
6. Sync and async SDK paths, proxy `POST /v1/responses`, streaming, error mapping, and cost/usage accounting.

Unsupported DeepSeek-specific parameters should follow the documented behavior rather than being silently transformed into Chat Completions parameters.

### References

- DeepSeek Responses API guide: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/responses_api
- DeepSeek Codex integration: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/agent_integrations/codex
- DeepSeek V4 Flash update: https://api-docs.deepseek.com/updates/
- Related bridge issue: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/27276
- Related DeepSeek filtering PR: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/30910
- Current DeepSeek provider transformation: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/litellm_internal_staging/litellm/llms/deepseek/chat/transformation.py
- Provider endpoint support metadata: https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/litellm_internal_staging/provider_endpoints_support.json

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK / Proxy / native Responses API provider translation

### LiteLLM version

Latest staging/main observed on 2026-08-03; the original gateway reproduction was on LiteLLM 1.89.3.

### Motivation, pitch

DeepSeek V4 Flash is now explicitly adapted for Codex and exposes a native Responses API. Adding a native LiteLLM provider route would let users keep LiteLLM's authentication, routing, observability, usage accounting, and proxy interface without losing DeepSeek's Responses-specific semantics or streaming events.

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified request for new provider capability (native DeepSeek Responses API support) that does not currently exist in LiteLLM - the provider only has chat/messages transformations, not a native Responses route. Per the rules, "Provider X is not supported" / new provider functionality is a feature request. There is no evidence of multiple users requesting this (single detailed requester), so it defaults to P3 despite the thorough write-up. It's a well-specified feature request that can be queued without further clarification from a maintainer - it clearly lays out scope, gating (v4-flash only), and required compatibility, so it doesn't need human judgement to route, though the decision of whether to build it is a product-direction call typically handled by maintainers triaging feature backlogs. Given it's a single, detailed, well-scoped request, needs_human can be false since it just needs queuing into the roadmap.

items.title: [Bug]: Vertex AI batch /v1/embeddings rows drop `input` and emit the chat `contents` shape
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

> Searched `is:issue` for `vertex batch embeddings`, `EmbedContentRequest`, `"no such field"`, and
> `_openai_batch_jsonl_entries_to_vertex_wrapped_requests`. No existing **issue** covers this.
>
> There is, however, an open **PR** that fixes exactly this:
> **[#35092 — fix(vertex_ai): translate /v1/embeddings batch rows to the Gemini embedding shape](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/35092)**
> (opened 2026-07-29, still open/unmerged as of filing, `Resolves LIT-4920`). I'm filing this anyway
> so the bug has a public issue to reference — PR #35092's "Relevant issues" section is empty, and
> anyone hitting this on a released version currently finds nothing when they search. Happy to close
> as soon as #35092 lands.

---
### Setup that triggers it

Submitting an embeddings batch job through the managed-files flow with a Vertex AI / Gemini
embedding model:

- `POST /v1/files` with `purpose=batch` and a JSONL file whose rows are `"url": "/v1/embeddings"`
- `POST /v1/batches` referencing that file
- Model configured as `vertex_ai/gemini-embedding-001` (any `gemini-embedding-*`)

### Expected

Each `/v1/embeddings` JSONL row should be translated into the Vertex AI embeddings batch-prediction
shape, carrying the row's `body.input` text through to Vertex.

### Actual

Every row — regardless of its `url` — is translated as if it were a **chat completions** request.
`_openai_batch_jsonl_entries_to_vertex_wrapped_requests()` reads `body["messages"]`, which does not
exist on an embeddings row, so it gets `[]`. The empty-messages defensive fallback then substitutes a
single blank content block, and **the actual `input` text is discarded entirely.**

Given this input row:

```json
{"custom_id": "req-1", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/embeddings",
 "body": {"model": "gemini-embedding-001", "input": "PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT"}}
```

LiteLLM emits, verbatim:

```json
{"request": {"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": " "}]}], "labels": {"litellm_custom_id": "req-1", "litellm_custom_id_raw": "b32_ojsxcljr"}}}
```

`PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT` appears nowhere in the output. It has been replaced by `" "`.

There are two independent defects visible in that one line:

1. **`input` is dropped.** The text to be embedded never reaches Vertex.
2. **The shape is wrong.** `contents`/`parts` is the `generateContent` (chat) shape. Vertex's
   embeddings batch request is `EmbedContentRequest`, which has **no `contents` field** — and no
   `labels` field either, so the `custom_id` smuggling would be the next failure even after fixing
   `contents`.

The only runtime signal on LiteLLM's side is a `WARNING`-level log line (full text in §4), which
explicitly says it is masking the problem rather than surfacing it:

> `Setting an empty content to prevent an 400 error.`

### Downstream effect, and how the failure is masked

Per the live Vertex AI runs documented in PR #35092 (real project in `us-central1`, real GCS bucket,
no mocks), the malformed row is **rejected** by Vertex per-row:

```json
{"custom_id": "req-1", "response": null,
 "error": {"code": "vertex_ai_error", "message": "... EmbedContentRequest ... no such field: 'contents'"}}
```

The masking is at the **job** level: the enclosing batch still reports `"status": "completed"` with
`"errors": null` even though every single row failed. So a caller polling `GET /v1/batches/<id>` and
checking job status sees a clean success, and only discovers the total failure if they parse the
output file row by row.

### Scope notes — what was and wasn't tested

**Tested by me (reproduced, v1.89.1):** the transformation-level `input` drop, via a direct call
into the vendored transformer. This needs no GCP credentials and is the repro in §3. I also
confirmed the equivalent chat-completions row round-trips correctly, isolating the defect to the
embeddings path rather than a general transformation failure.

**Not tested by me:** I did **not** run this against live Vertex AI. The per-row
`no such field: 'contents'` rejection and the `completed`/`errors: null` job-level masking described
above are from PR #35092's live runs, not my own observation. I'm citing them rather than claiming
them.

**Confirmed unaffected — live/synchronous embeddings.** This is isolated to the managed-files batch
path. Ordinary `/v1/embeddings` calls are fine, because they run through structurally separate code
that never touches the batch-files transformer:

- `vertex_ai/*` models → `vertex_embeddings/embedding_handler.py::VertexEmbedding.embedding()`,
  which calls `transform_openai_request_to_vertex_embedding_request(input=input, ...)` and POSTs
  directly to `:predict`. `input` flows straight through.
- `gemini/*` models, and `vertex_ai/*` models flagged `uses_embed_content=True` →
  `gemini_embeddings/batch_embed_content_handler.py::GoogleBatchEmbeddings.batch_embeddings()`.
  (Despite the name this is synchronous `:batchEmbedContents` — batching several texts into one HTTP
  call — not the async `/v1/batches` job API.) `input` flows straight through here too.

`grep -rn "GoogleBatchEmbeddings\|batch_embed_content_handler\|VertexEmbedding\b" litellm/proxy/ litellm/batches/ litellm/files/`
returns zero matches, i.e. the batch/files route handlers never delegate to either live handler.
This is consistent with the bug going unnoticed: people are using live embeddings successfully, and
that says nothing about the batch path.

### Steps to Reproduce

The defect is in a pure transformation function, so it reproduces with no proxy, no GCP project, and
no credentials.

**1. Install the affected version**

```bash
pip install litellm==1.89.1
```

**2. Run the embeddings row through the Vertex batch-files transformer**

```python
import json
from litellm.llms.vertex_ai.files.transformation import VertexAIJsonlFilesTransformation

t = VertexAIJsonlFilesTransformation()

row = {
    "custom_id": "req-1",
    "method": "POST",
    "url": "/v1/embeddings",
    "body": {"model": "gemini-embedding-001", "input": "PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT"},
}

out = t._transform_openai_jsonl_content_to_vertex_ai_jsonl_content([row])
print("OUTPUT:", json.dumps(out[0]))
print("SENTINEL PRESENT:", "PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT" in json.dumps(out[0]))
```

**3. Observe** — a `WARNING` is logged, the output carries the chat `contents`/`parts` shape instead
of an `EmbedContentRequest`, and the input text is gone:

```
OUTPUT: {"request": {"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": " "}]}], "labels": {"litellm_custom_id": "req-1", "litellm_custom_id_raw": "b32_ojsxcljr"}}}
SENTINEL PRESENT: False
```

- **Expected:** an `EmbedContentRequest`-shaped row containing `PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT`.
- **Observed:** a `generateContent`-shaped row containing `" "`. `SENTINEL PRESENT: False`.

**4. Control step — change only the row's `url` and `body` to the chat shape and repeat.** This
isolates the cause to the embeddings path:

```python
row = {
    "custom_id": "req-2",
    "method": "POST",
    "url": "/v1/chat/completions",
    "body": {"model": "gemini-2.0-flash-001",
             "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT"}]},
}
out = t._transform_openai_jsonl_content_to_vertex_ai_jsonl_content([row])
print("OUTPUT:", json.dumps(out[0]))
print("SENTINEL PRESENT:", "PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT" in json.dumps(out[0]))
```

Result — no warning, and the text survives:

```
OUTPUT: {"request": {"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT"}]}], "labels": {"litellm_custom_id": "req-2", "litellm_custom_id_raw": "b32_pe"}}}
SENTINEL PRESENT: True
```

So the transformer is not broken in general — it silently mishandles exactly the rows whose `url` is
`/v1/embeddings`.

**5. (Optional) End-to-end through the proxy**, if you have a Vertex project. Config:

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: gemini-embedding-001
    litellm_params:
      model: vertex_ai/gemini-embedding-001
      vertex_project: os.environ/VERTEX_PROJECT
      vertex_location: us-central1
```

`batch_embeddings.jsonl`:

```json
{"custom_id": "req-1", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/embeddings", "body": {"model": "gemini-embedding-001", "input": "hello world from litellm batch"}}
```

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/v1/files \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-1234" \
  -F purpose=batch -F 'model=gemini-embedding-001' \
  -F file=@batch_embeddings.jsonl
# then POST /v1/batches with the returned file id
```

Per PR #35092's live runs the job reports `"status": "completed"` / `"errors": null` while every row
in the output file carries the `no such field: 'contents'` error.

---

### Relevant log output

```shell
# Step 2 above — the embeddings row. The warning is the ONLY runtime signal, and it
# states outright that it is masking the problem instead of raising.
12:59:59 - LiteLLM:WARNING: transformation.py:1088 -
                No contents in messages. Contents are required. See
                https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/reference/rest/v1/projects.locations.publishers.models/generateContent#request-body.
                If the original request did not comply to OpenAI API requirements it should have failed by now,
                but LiteLLM does not check for missing messages.
                Setting an empty content to prevent an 400 error.
                Relevant Issue - https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/9733

# The emitted Vertex row. Note: shape is `contents`/`parts` (generateContent), NOT an
# EmbedContentRequest; and the input text has become " ".
EMBEDDINGS_ROW_OUTPUT: {"request": {"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": " "}]}], "labels": {"litellm_custom_id": "req-1", "litellm_custom_id_raw": "b32_ojsxcljr"}}}
SENTINEL_PRESENT: False

# Control: the same transformer on a /v1/chat/completions row. No warning, text preserved.
CHAT_ROW_OUTPUT: {"request": {"contents": [{"role": "user", "parts": [{"text": "PROOF_SENTINEL_TEXT"}]}], "labels": {"litellm_custom_id": "req-2", "litellm_custom_id_raw": "b32_pe"}}}
SENTINEL_PRESENT: True

# Downstream, from PR #35092's live Vertex AI runs (NOT observed by me): the malformed
# row is rejected per-row, while the enclosing batch still reports success.
{"custom_id": "req-1", "response": null, "error": {"code": "vertex_ai_error", "message": "... EmbedContentRequest ... no such field: 'contents'"}}
# ...yet: GET /v1/batches/<id>  ->  "status": "completed", "errors": null
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK (litellm Python package)

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.89.1

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a clear, well-reproduced bug: the Vertex AI batch-files transformer treats /v1/embeddings JSONL rows as chat completions, dropping the actual input text and emitting the wrong request shape (contents/parts instead of EmbedContentRequest), and adding an invalid `labels` field. This causes every row in an embeddings batch job to fail on Vertex AI, while the enclosing batch job silently reports "completed" with no errors, masking total failure. This affects the Vertex AI batch embeddings path broadly (any gemini-embedding-* model), with no workaround for the batch/files flow (live sync embeddings are unaffected, but that's a separate path). There's already a fix PR open (#35092) referenced, meaning this is a confirmed, reproducible defect needing to be tracked/merged rather than requiring open-ended investigation. Given the widely-used Vertex AI provider is affected for a core capability (batch embeddings) with silent failure masking (job reports success despite total row failure), and no workaround exists in the batch path, this warrants P1 severity. Since a fix already exists in an open PR and the bug is well understood with clear reproduction, a maintainer mainly needs to review/merge it, but because it's P1 impacting silent failures with misleading job status, it should still get human attention to confirm merge state and any residual scope.

items.title: [Security]: Responses ID security fails open for raw or ownerless response IDs
items.body:
### Summary

The Responses ID security hook only checks ownership when an ID can be decrypted into an encrypted LiteLLM response ID with nonempty owner metadata. Raw IDs and IDs returned unchanged after encryption setup fails bypass the ownership check, and an encrypted ID with empty user and team fields is accepted for every non-admin key

### Current behavior

The pre-call hook calls `check_user_access_to_response_id()` only when `_is_encrypted_response_id()` returns `True`. If decryption fails or the ID is not in the expected managed format, the hook forwards the ID without an ownership check

When `LITELLM_SALT_KEY` and `master_key` are both absent, `_encrypt_response_id()` logs at debug level and returns the provider response unchanged. This means a deployment with the security feature enabled can still return a raw response ID and later skip the security hook

The encrypted ID includes `user_api_key_dict.user_id or ""` and `team_id or ""`. The checker only rejects when either decoded field is truthy and differs from the caller. If both are empty, the function returns `True` for any non-admin caller

### Reproduction

The missing-key path can be exercised with `disable_responses_id_security` left at its default `False`, no `LITELLM_SALT_KEY`, and no `master_key`:

1. Make a successful Responses API request
2. Observe that the response ID is returned in its provider form because `_encrypt_response_id()` skipped encryption
3. Use a different valid LiteLLM key to retrieve, cancel, or list input items for that ID
4. The pre-call hook treats the raw ID as not encrypted and forwards it

The ownerless path can be tested directly:

~~~python
assert hook.check_user_access_to_response_id(
    response_id_user_id="",
    response_id_team_id="",
    user_api_key_dict=another_valid_key,
)
~~~

The assertion succeeds for a non-admin key even though no ownership relation was established

### Impact

A valid LiteLLM key can access another tenant's Responses API object when the provider ID is known or exposed, subject to the provider credential and endpoint behavior. Missing encryption configuration silently downgrades the feature from an ownership check to pass-through behavior

The security setting is enabled by default, so missing signing-key configuration should not silently disable its core guarantee

### Expected behavior

Fail startup or fail the Responses request when response ID security is enabled but no signing key is available. Every accepted response ID should have a verifiable ownership binding, or the proxy should perform a server-side ownership lookup for raw provider IDs

Treat an encrypted ID with no user and no team owner as invalid unless an explicit administrative or system path is being used

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, pre-call ID type gate
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `check_user_access_to_response_id`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `_encrypt_response_id`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/responses_id_security.py`, `_get_signing_key`

gold.rationale: This report describes a security control (Responses ID ownership security) that fails open under multiple conditions: raw/ownerless IDs bypass ownership checks, missing signing key silently disables encryption, and empty owner metadata is treated as accessible by any non-admin key. This is an auth/access-control bypass allowing cross-tenant access to another user's Responses API objects, with a plausible exploit path (a valid key can access another tenant's response by guessing/knowing the ID). This clearly matches the security category, taking precedence over bug/feature framing. Given it's enabled by default and affects a core security guarantee of the proxy for all users of the Responses API security feature, this is P0 - broken security control for most users on current release with no full workaround (feature is enabled by default and silently degrades). This requires maintainer judgement to assess exploit path, verify claims, and decide the fix approach (fail-closed behavior), so needs_human is true.

items.title: [Security]: Cached proxy-admin keys bypass blocked-key checks
items.body:
### Summary

A cached key whose role is `PROXY_ADMIN` returns from `user_api_key_auth()` before the normal `blocked` check. A stale local cache entry on another worker can therefore continue to authenticate after the key has been blocked in the database

### Current behavior

After loading a cached `UserAPIKeyAuth`, the proxy has a privileged early return for proxy-admin keys. That path checks expiration and updates request context, but it does not check `valid_token.blocked`

The ordinary non-admin path checks `valid_token.blocked` later

`block_key()` updates the database and attempts to delete the key from the local cache and the shared cache. The invalidation is not guaranteed to synchronously remove a stale entry from every worker. A worker that still serves the old cached admin object reaches the privileged early return and never consults the database

### Reproduction

Use two proxy workers with a shared database and cache:

1. Authenticate an admin key through worker B so its local cache contains `blocked=False`
2. Block the key through the management API or directly in the database
3. Make another request with the same key through worker B before its local cache refreshes
4. Observe that the request passes the admin early-return path, while a normal key would reach the blocked-key check

A focused test can construct a cached `UserAPIKeyAuth(user_role=PROXY_ADMIN, blocked=False)`, make the shared cache miss or stale, and assert that `user_api_key_auth()` does not authorize the key after an authoritative blocked record is present

### Impact

Blocking an admin key is not an immediate revocation guarantee across workers. The stale key can continue to access management and model routes for the cache lifetime or until invalidation succeeds

### Expected behavior

Run the blocked-key check before any privileged early return. For proxy-admin keys, either revalidate the blocked state against the database on every request or use a revocation version or generation that can be checked across workers without trusting the stale object

Add a multi-worker cache invalidation test that blocks a warmed admin key and verifies the next request is rejected

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, cached `PROXY_ADMIN` early return
- `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py`, normal blocked-key check
- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `_delete_cache_key_object`

gold.rationale: This is an authentication/authorization bypass: a blocked admin key can continue to authenticate and access privileged routes across workers due to a cache invalidation race condition. This is an auth bypass with a plausible exploit path (revoked/blocked admin credentials remain valid), which falls squarely under security per the rules, taking precedence over bug framing. Given it affects privileged admin access control and can allow continued unauthorized access after a key is explicitly blocked, this is a serious security issue affecting the core auth path shared by all proxy deployments with multiple workers - a widely used deployment pattern. There's no stated workaround, and it undermines a core security guarantee (revocation). This warrants P0 given the plausible exploit path and impact on privilege revocation guarantees, though it requires cache staleness/timing rather than being trivially exploitable, so P1 might also be reasonable — but since it's an auth bypass on admin-level keys with no workaround, treating as P0 is justified per the security modifier rules. Security issues always need human judgement to assess exploitability and design the correct fix (e.g., whether to add revalidation or versioning).

items.title: [Security]: JWT team_id_upsert creates arbitrary teams through a proxy-admin principal
items.body:
### Summary

When JWT authentication has `team_id_upsert` enabled, a signed JWT containing a team ID that is absent from the database can cause the proxy to create that team during request authentication. The upsert calls the normal team-creation endpoint with a synthetic `PROXY_ADMIN` principal

### Current behavior

`_get_team_db_check()` does the following when the team lookup returns no row:

~~~python
new_team_data = NewTeamRequest(team_id=team_id)
system_admin_user = UserAPIKeyAuth(user_role=LitellmUserRoles.PROXY_ADMIN)

created_team_dict = await new_team(
    data=new_team_data,
    http_request=mock_request,
    user_api_key_dict=system_admin_user,
)
~~~

The normal `new_team()` endpoint then skips non-admin team-limit checks and runs the creation flow as a proxy admin. The synthetic principal has no user ID and is not constrained to a pre-existing membership or team allowlist

The option defaults to `False`, but it is passed through the JWT team-claim resolution paths when enabled. Current hardening for provisional `x-litellm-team-id` headers does not remove this behavior for a genuine team claim in a signed JWT

### Reproduction

Configure JWT auth with team upsert enabled:

~~~yaml
general_settings:
  enable_jwt_auth: true
  litellm_jwtauth:
    team_id_jwt_field: tenant_id
    team_id_upsert: true
~~~

Use a valid token issued by the configured identity provider whose `tenant_id` is a previously nonexistent value such as `tenant-created-by-claim`. Send a normal model request. The authentication flow calls `_get_team_db_check()`, the team row is created through `new_team()`, and subsequent requests find the newly created team

The direct unit-level reproduction is to mock `TeamRepository.table.find_unique()` to return `None`, call `_get_team_db_check(..., team_id_upsert=True)`, and assert that `new_team()` receives `UserAPIKeyAuth(user_role=PROXY_ADMIN)`

### Impact

Any trusted identity-provider principal whose team or tenant claim is not constrained to an existing LiteLLM team can create rows and obtain a default team policy during ordinary authentication. This can cause team-row exhaustion and can turn an unprovisioned claim into an accepted team context

The JWT must still be valid and signed. This is an authorization and provisioning-boundary issue, not a JWT signature-forgery issue

### Expected behavior

Prefer requiring team IDs to be pre-provisioned and validating the claim against an explicit allowlist or membership mapping. If automatic provisioning is required, use a narrowly scoped provisioning path with bounded claims, safe default policy, audit metadata, and no broad proxy-admin authorization context

Add an integration test for a valid signed JWT with an unknown team claim and assert the configured policy for unknown teams, including whether the request is rejected or a restricted team is created

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `_get_team_db_check`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/handle_jwt.py`, JWT team resolution calls
- `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/team_endpoints.py`, `new_team`
- `litellm/proxy/_types.py`, `LiteLLM_JWTAuth.team_id_upsert`

gold.rationale: This report describes an authorization/provisioning-boundary flaw: when JWT auth has team_id_upsert enabled, a valid JWT with an unrecognized team claim triggers automatic team creation using a synthetic PROXY_ADMIN principal, bypassing normal team-creation authorization checks. This is a plausible exploit path (unprovisioned claim escalating to team creation with admin context), not just a bug or feature gap, so it falls under security per the category rules (takes precedence over bug/feature framing). Given it requires a valid signed JWT (not a bypass of auth entirely) but can lead to unauthorized resource creation and potential team-row exhaustion / policy abuse, and the option defaults to False (limiting exposure to those who enabled it), this is serious but not a full P0 (no default-on broad exploit, requires specific config). It fits P1: a significant authorization boundary violation affecting a security-sensitive path with no easy workaround other than disabling the feature. Security issues always require maintainer judgement, so needs_human is true.

items.title: [Security]: Raw provider file IDs bypass managed-file ownership checks
items.body:
### Summary

The files retrieve, content, and delete endpoints enforce LiteLLM API-key authentication but do not enforce tenant ownership for raw provider file IDs. Managed unified IDs go through the managed-file hook, while any other provider file ID is forwarded to the provider using the current team's or shared provider credentials

### Current behavior

In `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`:

- Unified managed IDs are routed through `ManagedFileRepository` and the managed-file hook
- Raw cloud-storage URIs are rejected
- Other raw IDs take the fallback branch, call `apply_team_provider_credentials()`, and invoke `litellm.afile_retrieve()`, `litellm.afile_content()`, or `litellm.afile_delete()`
- `validate_managed_files_requirement()` is currently used on the upload path and does not make retrieve, content, or delete reject raw provider IDs

If multiple tenants use the same provider account, knowledge of another tenant's provider file ID is enough to make the proxy ask the provider for that object under shared credentials. The provider may authorize the operation because it sees the shared account, not the LiteLLM tenant

### Reproduction

Use two LiteLLM teams that share provider credentials and a provider that accepts raw file IDs

1. Have team A create or otherwise obtain a provider file ID such as `file-abc123`
2. Authenticate as team B
3. Request `/v1/files/file-abc123`, `/v1/files/file-abc123/content`, and `DELETE /v1/files/file-abc123`
4. In a unit test, mock the three `litellm.afile_*` methods and assert that the raw ID reaches them without a managed-file ownership lookup

The same behavior applies when the raw ID is supplied through the provider-prefixed routes

### Impact

This can expose or delete another tenant's provider-backed file when provider credentials are shared across tenants. The attacker needs a valid LiteLLM key and a file ID, but the proxy's tenant boundary is not applied to this compatibility path

Related issues [#33989](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/33989) and [#28294](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/28294) discuss raw output file IDs from managed batch flows. They do not cover the generic files retrieve, content, and delete routes described here

### Expected behavior

Require a managed-file registration before retrieving, streaming, or deleting a file when multi-tenant isolation is enabled. Alternatively, make raw provider IDs an explicit compatibility opt-in and document that they are not tenant-isolated

The ownership check should cover all three operations, not only upload

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`, `get_file_content`
- `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`, `get_file`
- `litellm/proxy/openai_files_endpoints/files_endpoints.py`, `delete_file`

gold.rationale: This report describes a plausible cross-tenant authorization bypass: raw provider file IDs skip the managed-file ownership check, allowing one tenant to retrieve, stream, or delete another tenant's files when provider credentials are shared. This is a security/auth-bypass class issue with a real exploit path, so it takes precedence as 'security' per the rules. Given multi-tenant deployments sharing provider credentials are common and the affected code is core to the shared files endpoint path (retrieve/content/delete), and there's a plausible exploit with no workaround mentioned other than not sharing credentials, this warrants high urgency. It affects a shared core path (files endpoints used across providers) so severity is elevated, but exploit requires specific setup (shared credentials across tenants) narrowing broad impact slightly — still, data exposure/deletion of arbitrary tenant data is severe → P0/P1. Security issues always require human judgement per the rules.

items.title: [Security]: End-user budget checks fail open on database lookup errors
items.body:
### Summary

A database error while loading an end-user object is converted into `None`, which is indistinguishable from an end user that was not found. The centralized authorization path then omits the end-user budget check

### Current behavior

`get_end_user_object()` catches a broad `Exception` and returns `None`

The common-check construction only adds `_check_end_user_budget()` when an end-user object with a budget is available. When the lookup failed because the database was unavailable, the result is the same as the not-found case and no budget check runs

This is separate from failures while reading a spend counter. The `fail_closed_budget_enforcement` setting cannot restore a check that was removed because object lookup returned `None`

### Reproduction

Create an end-user row with a positive `max_budget`, then inject a repository failure:

~~~python
from unittest.mock import AsyncMock, patch

with patch(
    "litellm.proxy.auth.auth_checks.EndUserRepository.table.find_unique",
    new=AsyncMock(side_effect=RuntimeError("database unavailable")),
):
    end_user = await get_end_user_object(
        end_user_id="existing-end-user",
        prisma_client=prisma_client,
        user_api_key_cache=user_api_key_cache,
        proxy_logging_obj=proxy_logging_obj,
    )
    assert end_user is None
~~~

Run the normal common-check path for the same request. Since the object is `None`, `_check_end_user_budget()` is not scheduled. A request can proceed even though the configured end-user budget could not be evaluated

### Impact

A transient database outage or repository exception can disable budget enforcement for requests attributed to affected end users. Repeated traffic can continue until the lookup succeeds again, and the failure is logged as a generic lookup failure rather than a policy denial

A genuinely missing end user may still be intentionally treated as unbudgeted, so the fix needs to distinguish not-found from infrastructure failure

### Expected behavior

Return a typed not-found result separately from a database or cache error. Infrastructure errors should either fail the request closed when a budgeted end user is expected, or use a clearly documented fallback that cannot silently remove the budget check

Add a test that makes `find_unique()` raise and asserts the request is denied or the error is surfaced instead of treating the user as absent

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, `get_end_user_object`
- `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_checks.py`, centralized common-check construction

gold.rationale: A database/repository failure during end-user lookup is silently coerced to None, causing the centralized common-check path to skip the end-user budget check entirely. This is an unsafe default (fail-open) that allows budget enforcement to be bypassed under transient infrastructure failures, which is a plausible exploit/impact path (unbounded spend during outages) — this fits the security category due to the fail-open safety-critical behavior, taking precedence over classifying it as a plain bug. The issue affects the shared core auth/budget-enforcement path used by all proxy deployments with end-user budgets, so it's a widely applicable fail-open risk, but requires no active exploit chain beyond triggering a transient DB error, and there's a reasonable workaround (monitor/alert on DB failures) though not clearly stated by the reporter. Given it's a security fail-open on a shared core path affecting budget enforcement broadly, it warrants urgent maintainer attention to decide the correct closed-fail semantics and to distinguish not-found vs error cases carefully — this requires product/security judgement, so needs_human is true.

items.title: [Security]: Enabled drain endpoint accepts requests when no token is configured
items.body:
### Summary

Enabling the graceful drain endpoint without configuring a drain token makes `/health/drain` callable by any network-reachable client. A successful call starts process-wide shutdown and takes the worker out of rotation

### Current behavior

`health_drain()` intentionally does not use `user_api_key_auth` because Kubernetes `preStop` hooks commonly do not have proxy credentials

`_authorize_drain_request()` returns immediately when neither `general_settings.drain_endpoint_token` nor `DRAIN_ENDPOINT_TOKEN` is set:

~~~python
expected = _drain_endpoint_token()
if expected is None:
    return
~~~

The endpoint is therefore protected only by `enable_drain_endpoint`

### Reproduction

Enable the endpoint and omit the token:

~~~yaml
general_settings:
  enable_drain_endpoint: true
  # drain_endpoint_token is omitted
~~~

Then call it without credentials:

~~~bash
curl -i http://localhost:4000/health/drain
~~~

The request reaches `GracefulShutdownManager.start_shutdown()`, waits for the worker to drain, and causes readiness to fail until the process restarts. The endpoint is expected to be a `GET` route and may hold the client connection while draining

### Impact

Any caller able to reach the health port can trigger denial of service or repeatedly drain workers. This includes a misconfigured load balancer, a shared cluster network, or an internal service that can make arbitrary HTTP requests

The feature is disabled by default, which limits exposure, but the unsafe behavior begins as soon as an operator enables it without also configuring a secret

### Expected behavior

Fail closed when `enable_drain_endpoint` is true and no token is configured, preferably at startup or with a 401 response. If unauthenticated drain is required for a controlled environment, it should be an explicit separate opt-in rather than the implicit behavior of a missing secret

The deployment documentation and health probe examples should make the token requirement unavoidable

### Source

- `litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, `_drain_endpoint_token`
- `litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, `_authorize_drain_request`
- `litellm/proxy/health_endpoints/_health_endpoints.py`, `health_drain`

gold.rationale: The drain endpoint intentionally bypasses standard auth to support Kubernetes preStop hooks, but when enable_drain_endpoint is true and no token is configured, the code silently allows unauthenticated access rather than failing closed. This is an unsafe default that any network-reachable client can exploit to trigger denial of service (repeated shutdown/drain of workers), fitting the security category (unsafe default with plausible exploit path). It requires maintainer judgement on the right remediation approach (fail closed at startup vs 401, doc changes), and is a security issue so needs_human is true per rules. Impact is limited since the feature is opt-in and disabled by default, and a trivial workaround exists (just set the token), but once enabled it can cause real DoS to a proxy's health-checking path, affecting production availability. Given it's opt-in and requires misconfiguration, but the security nature and potential impact to production combined with "requires judgement" push to at least P1, and per rules any security report defaults needs_human=true.

items.title: Per-request x-mcp-{server_alias}-authorization header not applied to MCP server auth resolution (resolves as no-auth)
items.body:
**Environment**: litellm 1.81.14 (proxy), MCP server registered with no static `auth_type`/`auth_value`/`static_headers` — relying entirely on per-request client headers (the documented alternative to a shared static credential).

**Config**:
```yaml
mcp_servers:
  myserver:
    url: "http://internal-host:9099/mcp"
    transport: "http"
```

**Repro**: `POST /mcp/` a `tools/list` request with header `x-mcp-myserver-authorization: Bearer <token>`.

**Expected**: LiteLLM forwards `Authorization: Bearer <token>` to the upstream server. With `x-litellm-mcp-debug: true` set, the response should include `x-mcp-debug-auth-resolution: per-request-header`.

**Actual**: `x-mcp-debug-auth-resolution: no-auth`. The upstream MCP server receives no valid `Authorization` header at all (confirmed via a 401 from the upstream server's own access logs, captured at the same timestamp as the LiteLLM request). Because of this, any tool call that needs the caller's real per-user identity fails to resolve one — `tools/list` alone appears to "succeed" only because it doesn't require a valid identity to return tool schemas.

**Investigation notes**: Traced through `mcp_server_manager.py`:
- `server.server_name` correctly resolves to `"myserver"` (the YAML key), matching what `_get_mcp_server_auth_headers_from_headers()` parses from the request header (`x-mcp-{prefix}-authorization` → `server_alias="myserver"`).
- The lookup in `list_tools()`'s `_fetch_server_tools()` — `mcp_server_auth_headers.get(server.alias) or mcp_server_auth_headers.get(server.server_name)` — should match on the `server_name` fallback given the above, but `MCPDebug.resolve_auth_resolution()` still reports `no-auth`, meaning `mcp_server_auth_headers` was empty/falsy by the time resolution happens for this server, despite the header apparently being sent and named correctly per the documented `x-mcp-{server_alias}-{header_name}` format.

Happy to provide more detail/logs if useful — found this while integrating an internal MCP server behind the LiteLLM MCP gateway specifically to support per-user auth without a shared static credential.

gold.rationale: The MCP gateway's documented behavior is that per-request headers of the form x-mcp-{server_alias}-authorization should be forwarded to the upstream server when no static auth is configured. The reporter has traced through the code (mcp_server_manager.py, _fetch_server_tools, MCPDebug.resolve_auth_resolution) and shown that the alias/server_name matching logic appears correct but mcp_server_auth_headers is empty by the time resolution occurs, causing auth to silently resolve as no-auth and the upstream call to fail with 401. This is a clear violation of documented/intended behavior (a bug), not a missing feature or docs issue, since the mechanism exists but doesn't work as designed. This affects any deployment relying on per-user/per-request MCP auth without a static credential — a documented and presumably common pattern for MCP gateway usage, and it silently fails (no error surfaced, tools/list appears to succeed) which is dangerous. This impacts the MCP proxy path broadly for anyone using per-request auth headers instead of static credentials, which is likely to affect many self-hosted MCP integrations. No workaround is stated by the reporter other than falling back to static shared credentials (which defeats the purpose of per-user identity). Given it silently breaks a documented auth path with no clear workaround, and requires maintainer investigation to confirm root cause (looks like a header-parsing/threading bug where mcp_server_auth_headers isn't populated by the time it's checked), this needs human judgement to confirm and diagnose.
