items.title: [Feature]: Option to override client-supplied 'user' field with authenticated user_id
items.body:
## The Feature

Add a config option (e.g. `general_settings.override_user_param: true`) that makes the proxy always set `data["user"]` to the authenticated `user_api_key_dict.user_id`, ignoring any client-supplied value.

Currently, `proxy_server.py` only sets `data["user"]` when the client doesn't provide it:

```python
# users can pass in 'user' param to /chat/completions. Don't override it
if data.get("user", None) is None and user_api_key_dict.user_id is not None:
    data["user"] = user_api_key_dict.user_id
```

This is correct for deployments where a service account makes requests on behalf of multiple end users (the client is trusted to set `user`). But in deployments where LiteLLM is the authentication boundary, the client-supplied `user` should not be trusted; the proxy should override it with the identity it authenticated.

## Motivation

In multi-gateway corporate environments, there are typically multiple layers of LLM gateways. When LiteLLM handles end-user authentication (via API keys or JWT), the downstream gateway needs to know the authenticated identity for per-user rate limiting, budget enforcement, and audit logging. The `user` field in the OpenAI spec is the natural carrier for this, and LiteLLM already translates it across providers (e.g. Anthropic's `metadata.user_id`).

Today there's no way to prevent a client from spoofing the `user` field when LiteLLM is the auth boundary. A client authenticating as "alice" could send `"user": "bob"` and the downstream gateway would rate limit "bob" instead of "alice".

The three deployment patterns and their desired behavior:

1. LiteLLM authenticates end users -> override `user` with authenticated identity (needs this feature)
2. App-to-app auth, client sets user info -> passthrough (current default, no change)
3. No auth, passthrough -> passthrough (current default, no change)

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified request for new configurable behavior (proxy currently never overrides client-supplied 'user'; feature asks to add an option to override it with authenticated user_id). This is a feature request, not a bug, since current behavior is intentional per code comment. It has security motivation (prevents user spoofing in multi-gateway auth boundary scenarios) but is framed as an opt-in feature/config option rather than a vulnerability report demanding immediate fix - default behavior remains unchanged, so it doesn't meet the security category bar of an unsafe default with exploit. It's a single requester with a detailed write-up but no evidenced corroborating demand from others, so default P3. This is a product-direction decision about whether to add a new auth-boundary config option, requiring maintainer judgement on design and security implications.

items.title: [Bug]: spend rows popped from the queue are lost when a flush is cancelled
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

Spend rows are removed from the in-memory queue before the database write is
awaited, so any cancellation of a flush loses them permanently. There is no
requeue and no shielding.

`update_spend_logs_job` pops the batch under `_spend_log_transactions_lock` and
reassigns the remainder (litellm/proxy/utils.py:5549-5554), then awaits
`ProxyUpdateSpend.update_spend_logs`. If that await is cancelled or fails, the
rows are gone: the handler carries an explicit
`except Exception:  # Logs already removed from queue at start - don't put them back`
(litellm/proxy/utils.py:5420), and `asyncio.CancelledError` is not an `Exception`
subclass, so a cancellation is not even logged there.

Two live cancellation paths reach this code:

1. `scheduler.shutdown()` -- apscheduler's `AsyncIOExecutor.shutdown()` states in
   its own source that it cannot honor `wait=True` and cancels pending job
   coroutines, so a mid-flight `update_spend` run is aborted.
2. `_monitor_spend_logs_queue` is started as a bare `asyncio.create_task`
   (litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py:8042) with no reference kept, so nothing can
   await or stop it; it polls every `SPEND_LOG_QUEUE_POLL_INTERVAL` (2.0s) and
   pops through the same path.

Because writes go out in `BATCH_SIZE = 1000` chunks inside a batch of up to
10000 (litellm/proxy/utils.py:5356), a cancellation can also land after some
chunks are committed, leaving the batch partially written.

Expected: a cancelled or failed flush either commits or leaves the rows
recoverable.
Actual: the popped batch is discarded silently.

This is a data-integrity race, not attacker-controlled: `proxy_shutdown_event`
is reachable only from the FastAPI lifespan
(litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py:1179), so no request path can influence the
timing.

Note on why the obvious fixes do not work -- each was tested:

- Cancelling the monitor task before a final drain makes it worse. The drain's
  own awaits give a surviving monitor time to finish its write; cancelling it
  destroys the batch it already popped. Measured: 0 rows lost when left alone
  versus all 9 lost when cancelled.
- `asyncio.shield` around the flush is not sufficient on its own. The
  `wait_for` timeout returns, shutdown proceeds to `prisma_client.disconnect()`,
  and the shielded write then fails against a closed engine. It only helps if
  the shielded task is also awaited before the disconnect.
- Requeue-on-cancel is unsafe as-is. Replay is idempotent for
  `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` itself (`request_id` is `@id` and the insert uses
  `create_many(..., skip_duplicates=True)`, litellm/proxy/utils.py:5701), but
  `update_spend_logs_job` also runs `process_spend_logs_guardrail_usage`, which
  upserts `DailyGuardrailMetrics` with `{"increment": n}` per key
  (litellm/proxy/guardrails/usage_tracking.py:164) against
  `@@id([guardrail_id, date])`. A cancellation mid-loop followed by a replay
  double-counts the keys already applied. The `SPEND_LOGS_URL` branch
  (litellm/proxy/utils.py:5377-5387) posts with no dedup at all, and the
  aggregate spend paths use `{"increment": response_cost}` against destructively
  drained queues. So a naive requeue turns a bounded, logged under-count into a
  silent over-count on billing-adjacent aggregates.

A correct fix therefore needs both halves: shield the write and await it before
the engine is torn down, and add idempotency to the non-idempotent follow-on
aggregates. That is a change to the spend-writer contract across several
modules.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the proxy with a database and spend tracking enabled so the
   `update_spend` scheduler job and the spend-logs queue monitor are active.

2. Drive enough traffic that `prisma_client.spend_log_transactions` holds a
   batch, then cancel a flush while it is mid-write -- in practice, send SIGTERM
   so `scheduler.shutdown()` cancels the in-flight job:

   ```bash
   curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..." \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'

   kill -TERM $(pgrep -f "litellm --port 4000")
   ```

3. Count what reached the database:

   ```sql
   SELECT count(*) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE "startTime" > now() - interval '5 minutes';
   ```

4. Rows belonging to the batch that was popped but not yet committed are absent,
   and nothing in the logs reports them as dropped.


### Relevant log output

```shell

```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.94.0-rc.3

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented data-integrity bug: spend log rows are popped from the in-memory queue before the DB write is awaited, and cancellation (via scheduler shutdown or an unmanaged monitor task) results in silent, permanent loss of spend rows with no requeue/shielding. The code does not behave as documented/expected (spend should be durably persisted), qualifying as a bug rather than a feature or docs issue. It's not security since there's no attacker-controlled exploit path—only a shutdown-timing race. This affects the shared spend-logging path used by all proxy deployments with DB-backed spend tracking, which is a core/widely-used path, and results in silent data loss (billing-adjacent) with no workaround (the reporter explicitly showed the "obvious fixes" don't work). That warrants raising urgency above baseline; given it's data loss on a core path affecting most DB-enabled proxy deployments during any restart/SIGTERM, it fits P0/P1. Since it's not exploitable and requires a shutdown timing rather than constant breakage, and there's no simple workaround, but it does affect nearly all users with spend tracking on any restart — treat as P1 (major, core-path broken across restarts) rather than P0. This requires maintainer judgement: the issue explicitly explains why naive fixes (shield alone, requeue alone) don't work and require coordinated changes across several modules (idempotency in guardrail usage tracking, shielding, disconnect ordering) — a design/architecture decision, so needs_human = true.

items.title: [Bug]: in-memory spend buffers are dropped on proxy shutdown
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

In-memory spend buffers are silently dropped when the proxy shuts down.

`update_spend` (key/team/user/end_user spend) and `update_daily_tag_spend` are
apscheduler jobs that accumulate rows in in-memory buffers between intervals.
On shutdown:

- the scheduler is never stopped anywhere, so a job can still be mid-flight, and
- `proxy_shutdown_event` (litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py) goes straight to
  `await prisma_client.disconnect()` without flushing either buffer.

Everything not yet committed is lost. On a uvicorn worker recycle
(MAX_REQUESTS_BEFORE_RESTART) or any SIGTERM (rolling update, scale-down,
liveness kill) this happens on every single restart, because the replacement
worker only sees its own future traffic.

Observed symptoms in the recycle window: `ClientNotConnectedError` on
update_spend, "Daily tag spend batch upsert failed", and "Error in spend logs
queue monitor: Server disconnected without sending a response."

Expected: buffered spend rows are flushed to the DB before Prisma disconnects.
Actual: they are discarded.

Note that `proxy_shutdown_event` already guards the analogous case for
enterprise billing, with the comment "final flush of billable-request counts:
without it, up to one export interval of enterprise billing data is dropped on
every restart". Spend rows have no equivalent flush, though they have the same
failure mode -- and spend data is billing-relevant.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the proxy with a DB and spend tracking enabled (default when a
   `DATABASE_URL` is configured), so the `update_spend` scheduler job is
   registered.

2. Send traffic so spend rows accumulate in the in-memory buffer, then stop the
   proxy before the next scheduler interval fires (default batch write interval):

   ```bash
   # send a few completions against a virtual key
   curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-..." \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'

   # immediately trigger a graceful shutdown
   kill -TERM <proxy_pid>
   ```

3. Query the DB for those requests:

   ```sql
   SELECT count(*) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs" WHERE "startTime" > now() - interval '5 minutes';
   ```

4. The rows buffered since the last scheduler run are missing. The same applies
   to `LiteLLM_DailyTagSpend` for tag spend.

### Relevant log output

```shell
ClientNotConnectedError: Client is not connected to the query engine
Daily tag spend batch upsert failed
Error in spend logs queue monitor: Server disconnected without sending a response.
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.94.0-rc.3

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a genuine bug: documented/expected behavior (buffered spend gets flushed and persisted, as shown by the analogous enterprise billing flush) is violated — in-memory spend buffers (update_spend, update_daily_tag_spend) are silently dropped on shutdown, causing billing/spend data loss on every worker recycle or SIGTERM. This affects the shared spend-tracking path used by virtually all proxy deployments with a DB configured, and happens on every restart (common operational event: rolling deploys, autoscaling, MAX_REQUESTS_BEFORE_RESTART), with no workaround mentioned. Data loss of billing-relevant records on a widely used core path is severe — this qualifies for P0 given "data loss" and "broken for most users on current release" criteria, but there is a workaround-like mitigation (avoid restarts) that isn't really practical, so treat as P1 given it's an edge/timing-window issue (only rows since last batch interval) rather than total breakage, but it affects the shared core path for essentially all proxy+DB users. Given the shared-core-path modifier (raise one level) and no workaround, I'll set to P0 since it's data loss affecting billing accuracy for most proxy users. Actually reflecting further: impact is bounded to a small window of rows per restart, not to the majority of requests being broken — so P1 fits better (major feature/shared core path broken, painful but partial impact, no workaround). This requires maintainer judgement to confirm impact and decide on the flush fix, so needs_human=true.

items.title: [SAP provider] cache_control is stripped from messages — Anthropic prompt caching unusable
items.body:
When routing Anthropic models through the `sap/` provider (SAP AI Core Orchestration), `cache_control` markers placed on message content blocks are silently dropped during request transformation. As a result, Anthropic prompt caching never activates — responses come back with `cache_read` / `cache_creation` at 0.

### Why

The SAP chat message models (`SAPMessage`, `SAPUserMessage`, `TextContent`) do not define a `cache_control` field, and content is flattened to a plain string during validation, so the marker is discarded before the request is built. By contrast, litellm's native `anthropic` provider supports `cache_control` on messages and tools.

### Minimal repro

```python
from litellm.llms.sap.chat.models import SAPMessage
m = SAPMessage(role="system", content=[
    {"type": "text", "text": "…large static prompt…",
     "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}
])
print(m.model_dump(by_alias=True))
# -> {"role": "system", "content": "…"}   # cache_control gone
```

### Expected

`cache_control` on content blocks is preserved through `transform_request` so it can reach the model, consistent with Anthropic's prompt-caching API (https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/prompt-caching).

### Ask

Could the SAP provider be brought to parity with the anthropic provider on `cache_control` passthrough — i.e. accept the field on content blocks (system / user / tool) and preserve it through `transform_request`?

### Impact

Prompt caching is a key lever for controlling token cost on agentic workloads. Without passthrough, anyone routing Anthropic models through this provider re-sends the full static system prompt + tool schemas at full price on every turn.

cc @vasilisazayka @guilherme-segantini as potential maintainers of the SAP provider (based on recent commit history) — is this the right place to raise it, or can you point to the right owner?

Environment: litellm 1.89.3

gold.rationale: The SAP provider fails to preserve cache_control markers on message content, which is documented/expected behavior consistent with Anthropic's prompt-caching API and with litellm's own anthropic provider. This is a functional gap causing wrong behavior (cost/caching not activating) rather than a missing feature from scratch — the provider already handles messages/content but silently drops a field, leading to incorrect cost/token accounting (cache_read/cache_creation always 0). This matches the "bug" category per the rules ("incorrect cost or token accounting" is explicitly called out as a bug). It affects a narrower path (SAP provider users routing Anthropic models), so not most users of the library, but it's a real functional defect with a clear reproduction. No workaround is mentioned other than not using caching, so it stays at P2 given it's a subset of users (SAP provider only) affected, with a clear repro provided. It does not rise to P1 since SAP provider is a narrow/less widely used path, not the shared core path. Given the clear reproduction and well-scoped nature, a maintainer could route this without deep discussion, but since it involves a design/API extension (adding cache_control field support across multiple models to reach parity) and affects a specific provider integration, some judgement on scope might be needed, but the report is well-specified and reproducible enough to route directly to the SAP owning module.

items.title: [Feature]: Auto Router v2: derive a session key from request content when `session_id` is absent
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature


## Summary

`session_affinity` and `adaptive` both depend on a resolvable `session_id`. When the client doesn't send one, both silently degrade — affinity stops pinning, and the bandit has no key to attribute reward against. Nothing errors. The router just quietly stops doing the two things you enabled it for.

Proposal: add an optional fallback chain for deriving the session key, so a missing `session_id` degrades to a best-effort key instead of to nothing.

## Current behaviour

Per the Auto Routing docs:

> `session_id` is read from request metadata; when no `session_id` is resolvable the router classifies every turn as usual.

That's the documented path for `session_affinity`. For `adaptive: true`, the docs state that feedback attributes back to the model that actually served the previous response — but with no session key there is nothing to correlate a later turn against, so reward attribution has nowhere to land.

Net effect with both flags on and no `session_id`:

| Feature | Configured | Actual behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session_affinity: true` | pin first-turn model | no-op, reclassifies every turn |
| `adaptive: true` | Thompson-sample + learn | samples, but never learns |

The failure is silent. There's no warning at config load, no log line, and no response header indicating the session key was unresolvable.

## Why this matters

Two distinct populations hit this:

1. **Clients the operator doesn't control.** OpenWebUI, LibreChat, off-the-shelf SDKs, and internal tools that predate the gateway. The operator can enable `session_affinity` in `config.yaml` but cannot make those clients emit `x-litellm-trace-id`. This overlaps with #18429 (mapping arbitrary headers to `litellm_session_id`).
2. **Operators who enabled the flags and assume they work.** Since there's no signal, a team can run `adaptive: true` for weeks, see the bandit never converge, and have no way to tell whether the model priors are bad or the reward loop was never closed.

The second case is arguably worse than the feature not existing, because it produces confident-looking routing decisions backed by an empty posterior.

## Prior art

OpenRouter solves this with a three-tier fallback chain for its sticky routing key:

1. Explicit `session_id` if present (max 256 chars)
2. Otherwise the OpenAI-style `prompt_cache_key` request field
3. Otherwise a hash of the first system/developer message plus the first non-system message

Their stickiness is scoped **per account, per model, per conversation**, which is what keeps the derived hash from colliding across tenants — two different customers opening with `"hi"` do not share a routing key.

They also document the limitation honestly: agents that rewrite opening messages while summarising state, reorder tool context, or inject run metadata will change the hash and break stickiness. That's why they tell agent builders to send an explicit `session_id`.

## Proposal

Add an optional `session_key_fallback` to `complexity_router_config`, defaulting to `none` so existing behaviour is unchanged:

```yaml
complexity_router_config:
  session_affinity: true
  session_affinity_ttl_seconds: 3600
  session_key_fallback: prefix_hash   # none (default) | prompt_cache_key | prefix_hash
```

Resolution order when `prefix_hash` is set:

1. `metadata.session_id` / `x-litellm-session-id` / `x-litellm-trace-id`
2. `prompt_cache_key` from the request body
3. `sha256(user_api_key_hash + model_group + normalised_first_system_msg + normalised_first_user_msg)`

**Scoping is the security-critical part.** The derived key must include `user_api_key_hash` so the namespace is per-key. Without that, two tenants sharing a common system prompt would share a routing key and, with `session_affinity`, potentially a pinned deployment. Per-key scoping should be non-optional, not a config knob.

Normalisation should be conservative — trim whitespace and normalise line endings only. Anything more aggressive risks collapsing genuinely distinct conversations.

## Observability (worth shipping even without the fallback)

Independent of whether the fallback lands, the silent-degradation problem deserves a fix:

- Extend the existing decision log with the key source, e.g. `session_key_source=explicit|prompt_cache_key|prefix_hash|none`
- Emit a warning on the first N requests where `session_affinity` or `adaptive` is enabled but no session key resolved
- Optionally surface it as a response header alongside `x-litellm-adaptive-router-model`

This alone would have saved the debugging time that prompted this request.

## Known limitations

Stating these up front rather than having them raised as objections:

- **Prefix hashing is unreliable for agent loops.** Agents that mutate their opening messages break the hash. This proposal does not fix agentic session tracking; explicit `session_id` remains the correct answer there. The fallback is for human chat traffic and uncontrolled clients.
- **Collision risk within a single key.** Two conversations from the same key with identical openings would share a key. For `session_affinity` this is benign (both get pinned to the same model). For `adaptive` it introduces some reward noise. Acceptable given the alternative is no signal at all, but worth documenting.
- **Requires shared state across replicas.** The derived-key → model mapping needs the same Redis/Postgres backing that `session_affinity` already uses, so this shouldn't add a new dependency.

## Alternatives considered

- **Header mapping only (#18429).** Solves the uncontrolled-client case where a usable ID exists in *some* header. Doesn't help when no stable ID exists anywhere in the request.
- **Requiring `session_id` and failing loudly.** Cleaner semantics, but a breaking change for anyone currently running these flags without one.
- **Doing nothing, documenting harder.** Reasonable, but the observability gap remains — an operator still can't tell from logs whether their reward loop is closed.

## Environment

- LiteLLM version: `1.94`
- Deployment: `Docker`
- Backing store: `Postgres + Redis + Clickhouse + MiniO`
- Client(s) affected: `LangGraph agents, Continue.dev`

## Willing to contribute

Happy to open a PR for the `session_key_fallback` resolution chain and the `session_key_source` log field if the approach and the config surface look right. Would want maintainer input on where the resolution belongs relative to the existing `session_affinity` lookup before starting.


### Motivation, pitch

I was working on Autorouter v2 to route request to model tiers, I find it hard to instruct every developer to maintain session id as it is not mandatory for the agents to work. The silent degradation decreases the efficiency of the router and increases latency & cost

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### LiteLLM is hiring a founding backend engineer, are you interested in joining us and shipping to all our users?

Yes

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

https://www.linkedin.com/in/muhammad-fazil-92b5b722a?utm_source=share_via&utm_content=profile&utm_medium=member_ios

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified feature request proposing new configuration (session_key_fallback), fallback resolution logic, and observability improvements for the auto router when session_id is absent. No code is currently broken relative to documented behavior — the docs state this is the current behavior, so it's not a bug. It's a single requester (no corroboration of demand from multiple users, though solid reasoning), so per rules it defaults to P3 despite being detailed and well-argued. It touches the shared core routing path (session_affinity/adaptive), but the "many providers or shared core path affected" modifier is meant for widespread breakage, not a proposed enhancement — and a detailed write-up alone isn't evidence of demand. This is a product-direction call (whether to add fallback key derivation, security-sensitive scoping design) that a maintainer should weigh in on before queuing, so needs_human should be true despite feature-not-bug classification.

items.title: [Bug]: MCP DCR bridge forwards lowercase bearer token type and causes upstream 401
items.body:
## What happened?

An `oauth_delegate` server with `dcr_bridge: true` can complete DCR, PKCE authorization, and token exchange successfully but return zero tools because the bridge copies the upstream OAuth `token_type` value verbatim into the protected-resource Authorization header.

A standards-based remote MCP provider returns `token_type: "bearer"` in lowercase. LiteLLM seals that value and later emits `Authorization: bearer <token>` from `resolve_bridge_envelope`. This provider treats the scheme casing strictly and returns HTTP 401 `invalid_token`.

A provider-neutral direct DCR/PKCE probe using the exact same token proved:

- `Authorization: bearer <token>` -> MCP initialize HTTP 401, `invalid_token`
- `Authorization: Bearer <token>` -> MCP initialize HTTP 200
- tools/list -> HTTP 200 with 32 tools

No token value is logged; the probe correlates attempts by a truncated SHA-256 fingerprint.

## Expected behavior

Canonicalize a case-insensitive OAuth token type of `bearer` to the interoperable `Bearer` scheme before protected-resource egress. RFC 6749 defines the token type value as case insensitive. Other token types can remain unchanged.

Minimal change in `outbound_credentials/bridge_credentials.py`:

```python
authorization_scheme = (
    "Bearer" if grant.token_type.lower() == "bearer" else grant.token_type
)
upstream_authorization = (
    f"{authorization_scheme} {grant.access_token.get_secret_value()}"
)
```

## Version

Reproduced on LiteLLM commit `bae22aad7cfe09d0ef0e41ec12cf1c7d9d0cbbb2`, used by the in-progress DCR bridge canary.

gold.rationale: This is a clear bug: the MCP DCR bridge forwards the OAuth token_type verbatim without canonicalizing case, causing strict providers to reject the Authorization header with HTTP 401. This violates RFC 6749's case-insensitivity expectation for token_type and results in zero tools being returned - a functional break for a subset of providers that strictly enforce scheme casing. The reporter provided a clear reproduction, root cause, and even a minimal patch, so this can be routed directly to the owning module without further discussion. It affects only providers that strictly validate the Authorization scheme casing (a subset, not all providers), and a workaround might not be readily available to end users (they can't control upstream provider strictness), but it's not a security vulnerability, not a documentation issue, and not a feature request - it's a clear functional bug in the bridge_credentials module. Since it's narrowly scoped to providers with strict casing checks, and a fix is trivial and well-specified, this fits P2 (narrower path broken, subset affected). No regression indicated (this seems to be a first-time implementation issue in the DCR bridge, not a working feature that broke), so no raise. No workaround stated by reporter for end users, so no lower. Given the clear reproduction, fix, and specificity, needs_human can be false - this is routable without discussion.

items.title: [Bug]: Concurrent router budget-window resets can overwrite spend
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I searched open and closed issues before filing
- [x] I found no existing issue for last-write-wins spend resets in `RouterBudgetLimiting`

### What happened?

When a provider, deployment, or tag budget window is considered expired, `_handle_new_budget_window` resets the spend key with a plain `SET` to the current response's cost

Concurrent responses crossing the same window boundary can all enter the reset path. Each writes only its own cost, so the final counter contains whichever write wins instead of the sum of all response costs

The start-time and spend keys are also written separately, so another worker can observe a mixed window state. In multi-replica deployments this directly undermines the shared budget counter at the point where traffic crosses a budget boundary

A separate reliability concern in the same accounting path is that queued Redis increments are dispatched with `asyncio.create_task` and the queue is cleared immediately, so the sync method does not wait for the remote write to complete

The reproduction uses synthetic cache keys, timestamps, and costs and makes no provider or network call

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Check out commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`
2. Run this script from the repository root

```python
import asyncio

from litellm.caching.caching import DualCache
from litellm.router_strategy.budget_limiter import RouterBudgetLimiting


async def main():
    # Construct only the helper state to avoid starting its periodic task
    limiter = object.__new__(RouterBudgetLimiting)
    limiter.dual_cache = DualCache()

    await asyncio.gather(
        limiter._handle_new_budget_window(
            spend_key="provider_spend:synthetic:1h",
            start_time_key="provider_budget_start_time:synthetic",
            current_time=1000.0,
            response_cost=0.05,
            ttl_seconds=3600,
        ),
        limiter._handle_new_budget_window(
            spend_key="provider_spend:synthetic:1h",
            start_time_key="provider_budget_start_time:synthetic",
            current_time=1000.0,
            response_cost=0.07,
            ttl_seconds=3600,
        ),
    )

    stored = await limiter.dual_cache.async_get_cache(
        "provider_spend:synthetic:1h"
    )
    print(
        {
            "stored_spend": stored,
            "additive_expected": 0.12,
        }
    )


asyncio.run(main())
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
{'stored_spend': 0.07, 'additive_expected': 0.12}
```

The exact winner is scheduling-dependent. It may be `0.05` or `0.07`, but cannot correctly become `0.12` because the reset operation is assignment rather than accumulation

The direct helper call isolates the boundary operation. In normal flow, every response that reads the same expired `budget_start` can enter this helper concurrently

### Current-code analysis

Budget start time is read and initialized with separate cache operations rather than an atomic window claim

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L340-L351

The reset helper sets spend to one response cost, then sets start time in a second operation

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L353-L375

The expired-window branch calls that helper after a non-atomic read and comparison

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L446-L496

Provider, deployment, and tag success accounting all converge on `_increment_spend_for_key`, so the race is shared by each budget type

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L401-L444

Redis pipeline work is started in the background and the local queue is cleared without awaiting the write

https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c/litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py#L525-L548

### Suggested correction

Make window selection and spend accumulation one atomic operation in the shared backing store

One option is a Redis Lua script that identifies the active window, initializes it only when absent or expired, adds the response cost with `INCRBYFLOAT`, and applies the matching TTL to the window metadata and counter before returning the new total

A window identifier embedded in the spend key can avoid mixing a late increment from the old window into a newly reset counter

The in-memory path needs equivalent locking for the same logical key. Redis pipeline pushes should copy the pending operations, await the pipeline result, and clear or requeue only after success

Regression coverage should synchronize two reset calls at the boundary and assert additive spend for provider, deployment, and tag budgets, including a two-instance Redis case and pipeline failure/retry behavior

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

SDK Router and Proxy Router budgets

### What LiteLLM version are you on?

Commit `24123269ccb76f36298a2457589f08bd3141072c`

### Contact details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented, reproducible race condition in the router budget limiter causing incorrect spend accounting (last-write-wins instead of additive) across multiple deployments/workers. It behaves differently from documented/expected behavior (budget tracking should sum spend accurately) so it's a bug, not a feature request. It affects a shared core accounting path used by provider, deployment, and tag budgets in multi-replica deployments, which is a widely-used core path — this raises severity. There's no stated workaround for the race itself (mitigations would require code changes), and it can cause silent under-counting of spend which could let budgets be exceeded (financial/reliability impact) but not itself a security vulnerability. Given the shared core path is affected in multi-replica setups, this should be raised one level from a narrower P2 to P1. It requires judgement/reproduction confirmation and a design decision (Lua script, locking strategy) about how to properly fix, so a maintainer should review before routing/implementing.

items.title: [Docs]: REDIS_URL prod warning is stale; the perf gap it cites is fixed
items.body:
### What happened?

The caching docs still advise against `REDIS_URL` in production on performance grounds:

> we **don't** recommend using REDIS_URL in prod. We've noticed a performance difference between using it vs. redis_host, port, etc.

That guidance was correct when it was written, and it traces back to #3188. The cause was connection churn: the url path discarded the shared pool and opened roughly two new connections per request, which is ruinous over TLS because each one pays a fresh handshake.

Current code pools correctly, and the gap is gone. Measured against a local redis behind a TCP relay injecting a fixed one-way delay, with redis in the request path on every call (response caching with unique prompts, 500 requests, 50 concurrent workers):

| version | mode | req/s | connections opened |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.35.17 | url | 540 | 1002 |
| 1.35.17 | host/port | 742 | 50 |
| current (1.95.0) | url | 650 | 50 |
| current (1.95.0) | host/port | 690 | 50 |

Over TLS the old churn cost 83.9 req/s against 462.1 on current code, with 1007 connections against 52. On current code url and host/port are within run to run noise of each other, so the stated reason for the recommendation no longer holds. Full detail is in a comment on #3188.

The recommendation should not simply be deleted, because `REDIS_URL` still has a real caveat, just a different one. Only `url`, `timeout` and `max_connections` are forwarded into the pool in `get_redis_connection_pool`, so any setting supplied outside the URL string is silently dropped. A `REDIS_PASSWORD` set alongside a `REDIS_URL` never reaches the client, and the same applies to ssl options and socket timeouts. Everything has to be embedded in the URL itself, as in `redis://user:pass@host:6379/0?socket_timeout=5`.

So the suggested doc change is to drop the performance claim and replace it with the configuration caveat, noting that url-based setups must carry credentials and options inside the URL string.

### Relevant issues

Reason for the original guidance: #3188

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

N/A

gold.rationale: The code behaves as intended (pooling now works correctly for REDIS_URL); the documentation is simply outdated, citing a performance issue that has since been fixed. The issue proposes a specific, well-reasoned doc update (drop performance claim, add configuration caveat about REDIS_PASSWORD/options not being forwarded outside the URL). This is a clear docs issue, not a bug, since there's no code misbehavior claimed—only a documentation staleness problem. It's low urgency (cosmetic/doc accuracy), and the suggested fix is well-specified enough to route directly without maintainer discussion.

items.title: [Bug]: [Security]: Raw virtual key persisted in cleartext under `user_api_key_hash` in standard logging metadata
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

`StandardLoggingMetadata.user_api_key_hash` is emitted into long-lived logging sinks (e.g. the S3 request/response logs). It is meant to hold a **hash** of the virtual key, never the key itself. But both functions that build the standard logging metadata blind-copy `user_api_key_hash` verbatim from the caller's input metadata, so a **raw** `sk-...` virtual key (or a JWT) placed in that field is persisted in cleartext.

`user_api_key_hash` is a `StandardLoggingMetadata` field (`litellm/types/utils.py`), so it is included in the key set that both builders copy directly from input metadata:

`litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py` — `StandardLoggingPayloadSetup.get_standard_logging_metadata` (~line 4690):

```python
if isinstance(metadata, dict):
    for key in metadata.keys() & _STANDARD_LOGGING_METADATA_KEYS:
        clean_metadata[key] = metadata[key]  # type: ignore   # <-- copies user_api_key_hash verbatim

    user_api_key = metadata.get("user_api_key")
    if user_api_key and isinstance(user_api_key, str) and is_valid_sha256_hash(user_api_key):
        clean_metadata["user_api_key_hash"] = user_api_key
```

`litellm/litellm_core_utils/litellm_logging.py` — module-level `get_standard_logging_metadata` (~line 5532):

```python
if isinstance(metadata, dict):
    for key in StandardLoggingMetadata.__annotations__.keys():
        if key in metadata:
            clean_metadata[key] = metadata[key]  # type: ignore   # <-- same verbatim copy

    if metadata.get("user_api_key") is not None:
        if is_valid_sha256_hash(str(metadata.get("user_api_key"))):
            clean_metadata["user_api_key_hash"] = metadata.get("user_api_key")  # this is the hash
```

Note the only guarding logic present validates the *separate* `user_api_key` field with `is_valid_sha256_hash` before promoting it into `user_api_key_hash`. There is **no such guard on `user_api_key_hash` itself** — it is copied as-is by the loop above.

The proxy auth path normally hashes the key before it reaches logging, but several paths can place a raw value in this field: the `master_key is None` early-return in proxy auth, an SDK caller passing `user_api_key_hash` directly, or a future regression upstream of logging.

**Expected:** whatever is persisted under `user_api_key_hash` is always a hash — a raw `sk-...` key or JWT arriving in that field must be hashed at the logging boundary before it reaches any sink.

**Actual:** a raw `sk-...` key (or JWT) in the input `user_api_key_hash` is copied verbatim into the standard logging payload and written to the configured logging sinks (S3, etc.) in cleartext — a credential-in-cleartext leak in durable storage. The failure is silent (no error, no warning).

**Proposed fix:**

Sanitize the field at the logging boundary in both builders, delegating credential detection + hashing to the existing canonical auth helper `UserAPIKeyAuth._safe_hash_litellm_api_key` (single source of truth — covers `sk-` via `hash_token`, JWT as `hashed-jwt-<h>`, and strips a `Bearer ` prefix), so the stored hash matches what the auth layer produces elsewhere and attribution joins still work. Non-credential / already-hashed / non-string values pass through unchanged.

```python
def _sanitize_user_api_key_hash(value: Optional[Any]) -> Optional[str]:
    """Hash a raw virtual key/JWT so it is never persisted to a log sink in cleartext."""
    if not value or not isinstance(value, str):
        return value
    if is_valid_sha256_hash(value):
        return value
    candidate = value.strip()
    if candidate[:7].lower() == "bearer ":
        candidate = candidate[7:].strip()

    from litellm.proxy._types import UserAPIKeyAuth

    sanitized = UserAPIKeyAuth._safe_hash_litellm_api_key(candidate)
    return sanitized if sanitized != candidat
```

Applied at both builders right after the copy loop:

```python
clean_metadata["user_api_key_hash"] = _saniti_metadata.get("user_api_key_hash"))
```

**Related:**
- `UserAPIKeyAuth._safe_hash_litellm_api_key`py` — the canonical key/JWT hasher this fixreuses (the auth layer already calls it to hash keys before they are logged).
- `is_valid_sha256_hash` in `litellm/litellm_.py` — the existing guard used for the`user_api_key` promotion path; this fix reuses it for the short-circuit.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Reproduces with the `litellm` package alone (no proxy, no cloud, no provider):

```python
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.litellm_logging import (
    StandardLoggingPayloadSetup,
)

# A raw virtual key placed under user_api_key_hash (e.g. via the master_key=None
# early-return, an SDK caller, or a regression upstream of logging).
metadata = {"user_api_key_hash": "sk-1234567890abcdefghijklmnop"}

result = StandardLoggingPayloadSetup.get_standard_logging_metadata(metadata)
print(result["user_api_key_hash"])
```

2. Observe the output:

```
sk-1234567890abcdefghijklmnop
```

The raw `sk-...` key is returned verbatim in the standard logging metadata — and from there is written to the configured logging sinks (S3 request/response logs, etc.) in cleartext.

3. This is the bug: `user_api_key_hash` is documented and named as a hash and lands in durable, long-lived log storage, but a raw credential in that field is persisted unhashed. Same result for the module-level `get_standard_logging_metadata` and for a `Bearer sk-...` / whitespace-padded / raw-JWT value.

### Relevant log output

```shell

```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.94.0-rc.3

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a genuine security issue: a raw virtual key or JWT can be persisted in cleartext in durable logging sinks (S3, etc.) under a field named/documented as a hash, due to a verbatim copy without sanitization. There is a plausible exploit/leak path (credential exposure in long-lived logs), and it takes precedence over being classified as a bug per the category rules. It affects the shared logging path used across providers/sinks, warranting escalation. Security issues always require human judgement per the rules, and P0/P1 severity for credential leakage in durable storage affecting many users (any user using standard logging with certain auth paths) — no workaround stated, so treat as P0 given plausible exploit and data exposure at rest across all sinks.

items.title: [Bug]: [Security] print_verbose prints api_key and raw control chars to stdout when set_verbose=True (stdout path not redacted or sanitized)
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

Every `print_verbose` helper in the codebase prints its argument **raw** to stdout when `litellm.set_verbose is True`. Callers routinely pass dict-shaped diagnostic payloads (e.g. `model_call_details`) that contain `api_key` (and, on the proxy, master/virtual keys, and provider Bearer tokens), so the full secret is emitted verbatim to stdout and captured by container/pod log collectors. In addition, model- and request-controlled content reaches these same stdout paths (e.g. the async streaming line logger), so unescaped CR/LF/Unicode-separator/control characters allow log forging and terminal-escape injection (CWE-117).

The `verbose_logger` path is already redacted by `SecretRedactionFilter`; only the `set_verbose` stdout `print(...)` branch is unprotected. There are **multiple** copies of `print_verbose` across the code, and they share this same unredacted-stdout pattern:

- `litellm/utils.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/_logging.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/main.py::print_verbose` (prints provider streaming chunks — `line in async streaming`)
- `litellm/caching/caching.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/litellm_core_utils/streaming_handler.py::print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/utils.py::print_verbose` (redacts, but does not sanitize control chars)
- `litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/presidio.py::_OPTIONAL_PresidioPIIMasking.print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/batch_redis_get.py::_PROXY_BatchRedisRequests.print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/prompt_injection_detection.py::_OPTIONAL_PromptInjectionDetection.print_verbose`
- `litellm/proxy/hooks/parallel_request_limiter.py::_PROXY_MaxParallelRequestsHandler.print_verbose`

Representative offending snippet (`litellm/utils.py`):

```python
def print_verbose(print_statement, logger_only=False, log_level="DEBUG"):
    try:
        if log_level == "DEBUG":
            verbose_logger.debug(print_statement)   # redacted by SecretRedactionFilter
        ...
        if litellm.set_verbose is True and logger_only is False:
            print(print_statement)  # noqa: T201    # <-- RAW: not redacted, not sanitized
    except Exception:
        pass
```

**Expected:** the stdout path masks secrets (matching what `litellm/_logging.py`'s stdout write already does with `redact_secrets(...)`) and neutralizes control characters that could forge log lines or inject terminal escapes. Redaction should still honor the `LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS=true` opt-out.

**Actual:** the `api_key` value reaches stdout unredacted (exposing credentials to any log sink that captures stdout), and CR/LF/Unicode-separator/C0/C1/DEL characters pass through unescaped (log-injection / terminal-manipulation vector). No error is raised — the exposure is silent.

**Proposed fix:** redact then sanitize before every `set_verbose` stdout print, e.g. a single shared helper:

```python
# litellm/_logging.py
def _sanitize_log_message(message: str) -> str:
    for ch, esc in {
        "\r": "\\r", "\n": "\\n", "\x85": "\\x85",
        " ": "\\u2028", " ": "\\u2029",
    }.items():
        message = message.replace(ch, esc)
    return re.sub(r"[\x00-\x08\x0b\x0c\x0e-\x1f\x7f-\x9f]", "?", message)

def _redact_and_sanitize(value) -> str:
    return _sanitize_log_message(redact_secrets(str(value)))
```

and route each `print_verbose` stdout branch through `print(_redact_and_sanitize(print_statement))`. `redact_secrets` already exists in `litellm/_logging.py` and is a no-op when `LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS=true`; the sanitizer is independent of the opt-out.

**Related:**
- #24813 (merged) — added `SecretRedactionFilter` / the redaction infrastructure this fix reuses.
- The separate "`print_verbose` doesn't emit through `verbose_logger` when `set_verbose` is False" behavior (#32318 / PRs #32495, #32326) is deliberately **out of scope** for this security fix.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install current `main` / latest release (`pip install litellm`).
2. Run (no proxy, cloud, or provider credentials required):

```python
import litellm
from litellm.utils import print_verbose

litellm.set_verbose = True
print_verbose({
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "api_key": "sk-secret-DO-NOT-LEAK-1234567890abcdef",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}],
})
print_verbose("attacker\r\nFORGED-LOG-LINE injected")
```

3. Observe stdout:

```
{'model': 'gpt-4o', 'api_key': 'sk-secret-DO-NOT-LEAK-1234567890abcdef', 'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'hi'}]}
attacker
FORGED-LOG-LINE injected
```

The `api_key` is printed verbatim, and the CR/LF splits the second call into a forged extra log line. The same happens organically on real calls (many paths pass `model_call_details`, which carries `api_key`, through `print_verbose` when `set_verbose=True`), including the `litellm.main.print_verbose` path that logs provider streaming chunks.

### Relevant log output

```shell

```

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.94.0-rc.3 (also reproduces on latest release)

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: Credentials (api_key, master/virtual keys, provider Bearer tokens) are printed raw to stdout when set_verbose=True, exposing secrets to any log collector capturing stdout. Additionally, unsanitized control characters allow log forging/terminal-escape injection (CWE-117). This is a genuine vulnerability with a plausible exploit path (any environment with set_verbose enabled and log aggregation), so it takes precedence as security regardless of framing as a bug. It affects the shared core logging path used across the entire codebase (multiple print_verbose copies across core, proxy, caching, streaming, guardrails), so impact is broad. There's no workaround other than disabling verbose logging entirely, which defeats debugging. This requires maintainer judgement to confirm the exploit path, coordinate the shared fix across many files, and decide on the correct sanitization approach.

items.title: [Feature]: Prometheus exporter cannot attribute spend, latency or traffic to a region or call type
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### Context

Filing this at Krrish's request after a Discord thread. We run LiteLLM Proxy in production in front of Azure OpenAI deployments spread across several regions plus Bedrock, and we maintain a patched build of `litellm/integrations/prometheus.py` because the shipped exporter cannot answer the questions we need it to answer. This issue documents what we hit, what we changed, and which of those changes I think belong upstream. Happy to send each as a separate PR.

All line references are against `litellm_internal_staging` at `24123269ccb7`, since that is the default branch and where PRs land. The same lines are present on `main`.

cc @yucheng-berri, who owns most of the recent work in this file.

---

### Problem 1: rate-limit gauges silently drop a value of `0`

`set_llm_deployment_success_metrics` guards both gauges with a truthy check:

```python
# litellm/integrations/prometheus.py:2694
if remaining_requests:
    ...
    self.litellm_remaining_requests_metric.labels(**_labels).set(remaining_requests)

# litellm/integrations/prometheus.py:2708
if remaining_tokens:
    ...
    self.litellm_remaining_tokens_metric.labels(**_labels).set(remaining_tokens)
```

When a provider reports `0` remaining, meaning the quota is actually exhausted, Python reads it as falsy and the gauge is never updated. Prometheus keeps serving the last non-zero value, so an alert on `litellm_remaining_requests_metric == 0` never fires and a dashboard shows healthy headroom during an outage. `0` and "the provider sent no header" both end up indistinguishable.

The same file already handles this correctly elsewhere for the same two variables:

- `_async_set_router_remaining_metrics`, lines 2609 and 2617: `if not already_have_tokens and remaining_tokens is not None:`
- `litellm_remaining_api_key_requests_for_model`, lines 1843 to 1855: `if remaining_requests is None: remaining_requests = sys.maxsize`

So this is an internal inconsistency rather than a design choice.

Filed as #29214. It is now rebased onto `litellm_internal_staging`, retargeted off `main`, conflict-free, and carries a live before and after: with the fix the gauge reads `0`, without it the gauge keeps serving the previous request's `1` while the quota is gone.

---

### Problem 2: there is no region dimension anywhere in the exporter

`region` appears zero times in `litellm/integrations/prometheus.py` and zero times in `litellm/types/integrations/prometheus.py`.

For a single-region install that is fine. For anyone running the same logical model across multiple regions, every region collapses into one time series and the following questions have no answer today:

- Which region is being throttled? `litellm_remaining_requests_metric` carries `api_base`, so the raw URL is technically there, but it is a high-cardinality opaque string rather than a dimension you can group or alert on.
- What are we spending per region? `litellm_spend_metric` has no `api_base` at all.
- Is one region slower? `litellm_llm_api_latency_metric` and `litellm_llm_api_time_to_first_token_metric` have no `api_base` either.

That last point is the crux. `api_base` is present on 10 metrics, all deployment-level, and absent from 29 others including `litellm_spend_metric`, `litellm_requests_metric`, `litellm_total_tokens_metric`, `litellm_request_total_latency_metric` and `litellm_llm_api_latency_metric`. So "derive the region from `api_base`" is not available on the metrics where regional attribution actually matters.

**What we run:** a `region` label resolved in priority order from `litellm_params.region_name`, `litellm_params.aws_region_name`, `litellm_params.vertex_location`, then metadata equivalents. Those are explicit and authoritative. We additionally fall back to parsing the region out of `api_base`, which works well for us but is a heuristic, and I would keep it out of a first PR or put it behind its own flag.

---

### Problem 3: no `call_type` dimension

`call_type` also appears zero times in both files. Chat completions, embeddings, image generation and audio all land in the same `litellm_requests_metric` and `litellm_spend_metric` series. Embedding traffic is typically orders of magnitude higher volume and orders of magnitude lower cost than chat, so mixing them makes both the request-rate and the spend series hard to reason about.

`standard_logging_payload` already carries `call_type`, so this is label plumbing rather than new data collection.

---

### Problem 4 (question, not a claim): `litellm_images_generated_metric` coverage

`_increment_media_generation_metrics` (line 1487) sources the counter from `standard_logging_payload["metadata"]["usage_object"]["output_image_count"]`, and skips when the value is absent.

I have not verified upstream's behaviour against every image provider, so I am asking rather than reporting: is `output_image_count` expected to be populated for all image-generation paths, including Azure DALL-E and Bedrock image models? If some providers do not report it, the counter silently stays at zero for them and a fallback (for example the length of the returned image list on image call types) would help. I am glad to test and send a PR if this is a real gap.

---

### Proposed shape

Problems 2 and 3 are the same shape as #32126, which added `api_provider` to the token, latency, request and cache metrics because those were emitted from call sites that already had the value and there was no way to break the numbers down by provider without it. `region` and `call_type` are the next two dimensions in that list, and both are already available at the same call sites. I would follow that PR directly: add the labels to the default sets, one PR per label, with tests and before/after dashboards.

If you would rather not grow the default label sets, the file also has the opt-in pattern, `litellm.prometheus_emit_stream_label` and `litellm.prometheus_emit_rate_limit_labels`, the latter carrying the comment "Off by default so the metric's historical label set is preserved across upgrade". #30532 is an open request for more label control, so I understand if cardinality is a concern here. Either shape works for us. Tell me which you prefer and I will build it that way.

Suggested split, each one independent:

1. #29214, rebased and ready for review. The `0` fix, two lines plus a regression test.
2. `region` label, resolved only from explicit config fields.
3. `call_type` label.
4. Region inference from `api_base` for AWS and Azure, if you want it. This one is a heuristic, so I would keep it behind a flag regardless of what we decide for 2 and 3.
5. Image counter fallback, if Problem 4 turns out to be real.

---

### Changes we run that I am not proposing upstream

Including these for completeness since the offer was to share what we run in production. I do not think they belong in LiteLLM as-is, and here is why.

- **Pre-computed RPM and TPM gauges** from an in-process sliding window. `rate()` over the existing counters gives the same answer, our implementation sweeps every window under a lock on every request, and it produces wrong numbers under `PROMETHEUS_MULTIPROC_DIR` because each worker only sees its own share of traffic.
- **Moving the `litellm_proxy_total_requests_metric` increment into `async_log_success_event`.** This gives us fully-labelled counts, but it drops requests that never reach an LLM such as auth rejections and non-LLM routes, which changes what the metric means.
- **A reduced `LATENCY_BUCKETS` set**, 15 buckets instead of 35. It roughly halves histogram cardinality and I would happily discuss it separately, but changing bucket boundaries changes every existing `histogram_quantile()` result, so it is not something to slip into another PR.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

gold.rationale: This is a detailed, well-researched issue containing multiple distinct problems: (1) a concrete bug where falsy-zero check causes rate-limit gauges to silently drop 0 values, masking real quota exhaustion (a correctness bug in the prometheus exporter's alerting path); (2) a feature request to add a `region` dimension to metrics; (3) a feature request to add `call_type` dimension; (4) an open question about image generation metric coverage across providers. Per the rules, when multiple distinct problems are bundled together, the primary actionable and highest-severity item should drive classification. Problem 1 is a clear bug with reproduction (before/after behavior described, PR #29214 referenced) affecting alerting/observability correctness — this is the most severe and concrete claim, so category = bug. The other problems are feature requests (region/call_type labels) referencing precedent PR #32126, showing some evidenced demand shape but still essentially a single reporter's proposal - however this affects prometheus metrics used broadly for cost/latency monitoring across multiple providers, and the bug about zero-value gauges affects rate-limit alerting broken silently in production which impacts monitoring reliability for exporter users generally, though it's a narrower monitoring path with a workaround already found (patched build) - stated workaround lowers severity one level. Given it's a monitoring gauge issue (not a full outage-causing bug, workaround already applied by reporter), and affects a subset of users who use rate-limit gauges/alerting, I set urgency P2 (narrower path affected, workaround exists onset P1->P2). Since this bundles multiple distinct problems (4 separate issues) and requires maintainer judgement to decide which of the feature-shaped asks to accept and reproduce the zero-gauge bug, needs_human = true.

items.title: [Bug]: `ollama_chat` → Anthropic `/v1/messages` streaming sets `stop_reason: "end_turn"` (not `"tool_use"`) and emits a spurious empty leading text block when the turn contains a tool call
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When an `ollama_chat` model is served through the Anthropic `/v1/messages` adapter with `stream: true`, and the model returns a tool call, the streamed response is malformed in two ways:

1. The final `message_delta` carries `stop_reason: "end_turn"` even though the message contains a `tool_use` block. Per the Anthropic Messages spec it MUST be `stop_reason: "tool_use"`.
2. A spurious empty leading text block is emitted first — `content_block` index 0 is `{"type": "text", "text": ""}` (immediately followed by `content_block_stop`) — before the real content.

The `tool_use` block itself and its `input_json_delta` arrive correctly, so the data is on the wire; only the framing (`stop_reason` + the empty text block) is wrong.

**The identical request with `stream: false` is correct** — it returns `stop_reason: "tool_use"` with the full tool input. So this is specific to the streaming translation path.

### Why it matters

Anthropic-Messages tool-runners (Claude Code, the Anthropic SDK's `messages.stream`, and other `/v1/messages` clients) key off `stop_reason == "tool_use"` to decide whether to execute the emitted `tool_use` block. With `stop_reason: "end_turn"` they treat the turn as final assistant text and silently drop the tool call. Combined with the empty leading text block, a client that validates visible payload sees an "empty" turn. In our downstream (OpenClaw gateway) every local-model tool call fails closed — `payloads=0, tools=0`, "agent couldn't generate a response" — so local models via LiteLLM can never call a tool through the Anthropic transport.

### Expected output

- The final `message_delta` should carry `stop_reason: "tool_use"` whenever the streamed message contains at least one `tool_use` content block (matching the non-streaming response and the Anthropic spec).
- No empty leading `{"type": "text", "text": ""}` content block should be emitted (cf. #22930 on sanitizing empty text blocks).

### Steps to Reproduce

### Environment

- **LiteLLM:** v1.93.0 (`ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:v1.93.0`)
- **Provider:** `ollama_chat`
- **Endpoint:** `/v1/messages` (Anthropic Messages adapter), `stream: true`
- Reproduces deterministically across scale — from a **1-tool / ~284-input-token** request up to **40 tools / ~27,900 input tokens**. Independent of model reasoning (reproduces with thinking off), tool count, system-prompt size, and JSON-schema complexity. The only variable that flips it is `stream: true` vs `false`.

### Minimal reproduction

**1. `config.yaml`** (any tool-capable Ollama model):

```yaml
model_list:
  - model_name: qwen3
    litellm_params:
      model: ollama_chat/qwen3:8b
      api_base: http://localhost:11434
```

**2. Start the proxy:**

```bash
litellm --config config.yaml   # serves on :4000
```

**3. Streaming — BROKEN.** `/v1/messages` with `stream: true` and one tool:

```bash
curl -sN http://localhost:4000/v1/messages \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H 'x-api-key: sk-1234' \
  -H 'anthropic-version: 2023-06-01' \
  -d '{
    "model": "qwen3",
    "max_tokens": 512,
    "stream": true,
    "messages": [
      {"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in San Francisco? Use the get_weather tool."}
    ],
    "tools": [{
      "name": "get_weather",
      "description": "Get the current weather for a city",
      "input_schema": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["city"]
      }
    }]
  }'
```

**4. Non-streaming — CORRECT.** Same request, `"stream": false` — returns `stop_reason: "tool_use"` with the full tool input.



### Relevant log output

```shell
event: content_block_start
data: {"type": "content_block_start", "index": 0, "content_block": {"type": "text", "text": ""}}   <-- spurious empty text block

event: content_block_stop
data: {"type": "content_block_stop", "index": 0}

event: content_block_start
data: {"type": "content_block_start", "index": 2, "content_block": {"type": "tool_use", "id": "...", "name": "read", "input": {}}}

event: content_block_delta
data: {"type": "content_block_delta", "index": 2, "delta": {"type": "input_json_delta", "partial_json": "{\"path\": \"/tmp/ab/report.txt\"}"}}   <-- tool call is correct

event: content_block_stop
data: {"type": "content_block_stop", "index": 2}

event: message_delta
data: {"type": "message_delta", "delta": {"stop_reason": "end_turn"}, ...}   <-- WRONG: tool_use block present, must be "tool_use"

event: message_stop
data: {"type": "message_stop"}
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.93.0

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: The reported behavior violates the documented Anthropic Messages spec contract: stop_reason must be "tool_use" when a tool_use block is present, and streaming should not emit a spurious empty text block. The non-streaming path behaves correctly, confirming this is a code defect in the streaming translation logic specific to ollama_chat -> Anthropic /v1/messages adapter, not a docs issue or a question. This is a clear bug with detailed, deterministic reproduction steps. It affects a specific but widely-used integration path (streaming tool calls via Anthropic-compatible clients like Claude Code) — this breaks all tool-calling use cases over the streaming Anthropic-messages transport for ollama_chat models, and likely other providers using the same streaming translation code, since it's about the shared Anthropic streaming adapter logic. No workaround is stated (switching off streaming is a functional workaround, but that defeats the purpose of streaming for many production copilot/agent uses). Given the impact -- tool calls silently fail closed for any tool-capable streaming request via this transport -- this is significant, though scoped to one code path (Anthropic streaming translation with tool use), not "most users on a current release broken" universally. I'll set urgency P1 given it breaks a major feature (tool calling for streaming) for users going through this integration, with reproduction steps provided. It's a clear, well-specified bug report with clear repro and expected output, so a maintainer doesn't need to triage/investigate further before routing it to the owning module (though given severity, I'd still flag needs_human due to P1 threshold in the rules).

items.title: FAL.ai provider only supports a fraction of available models — hardcoded list vs. 200+ models on FAL
items.body:
## Description

When using the FAL.ai provider in LiteLLM, users can only access a small fraction of the models that FAL.ai actually offers. The provider uses hardcoded model-specific transformation classes rather than dynamically discovering models from FAL's API.

## Current Implementation

LiteLLM's FAL provider at `litellm/llms/fal_ai/image_generation/` currently has hardcoded support for **only these endpoints**:

| LiteLLM Model ID | FAL Endpoint |
|------------------|-------------|
| `fal-ai/nano-banana` | `fal-ai/nano-banana` |
| `fal-ai/gemini-25-flash-image` | `fal-ai/nano-banana` |
| `fal-ai/imagen4/preview` | `fal-ai/imagen4/preview` |
| `fal-ai/recraft/v3/text-to-image` | `fal-ai/recraft/v3/text-to-image` |
| `fal-ai/bria/text-to-image` | `bria/text-to-image/3.2` |
| `fal-ai/flux-pro/v1.1` | `fal-ai/flux-pro/v1.1` |
| `fal-ai/flux-pro/v1.1-ultra` | `fal-ai/flux-pro/v1.1-ultra` |
| `fal-ai/flux-schnell` | `fal-ai/flux-schnell` |
| `fal-ai/bytedance/seedream/v3/text-to-image` | `fal-ai/bytedance/seedream/v3/text-to-image` |
| `fal-ai/bytedance/dreamina/v3.1/text-to-image` | `fal-ai/bytedance/dreamina/v3.1/text-to-image` |
| `fal-ai/ideogram/v3` | `fal-ai/ideogram/v3` |
| `fal-ai/stable-diffusion` | Dynamic from model name |

That's only **~15 model endpoints** out of the **200+ models** that FAL.ai publicly offers.

## What's Missing (major model families)

FAL.ai offers many more model families that have **no LiteLLM support at all**:

### Image Generation (missing)
- FLUX 1.0 Pro, FLUX Dev, FLUX LoRA variants, FLUX Realism
- FLUX Fill (inpainting), FLUX Canny, FLUX Depth, FLUX Redux
- Midjourney
- SDXL, SDXL Turbo, Playground v2
- DALL-E 3 (via FAL)
- Clipdrop, Clipdrop Cleanup
- Various community/fine-tuned models

### Video Generation (entirely missing)
- Luma Ray (text-to-video, image-to-video)
- Runway Gen-3 Alpha, Gen-3 Turbo
- Kling (text-to-video, image-to-video)
- Pika
- Stable Video Diffusion
- Haiper

### Audio (entirely missing)
- ElevenLabs (TTS, voice cloning)
- Play.ht
- Cartesia
- Deepgram
- Bark

### Other (entirely missing)
- Face swapping, restoration, enhancement
- Upscaling (Real-ESRGAN, etc.)
- Background removal
- OCR
- 3D model generation
- LLM inference (via FAL)

## Root Cause

The provider maps to a specific transformation class per model via `get_fal_ai_image_generation_config()` in `litellm/llms/fal_ai/image_generation/__init__.py`. Models that don't match any of the ~15 hardcoded patterns fall through to the generic `FalAIImageGenerationConfig` which may not handle parameters correctly. There is no model discovery or dynamic parameter mapping.

## Suggested Improvements

1. **Model discovery**: Add auto-discovery of available models via FAL's REST API (e.g. `GET https://rest.fal.ai/v1/models`)
2. **Generic parameter passthrough**: For models without a specific transformation class, pass parameters through generically instead of requiring per-model implementations
3. **Broader category support**: At minimum add support for video and audio endpoints
4. **Documentation**: Clearly document which FAL models are supported vs. requiring manual passthrough

## References

- LiteLLM FAL source: `litellm/llms/fal_ai/`
- FAL API docs: https://fal.ai/docs
- FAL models catalog: https://fal.ai/models
- FAL REST API appears to expose a list of available models (though behind auth)

## Environment

- All LiteLLM versions with FAL.ai support

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented request to expand provider support for FAL.ai beyond the current ~15 hardcoded models to cover 200+ models including video, audio, and other categories that don't exist yet in LiteLLM. This is new functionality (model discovery, generic passthrough, new categories), not a bug fix — the existing hardcoded models still work as documented. It falls under 'feature' category since these are entirely missing capabilities (e.g., video/audio support don't exist at all). The request is detailed and well-argued by a single reporter, but per the rules a detailed write-up alone is not evidence of demand — no corroborating requests, maintainer signals, or multiple users are cited. FAL.ai is one provider among many in LiteLLM, not the shared core path, so it doesn't qualify for the 'many providers or core path affected' raise. This defaults to P3. Since this is a well-specified feature request/roadmap item that can be routed to the FAL module owners for prioritization without needing a maintainer conversation to clarify ambiguity, needs_human can be false — though it does propose a product-direction call (whether to build dynamic model discovery vs adding models incrementally), which arguably needs judgement. Given the scope (architectural change: dynamic discovery, generic passthrough) this is a product-direction question best decided by maintainer, so needs_human should be true.

items.title: Feature Request: Add WaveSpeed.ai as a supported inference provider (LLM API + Media Generation)
items.body:
## Feature Request: WaveSpeed.ai Provider

**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
WaveSpeed.ai is a unified AI platform offering both **LLM inference** (93+ models via OpenAI-compatible API) and **AI media generation** (1,000+ models for text-to-image, image-to-video, text-to-video, audio). Currently, LiteLLM does not support WaveSpeed.ai as a provider, requiring users to configure it manually as a custom endpoint.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Add WaveSpeed.ai as a first-class provider in LiteLLM for both:

### LLM Service
- OpenAI-compatible chat completions API at `https://api.wavespeed.ai/v1/chat/completions`
- Model names follow the pattern: `{provider}/{model}` (e.g. `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`, `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6`, `deepseek/deepseek-v4`, `google/gemini-2.5-flash`, etc.)
- Supports vision, tool use, and prompt caching
- API key authentication

### Media Generation (Image/Video/Audio)
- REST API for predictions at `https://api.wavespeed.ai/v1/predictions`
- Models include: Seedream 5.0, Seedance 2.0, FLUX 2, WAN 2.x, Kling, Luma, GPT-Image, etc.
- Asynchronous prediction workflow (submit → poll/get result)
- Supports webhooks for completion callbacks
- File upload API for input media

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
- Configuring WaveSpeed.ai as a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint for LLM (works but lacks model discovery, cost tracking)
- Manual REST API calls for media generation (no LiteLLM routing/fallback)

**Implementation pointers**
- LLM API: OpenAI-compatible, base URL likely `https://api.wavespeed.ai`
- Media API: Replicate-style prediction API at `https://api.wavespeed.ai/v1/predictions`
- Model list: https://wavespeed.ai/llm (93 LLM models)
- Documentation: https://wavespeed.ai/docs/
- API auth: Bearer token in Authorization header
- Supported providers in LLM catalog: OpenAI, Anthropic, Alibaba, DeepSeek, Google, MiniMax, Moonshot, Zhipu AI
- Media models: Seedream, Seedance, FLUX, WAN, Kling, Luma, Runway, Ideogram, Recraft, etc.

**Additional context**
- Website: https://wavespeed.ai
- LLM models page: https://wavespeed.ai/llm
- Documentation: https://wavespeed.ai/docs/
- Offers both prepaid credits and enterprise plans
- Supports coding agent integration (Cursor, Claude Code, etc.)

gold.rationale: This is a request to add a new provider (WaveSpeed.ai) for both LLM inference and media generation, which does not currently exist in LiteLLM. This is clearly a feature request for new provider support. There's no evidence of multiple users requesting this (single requester, detailed write-up but no corroboration), so per the rules it defaults to P3 despite the thorough justification. It is a well-specified feature request that can be queued for the provider-integration backlog without needing a maintainer conversation first to clarify scope, though a product-direction call on whether to support a new media-generation type API might be warranted. Given the complexity (two distinct APIs: chat completions and async media generation) and the product-direction nature of adding a wholly new provider type (prediction-based media API differs from existing patterns), a maintainer should weigh in before implementation.

items.title: Voxtral models not visible in Mistral API model list — only available as audio_transcription
items.body:
## Description

When configuring a Mistral AI API key in the LiteLLM proxy, the Voxtral models (e.g. `mistral/voxtral-mini-latest`) do **not** appear in the `/v1/models` endpoint or in any model list query. This is confusing for users who add Mistral as a provider and expect all Mistral models to be discoverable.

## Current Behavior

- Voxtral is **not listed** in the Mistral supported models table (chat completions)
- Voxtral only works via explicit `model_list` configuration with `model_info: {mode: audio_transcription}`
- Voxtral does **not** show up when querying `/v1/models` through the proxy
- Users must manually add it to `model_list` with the correct `mode: audio_transcription` to use it

## Expected Behavior

Voxtral should either:
1. Appear in the `/v1/models` endpoint (at minimum under a separate category like `audio_transcription`)
2. Or the Mistral provider documentation should **explicitly and prominently** state that Voxtral is only available via the audio transcription endpoint, not chat completions

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure LiteLLM proxy with a Mistral API key
2. Query `/v1/models` — no Voxtral models appear
3. Try to use Voxtral via chat completions — it fails
4. Voxtral only works when explicitly configured in `model_list` with `model: mistral/voxtral-mini-latest` and `model_info: {mode: audio_transcription}`

## Suggested Fix

1. Include audio models in the `/v1/models` response with their correct `mode` metadata
2. Update the Mistral provider docs to clearly indicate which models are chat vs audio transcription

## References

- [LiteLLM Mistral Provider Page](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/mistral) (Voxtral under "Audio Transcription" section)
- [Audio Transcription Docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/audio_transcription) (Mistral/Voxtral listed)
- [Voxtral Announcement](https://mistral.ai/news/voxtral/) (July 2025)

## Environment

- LiteLLM version: via docker image
- Mistral API key configured: Yes
- Voxtral model ID: `mistral/voxtral-mini-latest`

gold.rationale: The reporter describes existing documented behavior (Voxtral is only supported via audio_transcription mode, not chat completions) and requests either surfacing it in /v1/models or clarifying docs. This is a mix of a minor bug/feature (models endpoint not listing audio models with mode metadata) and a docs improvement request. Since the code behaves as designed (Voxtral works via audio_transcription mode) but the discoverability via /v1/models is missing and docs could be clearer, this is best categorized as docs/feature improvement. Given the primary ask is about model listing behavior not matching expectations, and it's a single reporter's request without evidence of widespread demand, treat as a feature-ish/docs enhancement rather than a critical bug. It's a narrow, well-specified issue that doesn't need maintainer judgement on scope - it can be routed as a docs/feature clarification. Urgency low since there's a workaround (manual model_list config) and it's a single reporter.
