items.title: [Feature]: `/v1/ocr` endpoint is not available in the Playground
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature

### Problem
The LiteLLM Playground currently does not expose the `/v1/ocr` endpoint as an available endpoint type.

When using the Playground, searching for "ocr" under **Endpoint Type** returns no results, even though OCR is a supported API endpoint.

### Expected Behavior
The Playground should list **/v1/ocr** as a supported endpoint type so users can:

- Test OCR requests directly from the Playground.
- Upload images/documents and validate OCR responses without using external tools.
- Keep the Playground feature-complete with the available API endpoints.

### Current Behavior
The `/v1/ocr` endpoint is not available in the Endpoint Type dropdown, making it impossible to test OCR through the Playground UI.

### Suggested Solution
Add `/v1/ocr` as a supported endpoint in the Playground and provide the corresponding UI for submitting OCR requests (image/document upload and request parameters), similar to how other endpoint types are supported.

### Motivation, pitch

I'm integrating and testing LiteLLM's OCR capabilities. While the API supports the `/v1/ocr` endpoint, there is currently no way to invoke it from the Playground because it is missing from the Endpoint Type selector.

Having OCR available in the Playground would make it much easier to:
- Quickly validate OCR integrations.
- Debug OCR requests and responses.
- Demonstrate OCR functionality without writing client code.
- Provide a consistent testing experience across all supported endpoints.

This would improve the developer experience and make the Playground a more complete interface for testing LiteLLM features.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

UI Dashboard

### LiteLLM is hiring a founding backend engineer, are you interested in joining us and shipping to all our users?

Yes

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

https://www.linkedin.com/in/shubham-kumar-9a6a13232/

gold.rationale: This is a request to add OCR endpoint support to the Playground UI, which is a new capability that doesn't currently exist. This is a well-specified feature request (add /v1/ocr to Endpoint Type dropdown with corresponding UI), but there is only a single requester with no corroborating evidence of demand from others. Per rules, feature requests default to P3 unless there's evidenced demand (multiple requesters, maintainer signal, or widely-used provider/core path affected). OCR playground UI is a narrow UI feature, not a core path, so it stays P3. Since it's well-specified and only needs queuing (not a product-direction judgement call about whether it should exist at all - it's a fairly clear feature addition), needs_human can be false.

items.title: onthebench.ai benchmarks LiteLLM: a review of our setup for fairness
items.body:
Hi, I run [onthebench.ai](https://onthebench.ai), an open benchmark that measures LLM-gateway overhead (latency, throughput, memory, streaming, protocol translation) on neutral hardware. LiteLLM appears on the board twice, the Python proxy and the Rust `/v1/messages` beta, each benchmarked separately. I want to make sure I'm testing both fairly.

How it works, so there are no surprises:
- Every gateway runs on the **same rig, same mock upstream, same load, same CPU pinning**, no per-gateway special-casing.
- Each entry is defined by a single file: [`gateways/litellm-python/gateway.sh`](https://github.com/GetBusbar/benchmarking/blob/main/gateways/litellm-python/gateway.sh) and [`gateways/litellm-rust/gateway.sh`](https://github.com/GetBusbar/benchmarking/blob/main/gateways/litellm-rust/gateway.sh). Those files are the whole story of how I configured them.
- Every number regenerates from committed JSON; the [method is documented here](https://onthebench.ai/gateways/method) and the whole thing is open source and re-runnable.

My guiding rule is that **a failure is my bug until proven the gateway's**. If a cell shows red or a number looks off, I'd rather find out I configured LiteLLM wrong than publish something unfair. So two asks, both optional:
1. **Look at your results** ([Python](https://onthebench.ai/gateways?gw=litellm-python), [Rust](https://onthebench.ai/gateways?gw=litellm-rust)) and the two `gateway.sh` files. If I've mis-set a flag, a version, an endpoint, or declared a capability you don't claim, tell me or open a PR, you're welcome to own your own `gateway.sh`.
2. If the setup looks fair, a thumbs-up is genuinely useful too.

Full disclosure: this is built and operated by the Busbar team, and busbar is also one of the entrants. Same harness for everyone, fully open, so you can verify exactly what I'm running.

Thanks for building LiteLLM.

gold.rationale: This is an outreach/notification from a third-party benchmark site asking LiteLLM maintainers to review their gateway.sh configuration for fairness. It's not a bug report, feature request, or documentation issue about LiteLLM's own docs/code. It doesn't ask "how to do something" in the sense of using the library, but it is a request for maintainer attention/validation of an external benchmark setup, which requires human judgement (product/community decision on whether to engage, verify config correctness, etc.). It best fits "question" category since no actual code misbehavior is claimed, just a request for review. Urgency is low since there's no functional impact on users; it's a courtesy check-in with optional asks. Needs human because it requires maintainer judgement on whether the benchmark config is accurate/fair, which is a domain-specific validation task, not something that can be auto-routed.

items.title: [Bug]: v1.93.0 regression — Model Armor post_call guardrail 500s every /v1/batches create ('NoneType' object has no attribute 'get')
items.body:
### What happens

With a Model Armor guardrail whose mode includes `post_call` applied to the request (via `default_on: true` or team/key guardrail settings), **every `POST /v1/batches` request against a `vertex_ai` model returns `500 {"error": {"message": "'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'"}}`** — while the Vertex batch prediction job is actually created successfully and keeps running as an orphan (the client never receives its ID).

Full traceback from the proxy pod (`ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:v1.93.0`, Python 3.13):

```
File "litellm/proxy/batches_endpoints/endpoints.py", line 273, in create_batch
    response = await proxy_logging_obj.post_call_success_hook(
File "litellm/proxy/utils.py", line 2305, in post_call_success_hook
    guardrail_response = await self._run_guardrail_with_metrics(
File "litellm/integrations/custom_guardrail.py", line 1171, in async_wrapper
    return self._process_response(
File "litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/model_armor/model_armor.py", line 357, in _process_response
    guardrail_response = metadata.get("_model_armor_response", {})
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'
```

**This is a `v1.93.0` regression.** The same `_process_response` code exists in `v1.92.0` ([`model_armor.py` L344-L346](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.92.0/litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/model_armor/model_armor.py#L344)), but in `v1.92.0` `ModelArmorGuardrail` declared no `get_supported_event_hooks`, and a configured `post_call` mode was not active — the same proxy setup (Model Armor with `post_call` applied to the calling team) served `/v1/batches` without errors on `v1.92.0`. `v1.93.0` added [`get_supported_event_hooks` listing `post_call` (`model_armor.py` L62-L70)](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.93.0/litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/model_armor/model_armor.py#L62), activating the hook for existing configurations and making the crash reachable. Upgrading `v1.92.0` -> `v1.93.0` with an unchanged guardrail config is sufficient to go from working to failing.

The 500 response carries no `x-litellm-call-id` header, which also makes these failures hard to correlate in logs.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Proxy config: a `vertex_ai` Gemini model, Vertex files enabled, and a Model Armor guardrail applied by default with a `post_call` mode:

   ```yaml
   model_list:
     - model_name: gemini-2.5-flash
       litellm_params:
         model: vertex_ai/gemini-2.5-flash
         vertex_project: <YOUR_PROJECT>
         vertex_location: us-central1

   files_settings:
     - custom_llm_provider: vertex_ai

   guardrails:
     - guardrail_name: model-armor-post
       litellm_params:
         guardrail: model_armor
         mode: [pre_call, post_call]
         default_on: true
         project_id: <YOUR_PROJECT>
         location: us-central1
         template_id: <YOUR_TEMPLATE>
   ```

   (`GCS_BUCKET_NAME` / `litellm_params.bucket_name` set so batch file storage works — uploads succeed in this setup.)

2. Client, standard OpenAI SDK, **no `metadata` param** (the SDK default):

   ```python
   from openai import OpenAI
   client = OpenAI(base_url="<PROXY>/v1", api_key="sk-...")

   f = client.files.create(
       file=open("batch_input.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="batch",
       extra_body={"target_model_names": "gemini-2.5-flash"},
   )   # succeeds

   client.batches.create(
       input_file_id=f.id, endpoint="/v1/chat/completions", completion_window="24h",
   )   # -> 500 "'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'"
   ```

3. Check Vertex (`GET .../batchPredictionJobs`): the job from the failed call exists and runs to `JOB_STATE_SUCCEEDED` — the 500 happens after job creation, in response post-processing.

Also reproducible without managed files (and without any enterprise-licensed feature, in case `target_model_names` routing is unavailable in your setup): `batches.create(..., extra_body={"custom_llm_provider": "vertex_ai"})` with a raw `gs://` `input_file_id` — same 500, so it is not specific to the managed-files path.

### Why it happens (verified against the `v1.93.0` tag)

The chain is fully traceable in the source:

1. [`litellm/proxy/batches_endpoints/endpoints.py` L111](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.93.0/litellm/proxy/batches_endpoints/endpoints.py#L111): `data["metadata"] = sanitize_openai_provider_metadata(data.get("metadata"))`.
2. [`litellm/proxy/common_utils/callback_utils.py` L478-L479](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.93.0/litellm/proxy/common_utils/callback_utils.py#L478): `sanitize_openai_provider_metadata` returns its input unchanged when falsy — so for the normal case of a batch request without client `metadata`, **`data["metadata"]` is now explicitly present with value `None`**.
3. [`endpoints.py` L273](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.93.0/litellm/proxy/batches_endpoints/endpoints.py#L273): the successful batch-create response is passed through `post_call_success_hook`, which runs all `post_call` + `default_on` guardrails on it.
4. [`model_armor.py` L355-L357](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.93.0/litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/model_armor/model_armor.py#L355): `metadata = request_data.get("metadata", {})` — the `{}` default only applies when the key is *absent*; here the key is present with `None`, so `metadata.get("_model_armor_response", {})` on the next line raises the `AttributeError`.

### Is this Model Armor-specific or generic to guardrails?

What we verified:

- The **crash itself is specific to Model Armor's `_process_response` override** ([`model_armor.py` L340-L372](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.93.0/litellm/proxy/guardrails/guardrail_hooks/model_armor/model_armor.py#L340)). The base [`CustomGuardrail._process_response` (`custom_guardrail.py` L880)](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/v1.93.0/litellm/integrations/custom_guardrail.py#L880) does not read `request_data["metadata"]`, so guardrails using the base implementation don't hit this particular AttributeError. Only Model Armor was tested live.
- Two **generic** ingredients enable it, and would expose any similarly written hook:
  - `/v1/batches` responses (job metadata, no model output) go through the same `post_call_success_hook` guardrail pipeline as chat completions (`endpoints.py` L273), even though there is no response content to inspect at batch-submission time.
  - On the batches route, `data["metadata"]` is normalized to `None` (`endpoints.py` L111), so any hook using the common `request_data.get("metadata", {})` pattern gets `None` instead of the intended `{}` default.

### Environment

- `ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database:v1.93.0` (proxy, Postgres-backed), Python 3.13
- Provider: `vertex_ai` (Gemini), batch via Vertex `batchPredictionJobs`
- Guardrail: `model_armor`, `default_on: true`, modes incl. `post_call`
- Confirmed workaround: disabling the guardrail's `post_call` application immediately restores `/v1/batches` (create → poll → results all succeed).

gold.rationale: This is a clearly reproduced regression introduced in v1.93.0: a new get_supported_event_hooks activation combined with a metadata sanitization change causes a None.get() AttributeError, crashing every /v1/batches create call when a post_call Model Armor guardrail is active. The Vertex batch job is created but the client never gets a response, leaving orphan jobs and no correlation ID header. This affects a widely-used provider path (vertex_ai batches) combined with a common guardrail feature, is a regression from a prior working version, and has clear reproduction steps and root-cause analysis pointing to exact code lines. It's a bug, not a feature or question, since documented/expected behavior (successful batch creation returning to caller) is violated. Given it's a regression breaking a core proxy endpoint for any user combining post_call guardrails, severity is high (P1), raised from baseline due to regression modifier, but not P0 since no data loss/security issue and vertex batches specifically. No workaround stated, so no downgrade. Because this is a well-documented regression with exact code pointers, though it involves a P1-level severity requiring reproduction confirmation and judgement on fix scope (metadata None-safety across guardrails), a maintainer should review to confirm scope of fix (just this line vs broader safety net for other guardrails).

items.title: LiteLLM forwards unsupported strict tool fields to Bedrock Claude models, causing 400 errors and hanging requests
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

When using PydanticAI with MCP tools through LiteLLM’s OpenAI-compatible proxy, some tool definitions contain `strict: true`.
LiteLLM forwards `strict` and `additionalProperties` to Bedrock Converse without accounting for the specific Claude model or Bedrock tool type. We have observed different failures across multiple Claude models.

This appears to be a regression introduced in LiteLLM [v1.90.0](http://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/releases/tag/v1.90.0) which began forwarding `strict` and `additionalProperties` to Bedrock Converse.
 
### Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Haiku 4.5
Bedrock reports that the compiled grammar exceeds its maximum allowed size. The deterministic Bedrock error is not returned promptly to the client. The request remains active for some minutes before nginx returns a 504 Gateway Time-out.
The same request and MCP tools succeed through LiteLLM when a PydanticAI `prepare_tools` (docs [here](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/capabilities/prepare-tools/)) hook forces `strict=False` on every tool definition. No schemas or application behavior are otherwise changed.
The original request also succeeds when sent directly to Bedrock.

### Claude Sonnet 5
This is already reported in https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/33193 and a [PR](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/33196) is open.
Bedrock immediately rejects a custom tool because LiteLLM forwards strict into `tools[].custom`, where that field is not permitted:
`tools.1.custom.strict: Extra inputs are not permitted`
We have not yet confirmed whether the proxy reports the same compiled-grammar error for this model.

LiteLLM has already introduced model-specific mitigations that strip strict for:
Opus 4.7/4.8 in [#31923](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/31923)
Claude Sonnet 4 in [#31943](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/31943)

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure LiteLLM model groups backed by Bedrock Converse for: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5 or Claude Haiku 4.5
2. Create a PydanticAI agent using LiteLLM’s OpenAI-compatible endpoint.
3. Attach 20-30 MCP tools for which PydanticAI generates tool definitions containing strict: true.
4. Send a prompt to Claude model.
5. Observe the compiled-grammar error in the LiteLLM proxy logs.
6. Observe that the caller remains blocked for a longer time than expected.
7. Observe that nginx eventually returns a 504 Gateway Time-out.
8. Repeat the same Sonnet 4.6 request with a PydanticAI prepare_tools hook that sets strict=False on every tool.

### Relevant log output

```shell
For Claude Sonnet 4.6 or Haiku 4.5:
litellm.exceptions.BadRequestError: litellm.BadRequestError: BedrockException -
{"message":"The model returned the following errors: Compiled grammar size
(410.4MB) exceeds maximum allowed size (300MB). Simplify your JSON schema
to reduce grammar complexity."}.
Received Model Group=eu.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6
Available Model Group Fallbacks=None


For Claude Sonnet 5:
pydantic_ai.exceptions.ModelHTTPError:
status_code: 400,
model_name: us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5,
body: {
  "message": "litellm.BadRequestError: BedrockException -
  {\"message\":\"The model returned the following errors:
  tools.1.custom.strict: Extra inputs are not permitted\"}.
  Received Model Group=us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5
  Available Model Group Fallbacks=None",
  "type": null,
  "param": null,
  "code": "400"
}
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.91.0

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a clear regression: LiteLLM v1.90.0 introduced forwarding of `strict`/`additionalProperties` to Bedrock Converse for Claude models without proper model-specific handling, causing 400 errors and hanging requests (504 timeouts) for multiple widely-used Claude models (Sonnet 4.6, Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5) via Bedrock, a core/shared provider path. There's already a related issue and PR open for one of the affected models, corroborating demand and confirming this is a known regression affecting the shared Bedrock tool-calling path. This is a functional bug (wrong behavior vs. documented/expected behavior, causing errors and hangs), not a docs or feature issue. Given it's a regression affecting a widely-used provider path (Bedrock Converse + multiple Claude models) with no full workaround (partial workaround only for one model via a client-side hook), this warrants high urgency. Base severity is P1 (major provider path broken, painful workaround exists for one case only) and regression modifier would push to P0, but workaround existing lowers it back down partially - however already many providers/models affected pushes it up. Given the severity (500s, hangs, timeouts) affecting multiple Claude models via Bedrock but a workaround exists (prepare_tools hook setting strict=False), I'll set urgency to P1 due to regression + shared core path affected, tempered by partial workaround. This requires maintainer judgement to reconcile multiple related PRs/issues and confirm the fix scope across models, so needs_human=true.

items.title: [Bug]: unpack_defs still hangs (unbounded) on recursive tool schemas — Bedrock & Vertex callers pass no byte budget
items.body:
Related (closed): #19098, #13151, #11372 — this looks like an incomplete fix for #19098.


### What happened?

A `/chat/completions` request whose tool `parameters` is a **recursive,
high-fan-in JSON Schema** (`$defs`/`$ref` where a type references itself and is
reused by many other defs — the shape Pydantic emits for recursive models)
causes `unpack_defs()` to expand **unboundedly**. It is CPU-bound, not just
memory: a ~23 KB tool schema expands past **510 MB within 30 s and does not
converge**, so the request never reaches the provider and the fronting
gateway/LB times out (~80 s) → **502**. Adding memory does not help.

Reproduced on both:
- **Bedrock** Converse (Claude), and
- **Vertex AI / Gemini**.

This is closely related to the closed #19098. That fix added a
`max_inlined_bytes` budget and a `ref_chain` cycle guard to `unpack_defs`, but
the bug persists because:

1. **Neither caller passes `max_inlined_bytes`**, so it defaults to `None`
   (unbounded) on exactly the two paths that trigger the blow-up.
2. The `ref_chain` guard only prevents **path cycles** (a def already on the
   current resolution chain). It does **not** prevent **diamond fan-out** — the
   same def reused across sibling branches — which is what a recursive,
   high-fan-in schema produces. Each reuse gets its own `copy.deepcopy` and is
   re-queued for full expansion → `O(fanout^depth)`.

Note: Anthropic/Bedrock Claude natively accepts JSON-Schema `$ref`, so this
force-expansion is not even required for that provider.

### Relevant code

- `litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/common_utils.py:958`
  — `resolved = copy.deepcopy(target_schema)` (per-`$ref` deep copy, re-queued)
- `common_utils.py:931` — `if ref_name in ref_chain:` (path-only cycle guard)
- `common_utils.py:940` — `max_inlined_bytes` budget exists but defaults to `None`
- Callers that do **not** pass a budget:
  - Bedrock Converse: `litellm/litellm_core_utils/prompt_templates/factory.py:5117`
  - Vertex/Gemini: `litellm/llms/vertex_ai/common_utils.py:601`

### Measured impact

Tool schema of ~23 KB with ~33 `$defs` / ~333 `$ref`s, several defs
self-referential and reused with high fan-in:

| Elapsed | deepcopy calls | cumulative inlined bytes |
|---|---|---|
| 30 s | ~690,000 | ~510 MB, still climbing (~17 MB/s) |

Does not converge; terminated by the external ~80 s gateway timeout → 502.

### Steps to reproduce

Standalone, no network — validated to hang on current source:

```python
import time, copy
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.prompt_templates.common_utils import unpack_defs

# Synthetic recursive, high-fan-in schema (fan-out 3, depth 14).
# Mirrors what Pydantic emits for recursive models.
defs = {
    f"N{i}": {"type": "object",
              "properties": {f"c{j}": {"$ref": f"#/$defs/N{i+1}"} for j in range(3)}}
    for i in range(14)
}
defs["N14"] = {"type": "object"}
schema = {"type": "object", "properties": {"root": {"$ref": "#/$defs/N0"}}}

t = time.perf_counter()
unpack_defs(schema, copy.deepcopy(defs))   # no max_inlined_bytes -> unbounded
print("done in", time.perf_counter() - t)  # does not return in reasonable time
```

Via the proxy: send any tool with such a schema to a Bedrock (`claude-*`) or
Vertex/Gemini model and observe the ~80 s hang → 502, CPU pegged.

### Suggested fix

- Arm the existing guard: pass `max_inlined_bytes` at both call sites
  (`factory.py:5117`, `vertex_ai/common_utils.py:601`), like the legacy path
  already does — fail fast with a clear error instead of hanging.
- Better: dedupe/memoize resolved subtrees for refs not on the current
  `ref_chain` (share instead of `deepcopy` per occurrence). This turns the
  exponential expansion into linear and also covers the recursive/diamond case
  the current `ref_chain` guard misses.

### Environment

- LiteLLM v1.95.0 (also reproduced on the `litellm_internal_staging` branch)
- Providers: Bedrock (Converse), Vertex AI / Gemini

gold.rationale: This is a genuine bug: an existing safety mechanism (max_inlined_bytes budget, ref_chain guard) added in a prior fix (#19098) is not actually applied at the two call sites that matter (Bedrock Converse and Vertex/Gemini), so the code violates its intended contract of bounding schema expansion. It's reproducible with a standalone script (no network needed), clearly evidenced with measurements (CPU pegged, 510MB+ and climbing, 502 after gateway timeout). This affects two widely-used providers (Bedrock and Vertex/Gemini) — both major integrations — and causes full request failure (502) with no workaround for schemas of this recursive shape. This is a regression/incomplete-fix of a previously closed issue affecting the shared core path (unpack_defs) used by multiple providers, causing complete failure for affected requests, so it warrants a high urgency. Since it affects any request with certain recursive tool schemas across two major providers, with no workaround, and pegs CPU (broader than a narrow subset), this is P1 — major feature/provider broken for a subset of users with no workaround, and given the shared core path is affected (raise one level modifier), leaning P0. However since it only affects requests with this specific recursive schema shape, most users are unaffected, so P1 is more appropriate than P0. Given the severity (CPU-bound hang, service outage risk, unbounded resource use) and that it affects multiple large fronting providers, I will set P1 severity, and since this involves judgement about proper fix approach (arm existing guard vs. rearchitect with memoization) and reproduction validation, needs_human should be true.

items.title: [Feature]: Partition DDL in SpendLogs cleanup causes service outage when it collides with routine PostgreSQL maintenance
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature

## Proposal

Allow the partition management path (`ensure_partitions` / `drop_partitions_older_than`) to run with `lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout` applied — scoped only to those DDL statements, so no other queries are affected. Sensible would be exposing them as env vars (or `general_settings` keys) with conservative defaults such as `lock_timeout=3s`, `statement_timeout=5s`.


### Motivation, pitch

## What happened in production

We run `vacuumdb --freeze` as a nightly cron on our Postgres cluster — standard practice to prevent transaction ID wraparound.
On one night, `vacuumdb --freeze` on `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` overlapped with the litellm partition cleanup tick.

Timeline:
1. `vacuumdb --freeze` starts, holds `ShareUpdateExclusiveLock` on `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` for the duration of the freeze pass.
2. litellm's `SpendLogsPartitionManager` fires and issues `DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "LiteLLM_SpendLogs_pYYYYMMDD"`, which needs `AccessExclusiveLock` on the parent to update `pg_inherits`.
3. The DDL is blocked waiting for VACUUM. Postgres's lock queue now has an `AccessExclusiveLock` *request* sitting at the front.
4. Every subsequent `INSERT` (which only needs `RowExclusiveLock`, normally compatible with VACUUM's lock) queues **behind** the DDL request, per Postgres's fair queueing rules.
5. Write traffic to `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` fully stalls until VACUUM finishes.

We mitigated by moving the two schedules apart. But this is a workaround, not a fix — any maintenance op that takes any lock higher than `AccessShareLock` on the parent can trigger the same outage: `VACUUM`, `VACUUM FREEZE`, `ANALYZE`, `pg_repack`, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, logical replication resync, or a future litellm feature that reads with a heavier lock.

## Root cause

`SpendLogsPartitionManager.ensure_partitions()` and `drop_partitions_older_than()` in `litellm/proxy/db/db_transaction_queue/spend_logs_partition_manager.py` issue DDL via `prisma_client.db.execute_raw` with no `lock_timeout` and no `statement_timeout`.
As a result, the DDL will wait as long as whatever holds a conflicting lock takes to finish, and the DDL's *wait itself* blocks all writers behind it.

## Why both lock_timeout and statement_timeout are needed

- `lock_timeout` bounds the time the DDL will *wait* to acquire its lock. This is the primary defense against the outage above,   where the DDL sits behind VACUUM and drags all INSERTs with it.

- `statement_timeout` bounds the time the DDL is *actually   running*. In rare edge cases — the DDL session gets stuck in   `idle in transaction`, a network hiccup leaves the connection half-open, or catalog contention makes the DDL itself slow — the DDL can hold `AccessExclusiveLock` well after `lock_timeout` is no longer relevant, and every writer stays blocked. `statement_timeout` is the safety net for that.

The two settings cover different failure modes (waiting for a lock vs. holding a lock too long), and both are needed for the cleanup path to be safe under real production conditions.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### LiteLLM is hiring a founding backend engineer, are you interested in joining us and shipping to all our users?

No

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented feature request to add lock_timeout/statement_timeout configuration to the partition management DDL path in SpendLogs cleanup, to prevent a real production outage caused by DDL blocking on locks held by routine Postgres maintenance (VACUUM). While it's framed as caused by a production incident, the ask itself is a new capability (exposing timeout settings) that doesn't exist yet — this is a feature, not a bug in existing documented behavior. The issue is a single detailed report from one reporter with no corroboration from other users, but it does describe a real outage-causing scenario affecting the shared SpendLogs partition management path used by all proxy DB users, which is a widely-used/core path. Per rules, feature requests default to P3, promoted to P2 on evidenced demand (widely-used provider or shared core path affected) — since SpendLogs partition management is core shared logic affecting many proxy deployments with Postgres, this qualifies for the "shared core path affected" raise. No regression modifier applies (this behavior always lacked timeouts). No workaround-lower modifier needed. This requires product-direction judgement (should timeouts be exposed as configurable settings, what defaults) so a maintainer should review before routing/implementation.

items.title: [Bug][Security] litellm.utils.print_verbose leaks api_key to stdout when set_verbose=True (stdout path not redacted, unlike _logging.print_verbose)
items.body:
## What Happened

`litellm/utils.py::print_verbose` prints its argument **raw** to stdout when `litellm.set_verbose is True`. Callers routinely pass dict-shaped diagnostic payloads (e.g. `model_call_details`) that contain `api_key` (and, on the proxy, master/virtual keys), so the full secret is emitted verbatim to stdout and captured by container/pod log collectors. The sibling `litellm/_logging.py::print_verbose` already redacts its stdout path via `redact_secrets(...)`; `utils.py` is the remaining inconsistent path.

## Reproduction

A maintainer can reproduce this with only the `litellm` package — no proxy, cloud, or specific provider required.

1. Install current `main` / latest release (`pip install litellm`).
2. Run:

```python
import litellm
from litellm.utils import print_verbose

litellm.set_verbose = True
print_verbose({
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "api_key": "sk-secret-DO-NOT-LEAK-1234567890abcdef",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}],
})
```

3. Observe stdout.

(This also fires organically on any real completion call — many code paths pass `model_call_details`, which carries `api_key`, through `print_verbose` when `set_verbose=True`. It is provider-agnostic; `sk-` and generic `api_key`/`api-key`/`apikey` dict-repr shapes are all affected.)

## Expected Behavior

The secret should be masked on the stdout path, matching what `litellm/_logging.py::print_verbose` already does (`print(redact_secrets(str(print_statement)))`) and the `SecretRedactionFilter` applied to the `verbose_logger` path. Redaction should still honor the `LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS=true` opt-out.

## Actual Behavior

The API key is printed verbatim:

```
{'model': 'gpt-4o', 'api_key': 'sk-secret-DO-NOT-LEAK-1234567890abcdef', 'messages': [{'role': 'user', 'content': 'hi'}]}
```

The `api_key` value reaches stdout unredacted, exposing credentials to any log sink that captures stdout (and creating a log-injection vector).

## Root Cause

`litellm/utils.py` (current `main`, lines 482-497):

```python
def print_verbose(
    print_statement,
    logger_only: bool = False,
    log_level: Literal["DEBUG", "INFO", "ERROR"] = "DEBUG",
):
    try:
        if log_level == "DEBUG":
            verbose_logger.debug(print_statement)   # redacted by SecretRedactionFilter
        elif log_level == "INFO":
            verbose_logger.info(print_statement)
        elif log_level == "ERROR":
            verbose_logger.error(print_statement)
        if litellm.set_verbose is True and logger_only is False:
            print(print_statement)  # noqa: T201    # <-- RAW, not redacted (line 495)
    except Exception:
        pass
```

Compare `litellm/_logging.py::print_verbose` on the same `main` (lines 413-416), which already redacts its stdout write:

```python
def print_verbose(print_statement):
    ...
            print(redact_secrets(str(print_statement)))  # noqa: T201
```

`redact_secrets()` is already the exported public helper in `litellm/_logging.py` and is a no-op when `LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS=true`.

## Environment

- litellm version: reproduces on current `main` (pyproject `version = "1.95.0"`); the `utils.py` stdout path has never been redacted.
- Provider: any (the leaked field is `api_key` in the generic call-details payload, not provider-specific).
- Trigger condition: `litellm.set_verbose = True` (or `LITELLM_LOG=DEBUG`-style verbose usage) with `logger_only=False` (the default).

## Proposed Fix

Wrap the stdout fallback in `redact_secrets(str(...))`, matching `litellm/_logging.py`:

```python
from ._logging import redact_secrets  # already exported
...
        if litellm.set_verbose is True and logger_only is False:
            print(redact_secrets(str(print_statement)))  # noqa: T201
```

No signature/API change; only the content of an already-emitted debug line changes, and only for strings matching known credential shapes. Suggested test: `tests/test_litellm/test_print_verbose_secret_redaction.py` asserting the secret never reaches stdout when `set_verbose` is on (fails pre-fix, passes after) and that the `verbose_logger` path stays redacted.

## Related

- #24813 (merged) — added `SecretRedactionFilter` / the redaction infrastructure this fix reuses.
- #32318 / PRs #32495, #32326 — the separate "`print_verbose` doesn't emit through `verbose_logger` when `set_verbose` is False" behavior; deliberately out of scope for this security fix.

A fix PR (wrap the `set_verbose` stdout branch in `redact_secrets`) will follow.

gold.rationale: This is a credential exposure issue: API keys (and potentially proxy master/virtual keys) are printed unredacted to stdout via litellm/utils.py::print_verbose, an inconsistency with the already-redacted _logging.py path. This is a plausible exploit path (log collectors capturing secrets in plaintext), so per the rules it takes precedence as security regardless of it being framed as a bug. It affects the shared core logging path used across all providers when set_verbose/debug logging is enabled, which is a widely used path, but has a straightforward workaround (avoid set_verbose=True, or disable via LITELLM_DISABLE_REDACT_SECRETS is unrelated) - actually there's no real workaround to avoid the leak other than not using verbose mode, but disabling verbose mode is itself a workaround. Given it's a credential leak affecting many users' logs when debug/verbose mode is enabled (common in production troubleshooting), and no simple fix without code change, this warrants P1. Security issues always need human judgement/review before routing.

items.title: [Feature]: Componentized chart — pod-hardening hook parity with litellm-helm
items.body:
The componentized chart is missing pod-hardening hooks that `litellm-helm` already
has. Please add, matching `litellm-helm` field names so values stay portable:

- `securityContext` + `podSecurityContext` (per component)
- `extraContainers` (per component)
- `podLabels` (per component)
- `lifecycle` + `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (per component)
- `volumes` / `volumeMounts` on the **migrations Job** (deployments got this in 1.93.0; the Job didn't)
- `migrationJob.serviceAccountName` (independent Job SA; see #21344, #20571)

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified feature request asking for parity with an existing chart (litellm-helm), listing concrete field names to add. It's not a bug (nothing broken), not docs, not a question. It references prior related issues (#21344, #20571), which shows some corroboration/history of demand for related functionality (e.g., independent Job SA), but this is still primarily a single detailed feature request. Given the referenced related issues indicating recurring demand for parts of this (serviceAccountName for migration job), and that it touches the shared chart core path (affecting all component deployments), it warrants a slight promotion to P2. It doesn't require deep judgement about direction—chart parity is a fairly clear, well-scoped ask—so it can be queued without a maintainer conversation.

items.title: Clear license boundaries between MIT and Enterprise features
items.body:
# Clear license boundaries between MIT and Enterprise features

## Summary

I'm trying to use LiteLLM in compliance with its licenses. The root `LICENSE` says code outside `enterprise/` is MIT-licensed. But I found that many features documented as "Enterprise" have their gating logic and, in many cases, their entire implementation in MIT-licensed files. So I can't determine which features I can legally use without a subscription. I'm asking for clear, physically-enforced boundaries.

## The Problem

The root `LICENSE` draws a clear rule:

> All content that resides under the "enterprise/" directory [...] is licensed under the license defined in "enterprise/LICENSE".
> Content outside of the above mentioned directories [...] is available under the MIT license.

So I should be able to look at any file path and know its license. But the current codebase doesn't follow this boundary:

### Category A: Enterprise feature gating in MIT files (25+ files)

A grep for `premium_user`, `_premium_user_check`, and `not_premium_user` shows that the enforcement mechanism for enterprise features lives almost entirely in MIT-licensed files:

| MIT file | What it gates |
|---|---|
| `litellm/proxy/common_utils/callback_utils.py` | Llama Guard, secret hiding, OpenAI Moderation, Google Text Moderation, Llm Guard, BlockedUser, BannedKeyword |
| `litellm/proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py` | Guardrails, policies, logging, content moderation (6 checkpoints) |
| `litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py` | Enforced params, IP ACLs, Swagger branding, request size limits |
| `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/key_management_endpoints.py` | Key regenerate, tags on keys, model_max_budget, premium metadata fields |
| `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/team_endpoints.py` | Team admin assignment |
| `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/scim/scim_v2.py` | All SCIM v2 endpoints |
| `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/ui_sso.py` | SSO UI settings (5-user free limit enforcement) |
| `litellm/proxy/management_helpers/audit_logs.py` | Audit log creation |
| `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/common_utils.py` | Metadata field premium validation |
| `litellm/proxy/management_endpoints/model_management_endpoints.py` | Model management checks |
| `litellm/proxy/spend_tracking/spend_management_endpoints.py` | `/spend/report` endpoint |
| `litellm/proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py` | JWT auth, IP-based access control |
| `litellm/proxy/auth/oauth2_check.py` | OAuth2 token validation |
| `litellm/proxy/auth/auth_utils.py` | `allowed_routes`, max request/response size |
| `litellm/proxy/auth/route_checks.py` | `admin_only_routes` |
| `litellm/proxy/fine_tuning_endpoints/endpoints.py` | All fine-tuning endpoints |
| `litellm/proxy/common_utils/http_parsing_utils.py` | `max_file_size_mb` for audio |
| `litellm/secret_managers/hashicorp_secret_manager.py` | HashiCorp Vault |
| `litellm/secret_managers/cyberark_secret_manager.py` | CyberArk |
| `litellm/secret_managers/google_secret_manager.py` | Google Secret Manager |
| `litellm/integrations/custom_guardrail.py` | Premium custom guardrail |
| `litellm/integrations/gcs_pubsub/pub_sub.py` | GCS PubSub |
| `litellm/integrations/gcs_bucket/gcs_bucket.py` | GCS Bucket logging |
| `litellm/integrations/SlackAlerting/slack_alerting.py` | Custom email alerting |
| `litellm/integrations/azure_storage/azure_storage.py` | Azure Blob Storage |
| `litellm/router_strategy/budget_limiter.py` | Tag-based budgets |
| `litellm/proxy/_types.py` | The `not_premium_user` error message definition |

All of these files are outside `enterprise/`. By the repository's own license terms, they are MIT-licensed.

### Going deeper: where is the implementation code?

I then checked whether these MIT files import from `enterprise/` to get the actual business logic. The results split into two groups:

**Group 1: MIT gate, Enterprise implementation (6 files)**

These MIT files import runtime logic from `enterprise/` modules. When the gate passes, `enterprise/` code executes:

| MIT file | Enterprise modules it imports |
|---|---|
| `proxy/common_utils/callback_utils.py` | `enterprise.enterprise_hooks.*`, `litellm_enterprise.enterprise_callbacks.*` (7 guardrails) |
| `proxy/management_endpoints/key_management_endpoints.py` | `litellm_enterprise.proxy.management_endpoints.key_management_endpoints` |
| `proxy/auth/user_api_key_auth.py` | `litellm_enterprise.proxy.auth.user_api_key_auth` |
| `proxy/auth/route_checks.py` | `litellm_enterprise.proxy.auth.route_checks` |
| `integrations/custom_guardrail.py` | `litellm_enterprise.integrations.custom_guardrail` |
| `proxy/management_endpoints/ui_sso.py` | `litellm_enterprise.proxy.auth.custom_sso_handler` (conditional) |
| `proxy/proxy_server.py` | Conditional `import enterprise` |

**Group 2: MIT gate, MIT implementation with zero enterprise imports (19 features)**

These files import nothing from `enterprise/`. Every line of code is MIT-licensed:

| MIT file | Enterprise imports |
|---|---|
| `proxy/management_endpoints/scim/scim_v2.py` + `scim_transformations.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/litellm_pre_call_utils.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/management_endpoints/team_endpoints.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/spend_tracking/spend_management_endpoints.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/fine_tuning_endpoints/endpoints.py` | 0 |
| `router_strategy/budget_limiter.py` | 0 |
| `secret_managers/hashicorp_secret_manager.py` | 0 |
| `secret_managers/cyberark_secret_manager.py` | 0 |
| `secret_managers/google_secret_manager.py` | 0 |
| `integrations/gcs_pubsub/pub_sub.py` | 0 |
| `integrations/gcs_bucket/gcs_bucket.py` | 0 |
| `integrations/azure_storage/azure_storage.py` | 0 |
| `integrations/SlackAlerting/slack_alerting.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/auth/auth_utils.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/auth/oauth2_check.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/common_utils/http_parsing_utils.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/management_endpoints/model_management_endpoints.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/management_helpers/audit_logs.py` | 0 |
| `proxy/management_endpoints/organization_endpoints.py` (see below) | 0 |

Organization management deserves a separate note. All 5 source files (endpoints, auth checks, repository, models) live in `litellm/` with zero `enterprise/` imports and zero `premium_user` checks. The backend API has no license gate. The only restriction is in the official Admin Dashboard UI (`OrganizationsPanel.tsx:128`), which hides the feature behind `if (!premiumUser)`. But the UI itself is MIT-licensed code (`ui/litellm-dashboard/`, outside `enterprise/`). If you call the API directly or build your own UI, you're not "bypassing" anything -- the backend was never gated.

### The gating mechanism itself is fully in MIT

The entire enforcement infrastructure lives in MIT files:

- `premium_user: bool`: defined in `litellm/proxy/proxy_server.py` (MIT)
- `_premium_user_check()`: defined in `litellm/proxy/utils.py` (MIT)
- `CommonProxyErrors.not_premium_user`: defined in `litellm/proxy/_types.py` (MIT)
- `LicenseCheck.is_premium()`: defined in `litellm/proxy/auth/litellm_license.py` (MIT); returns `False` when `LITELLM_LICENSE` is unset with no cryptographic verification

The `enterprise/` directory has zero independent gating infrastructure. All 9 files in `enterprise/` that check `premium_user` import it from the MIT area:

```python
from litellm.proxy.proxy_server import premium_user
```

### The frontend adds a second, independent gating layer (also MIT-licensed)

The Admin Dashboard (`ui/litellm-dashboard/`) is outside `enterprise/` and therefore MIT-licensed. It has its own premium gating system driven by the JWT `premium_user` claim, checked in 24+ components. This is a parallel control layer, independent of the backend API gates.

**Frontend-only gating (8 features -- UI blocks, backend has no license check):**

These features are gated in the MIT-licensed Dashboard but completely unprotected in the MIT-licensed backend API. If you use the API directly or build your own client, you're not bypassing anything -- the backend was never gated:

| Feature | UI location | Backend status |
|---|---|---|
| Organization management | `OrganizationsPanel.tsx:128` -- full page replaced with upsell banner | `organization_endpoints.py` (1235 lines) -- zero `premium_user` references. All CRUD endpoints are open |
| Pass-through endpoint authentication | `PassThroughSecuritySection.tsx:26` -- auth field silently stripped, upsell shown | `pass_through_endpoints.py:2749` -- premium gate was deliberately removed in PR #26827 with the rationale "the safe option has to be free." The UI never caught up |
| Deleted Keys listing | `DeletedKeysPage.tsx:17` -- "Coming soon to Enterprise" banner | `/key/list?status=deleted` -- no premium check |
| Deleted Teams listing | `DeletedTeamsPage.tsx:13` -- same banner pattern | Team listing -- no premium check |
| Email logo URL | `email_settings.tsx:75` -- field hidden, input disabled | `/config/update` -- no premium check on any env var |
| Email support contact | Same as above | Same as above |
| Region outage alerts toggle | `settings.tsx:630` -- replaced with "Enterprise Feature" upsell button | `/config/update` -- no premium check |
| Region outage alert TTL | `alerting/dynamic_form.tsx:62` -- input replaced with upsell button | `/config/update` -- no premium check; backend marks this field as `premium_field: true` in the API response metadata, but doesn't enforce it |

These eight features all follow the same pattern: MIT-licensed Dashboard code blocks access, MIT-licensed backend API has no gate. Using a custom UI or calling the API directly is not circumvention -- it's using MIT-licensed software as the MIT license permits.

**Consistent gating (both UI and backend enforce):**

The remaining UI gates correspond to backend checks: audit logs, SSO, key-level guardrails/policies/prompts/tags/logging, key regenerate/rotate, team admin assignment, team-BYOK model, allowed IPs, pass-through routes. For these, the UI adds a visual gate in addition to the backend enforcement.

## Why This Is a Compliance Problem

The repository's `LICENSE` draws a clean line: files in `enterprise/` -> Enterprise License; everything else -> MIT. In practice, that line doesn't hold:

1. For Group 2 features (19 features), **all code including the gate is MIT-licensed**. The official docs call them "Enterprise," but the license says MIT. Which takes precedence? If I use these features, am I violating the Enterprise License or exercising my MIT rights?

2. For Group 1 features (7 files), the gate is in MIT code but execution crosses into `enterprise/`. Is the mere act of crossing that boundary at runtime a license violation, even though the code that initiates the crossing is MIT-licensed?

3. The gate is a boolean defaulting to `False`. There is a proper RSA-signed license verification path in the codebase (`litellm/proxy/auth/litellm_license.py`), but only one file (`enterprise/litellm_enterprise/proxy/management_endpoints/internal_user_endpoints.py`) uses the verified `premium_user_data` for enforcement. All other checks use the unverified boolean.

4. The frontend adds another dimension. The Admin Dashboard (MIT-licensed, `ui/litellm-dashboard/`) has 24+ premium-gated components. For 8 features, the Dashboard blocks access while the backend API has no license check at all. If I build my own UI client that talks to the same MIT-licensed backend API, am I "circumventing" anything? The backend was never gated. The "gate" is a React `if` statement in code I'm not required to use.

## What I'm Asking For

I want to use LiteLLM in full compliance with its licenses. To do that, I need to be able to trust that file location determines license. My requests:

1. **Please clarify the license status of the 19 Group 2 features** whose entire codebase is MIT-licensed. Are they MIT-licensed (in which case the boolean gate should be removed) or Enterprise-licensed (in which case the code should be moved to `enterprise/`)?
2. **Please clarify the 8 frontend-only gated features.** Organization management, pass-through auth, deleted keys/teams listing, email branding, and region outage alerts have no backend license check. If these are genuinely enterprise features, the backend API should enforce it. If the backend was intentionally left open (as with pass-through auth in PR #26827), the Dashboard gates should be removed.
3. **Please move Enterprise enforcement logic into `enterprise/`.** The `_premium_user_check()` function, the `CommonProxyErrors.not_premium_user` definition, and the gating checks should physically reside under the Enterprise License they enforce. Otherwise the gate itself is subject to MIT's "modify" permission.
4. **Please use the existing RSA verification consistently** if features genuinely require a subscription. A boolean that defaults to `False` when no env var is set is not a license enforcement mechanism; it's a configuration flag.
5. **Please update the documentation** to clearly mark which specific files or API endpoints are Enterprise-licensed, so users can make informed compliance decisions without reverse-engineering the import graph -- across both the backend and the Dashboard frontend.

The current state creates legal ambiguity for anyone trying to use this software responsibly. I'm not looking to bypass anything. I'm asking for the code to match the license it ships with.

gold.rationale: The issue raises a licensing/legal-boundary concern: it claims that enterprise-gated feature logic actually resides in MIT-licensed files, creating ambiguity about what can legally be used without an enterprise license. This isn't a security vulnerability (no exploit path, credential exposure, or injection), nor a simple question or docs issue — it's a claim that the codebase's licensing structure doesn't match its stated license boundaries, which is a product/legal-structure concern requiring maintainer and possibly legal judgement. It doesn't fit cleanly as a "bug" in code behavior, but is closest to a structural/documentation-vs-implementation mismatch requiring a policy decision — best categorized as a question about licensing intent that requires maintainer clarification (not a well-specified feature or docs fix). Given the complexity, this requires a maintainer/legal judgement call to resolve and cannot be auto-routed. It is not P0/P1 in the sense of broken functionality, but it does affect many users' ability to legally understand and use the software, so it's more than cosmetic — however, no concrete widespread technical breakage or exploit is claimed, so P2 with human review is appropriate given the licensing-clarity implications and need for maintainer/legal judgement.

items.title: [Bug]: Nullable DailyTagSpend conflict columns cause duplicate inserts and database CPU exhaustion
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

`LiteLLM_DailyTagSpend` can accumulate many physical rows for the same logical spend key when `custom_llm_provider` is `NULL`. The repeated inserts increase table/index size and can make daily-spend flushes consume most of the PostgreSQL CPU. Spend reporting also becomes fragmented across duplicate rows.

I expected repeated daily tag-spend updates for the same `(tag, date, api_key, model, custom_llm_provider, mcp_namespaced_tool_name, endpoint)` key to update one row.

The current implementation does not enforce that behavior when a conflict column is nullable:

1. The Prisma schema makes `tag`, `model`, `custom_llm_provider`, `mcp_namespaced_tool_name`, and `endpoint` nullable, then includes all of them in a normal composite unique constraint: [`schema.prisma#L878-L900`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/3f9b71c1a45e870d1789ee105bd59b9274bb0d74/litellm/proxy/schema.prisma#L878-L900).
2. PostgreSQL treats `NULL` values as distinct in a normal unique constraint, so the constraint permits multiple otherwise-identical rows when any conflict column is `NULL`.
3. `_update_daily_spend` also constructs inconsistent upsert values. The `where` selector converts a missing provider to `""`, while the create payload preserves `None`: [`db_spend_update_writer.py#L1513-L1539`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/3f9b71c1a45e870d1789ee105bd59b9274bb0d74/litellm/proxy/db/db_spend_update_writer.py#L1513-L1539).

```python
# where
"custom_llm_provider": transaction.get("custom_llm_provider") or "",

# create
"custom_llm_provider": transaction.get("custom_llm_provider"),
```

The selector therefore looks for an empty string while a create writes `NULL`. The next flush does not select that row, and PostgreSQL's unique constraint does not reject another `NULL`, so another row can be inserted.

The same generic function writes the user, team, organization, end-user, agent, and tag daily-spend tables, whose composite constraints also contain nullable columns. `DailyTagSpend` was the table where the operational impact was observed, but the invariant should be reviewed for all six tables.

In one anonymized PostgreSQL 16 deployment running LiteLLM 1.94.0:

- `LiteLLM_DailyTagSpend` reached approximately 5.15 million rows and 3.47 GB including indexes.
- A one-day sample found 1,647 duplicate physical rows across six logical keys.
- The largest logical-key group contained approximately 804 physical rows.
- Daily tag-spend upserts dominated database execution count and drove sustained high CPU.
- The deployment had 28 proxy workers. Each worker initializes the scheduler, which amplifies pressure when many flushes are active, although locking can limit simultaneous execution.

The current upstream code at commit [`3f9b71c1a45e870d1789ee105bd59b9274bb0d74`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/3f9b71c1a45e870d1789ee105bd59b9274bb0d74) still contains the schema and create/lookup mismatch.

The writer also issues as many as 100 individual Prisma upserts per batch ([`db_spend_update_writer.py#L1472-L1500`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/3f9b71c1a45e870d1789ee105bd59b9274bb0d74/litellm/proxy/db/db_spend_update_writer.py#L1472-L1500), [`#L1587-L1593`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/3f9b71c1a45e870d1789ee105bd59b9274bb0d74/litellm/proxy/db/db_spend_update_writer.py#L1587-L1593)). That is not the correctness bug, but it magnifies the database cost once duplicate-producing keys are flushed repeatedly.

Possible fixes:

- Choose one canonical representation for every conflict-key field and use it consistently in the aggregation key, `where`, and `create` payloads.
- Backfill/deduplicate existing rows, then enforce the chosen invariant at the database layer, for example with non-null canonical values or a PostgreSQL `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` unique constraint where supported.
- Add a PostgreSQL integration test that performs the same upsert twice with each nullable conflict field set to `None` and asserts that only one physical row exists and its counters were incremented. Mock-only tests cannot detect PostgreSQL's `NULL` uniqueness behavior.
- Consider a set-based upsert per batch to reduce query execution count independently of the correctness fix.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Use PostgreSQL with the current `LiteLLM_DailyTagSpend` schema.
2. Process the same daily tag-spend transaction more than once with `custom_llm_provider=None` and all other logical-key values unchanged. This can be exercised through `_update_daily_spend` using `entity_type="tag"`; the current test suite already permits `None` in this field but only mocks the Prisma table call.
3. Alternatively, the database behavior can be demonstrated directly with the equivalent conflict key:

```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE daily_tag_spend_repro (
    tag text,
    spend_date text NOT NULL,
    api_key text NOT NULL,
    model text,
    custom_llm_provider text,
    mcp_namespaced_tool_name text,
    endpoint text,
    api_requests bigint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    UNIQUE (
        tag,
        spend_date,
        api_key,
        model,
        custom_llm_provider,
        mcp_namespaced_tool_name,
        endpoint
    )
);

INSERT INTO daily_tag_spend_repro
    (tag, spend_date, api_key, model, custom_llm_provider,
     mcp_namespaced_tool_name, endpoint, api_requests)
VALUES
    ('repro-tag', '2026-01-01', 'repro-key', 'repro-model', NULL, '', '', 1)
ON CONFLICT (
    tag, spend_date, api_key, model, custom_llm_provider,
    mcp_namespaced_tool_name, endpoint
)
DO UPDATE SET api_requests = daily_tag_spend_repro.api_requests + 1;

-- Run the same INSERT a second time, then inspect the result.
SELECT tag, spend_date, api_key, model, custom_llm_provider,
       mcp_namespaced_tool_name, endpoint,
       COUNT(*) AS physical_rows,
       SUM(api_requests) AS requests
FROM daily_tag_spend_repro
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7;
```

4. Observe `physical_rows = 2` and two rows with `api_requests = 1`, instead of one row with `api_requests = 2`.
5. On a LiteLLM database, duplicate logical keys can be detected with:

```sql
SELECT
    tag,
    date,
    api_key,
    model,
    custom_llm_provider,
    mcp_namespaced_tool_name,
    endpoint,
    COUNT(*) AS physical_rows
FROM "LiteLLM_DailyTagSpend"
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY physical_rows DESC;
```

### Relevant log output

```shell
No application error is required. The upserts succeed as inserts because PostgreSQL considers NULL conflict-key values distinct.
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.94.0; also verified in upstream commit 3f9b71c1a45e870d1789ee105bd59b9274bb0d74

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-documented, reproducible bug: nullable columns in composite unique constraints combined with inconsistent NULL/empty-string handling between the `where` and `create` payloads in `_update_daily_spend` cause duplicate physical rows across six daily-spend tables. This affects the shared core spend-tracking path used by all providers/deployments, leading to database CPU exhaustion and fragmented spend reporting in production. It matches "bug" category (behavior violates documented/intended uniqueness contract). Given it affects the shared core path across six tables and causes severe operational impact (CPU exhaustion, multi-GB bloat) with no stated workaround, and shared-core-path issues raise urgency one level, this warrants P1. It needs human review because it's a significant correctness/performance issue spanning schema changes, backfill strategy, and multiple tables — a judgement call on the fix approach (schema migration vs. code fix) is required before routing.

items.title: [Bug]: "Models + Endpoints" page shows "No models found" even though the models work
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### What happened?

On our proxy, users are given access to models by tier (e.g., "economy", "standard", "premium") rather than by listing each model.

For those users, the Models + Endpoints page in the UI says "No models found".

The same users see the full model list in the Playground and in the model dropdown when creating a key, and their requests to those models work fine. So the access is there, just that one page is blank.

If I change a user so they list the model names individually instead of the tier, the page starts working for them.

Users are internal users (w write) and are not in any team.

Version: v1.91.0. 

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Set up models in your proxy with different groups (e.g. `economy`)
2. Create a new internal user with write and no team, assign it to that model list
3. Log in with the user, go to the "_Models + Endpoints_" page. No model is available


### Relevant log output

```shell
N/A
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

UI Dashboard

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.91.0

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: The Models + Endpoints page fails to resolve model access when a user is assigned via a model access group (tier) rather than explicit model names, even though the underlying access and functionality (Playground, key creation, actual requests) work correctly. This is a clear discrepancy between expected behavior (page should reflect actual access) and actual UI behavior, indicating a bug in how the UI resolves access-group-based model lists. It's reproducible with clear steps, affects a specific but plausibly common admin configuration pattern (tiered model access), and has a workaround (list models individually instead of using tiers), though that workaround defeats the purpose of access groups. This affects a subset of users (those using access-group-based assignment) rather than all users, so it's not P0/P1 severity, but it's a legitimate functional gap in the UI Dashboard module affecting an evidently used feature. Given clear reproduction steps and specific version, this can be routed directly to the UI Dashboard/model access group owners without further clarification.

items.title: [Bug]: Headroom compression guide pins a stale, pre-fix version and the documented setup doesn't achieve real compression
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

Searched `litellm/litellm` issues for existing reports on the Headroom compression guide — found none specific to this.

### What happened?

The Headroom guardrail deploy guide (`docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/headroom#deploy-headroom`) pins `headroom-ai[proxy]==0.27.0` in its example Dockerfile. Following the guide exactly as written has two problems:

1. `headroom-ai==0.27.0` predates a crash fix in Headroom's own repo (`headroomlabs-ai/headroom#1114`, fixed in `0.31.0`/`0.32.0`) for its `HeadroomCallback` integration path — anyone following the pinned version can still hit `AttributeError: 'HeadroomCallback' object has no attribute 'async_post_call_success_hook'` on real requests, even though that issue is already closed upstream as fixed.

2. More importantly: following the guide's own `guardrail: headroom` / `mode: pre_call` example exactly as documented — correct network topology (sidecar), correct request schema once the undocumented required `model` field is added — results in `tokens_saved: 0` for realistic tool-output/RAG/JSON-shaped payloads, which is presumably the traffic this guardrail is meant for. Root cause is two independently-gated default protections inside Headroom's own `ContentRouter` (`skip_user_messages`, `protect_recent_code`). The guide's page only explains one related default ("`requests_compressed` can be 0 ... unless `HEADROOM_COMPRESS_USER_MESSAGES` is set") — it doesn't mention the second rule that also has to be defeated, or that defeating the first alone isn't enough. Filed the underlying compression-defaults bug upstream: `headroomlabs-ai/headroom#2457`.

**Expected:** the guide either notes the version floor needed to avoid the fixed crash, or at minimum flags that the documented default setup does not produce real compression for typical structured/JSON content without additional, currently-undocumented config changes — so people following the guide as written don't end up with a guardrail that silently no-ops.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Follow `docs.litellm.ai/docs/proxy/headroom#deploy-headroom` exactly: build the documented Dockerfile (`headroom-ai[proxy]==0.27.0`), run it as a sidecar, wire the `guardrail: headroom` block into `litellm_config.yaml` as shown.
2. Send a chat completion with `"guardrails": ["headroom-compression"]` and a large, realistic tool-output/JSON payload.
3. Observe: the request succeeds (no networking/crash issue), but Headroom's own `/v1/compress` response for that payload shows `tokens_saved: 0` — full reproduction and root-cause source citations in `headroomlabs-ai/headroom#2457`.

### Relevant log output

Representative response from Headroom's own `/v1/compress` endpoint for a realistic tool-output-shaped payload sent through the exact guide-documented setup:

```json
{"tokens_before": 5114, "tokens_after": 5114, "tokens_saved": 0, "compression_ratio": 1.0, "transforms_applied": ["router:protected:user_message"]}
```

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Docs

### What LiteLLM version are you on ?

v1.93.0

gold.rationale: The issue reports that the docs for the Headroom guardrail deploy guide pin a stale version (which is affected by an already-fixed upstream crash) and that following the documented setup exactly does not achieve real compression due to undocumented default protections. The code/integration itself works as intended when configured correctly (root cause is upstream, already filed separately); the actual problem here is that the LiteLLM docs are incomplete/misleading, causing users to end up with a silently no-op guardrail. This matches the docs category exactly: the documentation is missing important configuration details and pins an outdated version reference. It's not a security issue, not a question, and not asking for a new feature. The urgency is moderate — it's a doc gap that could confuse many users trying to deploy this specific guardrail integration, but it's narrow in scope (affects only Headroom guardrail users) and has a filed upstream issue with root cause identified, plus workaround (adjust config, pin higher version) essentially available once known. This fits P2 (narrow path, workaround exists via upstream fix version). Given clear reproduction steps, root cause identified, and a well-specified ask (update docs with version floor and configuration caveat), this can be routed without maintainer conversation — needs_human should be false.

items.title: [Feature]: allow overriding the UI login authentication with a custom function (`custom_ui_auth`)
items.body:
### Check for existing issues

- [x] I have searched the existing issues and checked that my issue is not a duplicate.

### The Feature

Add a `custom_ui_auth` option to `general_settings` in the proxy config, similar to the existing `custom_auth` option. When set, it points to a custom async function with the signature `async def custom_ui_auth(request, username, password) -> UserAPIKeyAuth` that the proxy calls instead of the built-in `authenticate_user` whenever a user logs into the Admin UI (both `POST /login` and `POST /v2/login`).

```yaml
general_settings:
  custom_ui_auth: custom_ui_auth.custom_ui_auth
```

```python
# custom_ui_auth.py
from fastapi import Request
from litellm.proxy._types import UserAPIKeyAuth

async def custom_ui_auth(request: Request, username: str, password: str) -> UserAPIKeyAuth:
    # validate username/password against your own identity provider
    ...
    return UserAPIKeyAuth(user_id=..., user_email=..., user_role=...)
```

### Motivation, pitch

`custom_auth` already lets you replace `user_api_key_auth` for API requests, but the Admin UI login form (`/login` and `/v2/login`) always calls the built-in `authenticate_user`, which only checks the master key, Prisma-stored users, or SSO. Teams that authenticate users against an internal identity system (LDAP, a homegrown user table, etc.) have no way to let those users log into the Admin UI without also standing up SSO or shoehorning credentials into the Prisma user table. A `custom_ui_auth` hook, mirroring the existing `custom_auth` pattern, closes that gap and lets self-hosted proxies plug in their own login logic while keeping the rest of the UI auth flow (cookie/token issuance) unchanged.

### What part of LiteLLM is this about?

Proxy

### LiteLLM is hiring a founding backend engineer, are you interested in joining us and shipping to all our users?

No

### Twitter / LinkedIn details

_No response_

gold.rationale: This is a well-specified feature request asking for a new configuration hook (`custom_ui_auth`) mirroring the existing `custom_auth` pattern, to allow custom authentication for the Admin UI login. The behavior does not currently exist, so this is a feature request, not a bug. There is no evidence of multiple users requesting this or maintainer intent signaled, so it defaults to P3 despite being a detailed write-up (a detailed write-up alone does not justify promotion per the rules). It's a single requester with a clear, well-specified ask that could be queued for the proxy auth module without further clarification needed to route it, though the decision of whether to build it is a product-direction call.
